We have instead trained a neural network to perform equivalent corrections. resulting in a significant speed-up. We have examined hardware implementations using both analog and digital electronic networks. Both had an acceptably small error of 0.5% compared to the iterative results. Additionally. we verified that the neural network correctly generalized the solution of the problem to include patterns not contained in its training set. We have experimentally verified this approach on a Cambridge Instruments EBMF 10.5 exposure system.

paragraphs: Electron scattering can distort patterns written by an electron beam, producing proximity effects that require correction. Iterative correction methods are effective but computationally expensive. This paper trains a neural network to calculate equivalent corrections, with the goal of reducing the time needed to prepare the corrected pattern.

The authors examine both analog and digital electronic implementations. Each produces an error of 0.5% relative to the iterative results, which the abstract describes as acceptably small. The neural approach also delivers a significant speed-up. This comparison establishes how closely the faster computation reproduces the correction supplied by the iterative method.

The study additionally verifies that the network generalizes to patterns absent from its training set and experimentally checks the approach on a Cambridge Instruments EBMF 10.5 exposure system. These findings connect computational approximation to practical pattern writing. The contribution is a learned replacement for an expensive correction calculation, supported by agreement with iterative results, tests on previously unseen patterns, and experimental verification on an exposure system.
summary.tldr: A neural network accelerates electron-beam proximity correction, matching iterative results within 0.5% error in analog and digital implementations.

title: Proximity Effect Corrections in Electron Beam Lithography Using a Neural Network

abstract: This paper will address an important question in machine learning: What kind of network architectures work better on what kind of problems? A projection pursuit learning network has a very similar structure to a one hidden layer sigmoidal neural network. A general method based on a continuous version of projection pursuit regression is developed to show that projection pursuit regression works better on angular smooth func(cid:173) tions than on Laplacian smooth functions. There exists a ridge function approximation scheme to avoid the curse of dimensionality for approxi(cid:173) mating functions in L2(¢d).

A projection pursuit learning network has a very similar structure to a one hidden layer sigmoidal neural network. A general method based on a continuous version of projection pursuit regression is developed to show that projection pursuit regression works better on angular smooth func(cid:173) tions than on Laplacian smooth functions. paragraphs: This paper asks which kinds of target functions are well suited to particular network architectures. It studies projection pursuit learning networks, whose structure closely resembles a neural network with one sigmoidal hidden layer. The focus is approximation: how the form of a network interacts with the mathematical properties of the function it is meant to represent.

The authors develop a general method based on a continuous version of projection pursuit regression. Their analysis shows better approximation behavior for angular smooth functions than for Laplacian smooth functions. These are different mathematical notions of smoothness, so the finding makes the type of regularity in the target function relevant to architecture choice.

The paper also establishes the existence of a ridge-function approximation scheme that avoids the curse of dimensionality in the stated L2 setting. Together, these results connect approximation difficulty with both function structure and representation. The contribution gives theoretical reasons to consider how a problem's smoothness aligns with projection-based representations when evaluating whether that architecture is suitable.
summary.tldr: The paper links projection pursuit approximation quality to function smoothness and establishes a ridge-function scheme that avoids dimensionality's usual burden.

title: Some Approximation Properties of Projection Pursuit Learning Networks

abstract: We propose and empirically evaluate a method for the extraction of expert(cid:173) comprehensible rules from trained neural networks. Our method operates in the context of a three-step process for learning that uses rule-based domain knowledge in combination with neural networks. Empirical tests using real(cid:173) worlds problems from molecular biology show that the rules our method extracts from trained neural networks: closely reproduce the accuracy of the network from which they came, are superior to the rules derived by a learning system that directly refines symbolic rules, and are expert-comprehensible.
originalAbstract: We propose and empirically evaluate a method for the extraction of expert(cid:173) comprehensible rules from trained neural networks. Our method operates in the context of a three-step process for learning that uses rule-based domain knowledge in combination with neural networks. Empirical tests using real(cid:173) worlds problems from molecular biology show that the rules our method extracts from trained neural networks: closely reproduce the accuracy of the network from which they came, are superior to the rules derived by a learning system that directly refines symbolic rules, and are expert-comprehensible.

paragraphs: This paper proposes a way to extract rules that domain experts can understand from trained neural networks. The method belongs to a three-step learning process that combines existing rule-based knowledge with neural-network learning. Its purpose is to make the learned result available in a form that people can inspect and interpret.

The authors evaluate the method on real molecular-biology problems. The extracted rules closely reproduce the accuracy of the networks from which they were obtained. This is important because turning a trained network into a readable representation is useful only if that representation retains the predictive behavior that made the network valuable.

The rules also outperform those produced by a system that directly refines symbolic rules, and the authors report that experts can comprehend them. These findings support a workflow in which symbolic knowledge and neural learning contribute to the same process. Rule extraction provides the connection back to an understandable description after the network has learned.
summary.tldr: Extracted expert-readable rules retain neural-network accuracy and outperform direct symbolic-rule refinement on molecular-biology problems.

title: Interpretation of Artificial Neural Networks: Mapping Knowledge-Based Neural Networks into Rules

abstract: Experimental research on Artificial Neural Network (ANN) algorithms requires either writing variations on the same program or making one monolithic program with many parameters and options. By using an object-oriented library, the size of these experimental programs is reduced while making them easier to read, write and modify. An efficient and flexible realization of this idea is Connection(cid:173) ist Layered Object-oriented Network Simulator (CLONES). CLONES runs on UNIX1 workstations and on the 100-1000 MFLOP Ring Array Processor (RAP) that we built with ANN algorithms in mind. In this report we describe CLONES and show how it is implemented on the RAP.

paragraphs: Neural-network research often involves implementing many closely related experimental programs. The authors identify two burdensome approaches: repeatedly writing program variants or maintaining one large program with many settings. This paper presents an object-oriented library intended to make experimental software smaller and easier to read, write, and modify.

The implementation is CLONES, the Connectionist Layered Object-oriented Network Simulator. The library approach allows experimental programs to use shared software components. Its importance lies in supporting algorithm variation without requiring each experiment to contain a full independent implementation of the surrounding neural-network software.

CLONES runs on UNIX workstations and on the authors' Ring Array Processor, hardware built with neural-network algorithms in mind and described as operating in the 100–1000 MFLOP range. The paper explains the simulator and its implementation on that processor. The contribution connects flexible experimental programming with specialized computing hardware, addressing both the organization of research code and the platform on which that code executes.
summary.tldr: CLONES uses an object-oriented library to simplify neural-network experiments on UNIX workstations and a specialized Ring Array Processor.

title: Software for ANN training on a Ring Array Processor

The degree to which the re(cid:173) suIting internal (i.e. hidden unit) representations reflect global proper(cid:173) ties of the environment depends upon several parameters of the learning procedure. Architectural bottlenecks. noise. and incremental learning of landmarks are shown to be important factors in maintaining topograph(cid:173) ic relationships at a global scale.

The degree to which the re(cid:173) suIting internal (i.e. hidden unit) representations reflect global proper(cid:173) ties of the environment depends upon several parameters of the learning procedure. Architectural bottlenecks. noise. and incremental learning of landmarks are shown to be important factors in maintaining topograph(cid:173) ic relationships at a global scale.

paragraphs: This paper asks whether learning local relationships can produce an internal representation of an environment's larger structure. The authors use a variant of an encoder network whose input and output units represent nodes in a graph. Its training task maps a location to a set of neighboring locations, giving the network local associations to learn.

The authors then examine the hidden-unit representations produced by that task. The question is how well these representations preserve global topographic relationships across the environment. Successfully learning which locations are neighbors is one issue; organizing the internal representation so that larger-scale relationships remain meaningful is a further property of the learned system.

The reported findings identify architectural bottlenecks, noise, and incremental learning of landmarks as important factors in maintaining global topography. The extent of global organization depends on choices in the learning procedure. The paper therefore links the emergence of large-scale structure to specific features of architecture and training, showing how a local prediction task can support a more globally organized representation.
summary.tldr: Learning neighborhood associations can yield globally organized representations, with bottlenecks, noise, and landmark learning playing important roles.

title: Emergence of Global Structure from Local Associations

abstract: We analyze how data with uncertain or missing input features can be incorporated into the training of a neural network. The gen(cid:173) eral solution requires a weighted integration over the unknown or uncertain input although computationally cheaper closed-form so(cid:173) lutions can be found for certain Gaussian Basis Function (GBF) networks. We also discuss cases in which heuristical solutions such as substituting the mean of an unknown input can be harmful.
originalAbstract: We analyze how data with uncertain or missing input features can be incorporated into the training of a neural network. The gen(cid:173) eral solution requires a weighted integration over the unknown or uncertain input although computationally cheaper closed-form so(cid:173) lutions can be found for certain Gaussian Basis Function (GBF) networks. We also discuss cases in which heuristical solutions such as substituting the mean of an unknown input can be harmful.

paragraphs: This paper examines how to train neural networks when some input features are missing or uncertain. Such examples do not provide a single fully known input vector. The authors analyze how their uncertainty can be included in learning, so that incomplete examples can contribute without treating unknown values as if they had been observed.

The general solution uses weighted integration over the unknown or uncertain input. In plain terms, the training calculation accounts for possible input values with appropriate weights. This retains the distinction between an observed value and a range of plausible values. For certain Gaussian basis function networks, the authors identify less expensive closed-form solutions.

The paper also discusses situations in which replacing a missing input with its mean can be harmful. That substitution compresses uncertainty into one value, whereas the proposed general treatment carries uncertainty into the calculation itself. The contribution combines a principled formulation with computational shortcuts for particular networks, while identifying why a convenient replacement heuristic can give an unsuitable training signal.
summary.tldr: Training with uncertain inputs calls for weighted integration, with efficient solutions available for certain Gaussian basis function networks.

title: Training Neural Networks with Deficient Data

abstract: The paper presents a rapid speaker-normalization technique based on neural network spectral mapping. The neural network is used as a front-end of a continuous speech recognition system (speaker(cid:173) dependent, HMM-based) to normalize the input acoustic data from a new speaker. The spectral difference between speakers can be reduced using a limited amount of new acoustic data (40 phonet(cid:173) ically rich sentences). Recognition error of phone units from the acoustic-phonetic continuous speech corpus APASCI is decreased with an adaptability ratio of 25%. We used local basis networks of elliptical Gaussian kernels, with recursive allocation of units and on-line optimization of parameters (GRAN model). For this ap(cid:173) plication, the model included a linear term. The results compare favorably with multivariate linear mapping based on constrained orthonormal transformations.
originalAbstract: The paper presents a rapid speaker-normalization technique based on neural network spectral mapping. The neural network is used as a front-end of a continuous speech recognition system (speaker(cid:173) dependent, HMM-based) to normalize the input acoustic data from a new speaker. The spectral difference between speakers can be reduced using a limited amount of new acoustic data (40 phonet(cid:173) ically rich sentences). Recognition error of phone units from the acoustic-phonetic continuous speech corpus APASCI is decreased with an adaptability ratio of 25%. We used local basis networks of elliptical Gaussian kernels, with recursive allocation of units and on-line optimization of parameters (GRAN model). For this ap(cid:173) plication, the model included a linear term. The results compare favorably with multivariate linear mapping based on constrained orthonormal transformations.

paragraphs: The paper addresses the difficulty of applying a speech recognizer trained for one speaker to a new speaker. It places a neural network before a speaker-dependent, hidden Markov model recognizer. This front end maps the new speaker's acoustic spectra to reduce differences between speakers before recognition takes place.

The mapping uses a generalized resource allocating network with local, elliptical Gaussian units and an additional linear term. Units are allocated recursively, and parameters are optimized online. This gives the spectral mapping an adaptable structure while allowing its parameters to change as acoustic data arrives. The reported normalization uses 40 sentences chosen to provide broad phonetic coverage.

On the APASCI continuous speech corpus, the method reduces phone recognition errors and reports an adaptability ratio of 25%. That figure is the stated adaptation measure, rather than a claim of 25% overall recognition accuracy. The results compare favorably with a multivariate linear mapping using constrained orthonormal transformations, supporting the usefulness of this neural front end for speaker adaptation.
summary.tldr: An adaptive neural spectral mapping improves speaker-dependent speech recognition for a new speaker using 40 phonetically rich sentences.

title: Connectionist Speaker Normalization with Generalized Resource Allocating Networks

abstract: Human subjects are known to adapt their motor behavior to a shift of the visual field brought about by wearing prism glasses over their eyes. We have studied the analog of this effect in speech. U sing a device that can feed back transformed speech signals in real time, we exposed subjects to alterations of their own speech feedback. We found that speakers learn to adjust their production of a vowel to compensate for feedback alterations that change the vowel's perceived phonetic identity; moreover, the effect generalizes across consonant contexts and to different vowels.
originalAbstract: Human subjects are known to adapt their motor behavior to a shift of the visual field brought about by wearing prism glasses over their eyes. We have studied the analog of this effect in speech. U sing a device that can feed back transformed speech signals in real time, we exposed subjects to alterations of their own speech feedback. We found that speakers learn to adjust their production of a vowel to compensate for feedback alterations that change the vowel's perceived phonetic identity; moreover, the effect generalizes across consonant contexts and to different vowels.

paragraphs: This paper investigates whether speakers adapt their speech movements when the sound they hear from their own voice is altered. The motivating comparison is adaptation to prism glasses, which shift visual feedback and cause people to adjust their movements. Here, the researchers ask whether changing auditory feedback produces a corresponding adjustment in speech production.

The experiment uses a device that transforms speech signals and returns them to speakers in real time. The alterations change the perceived phonetic identity of a vowel, meaning that speakers hear their production as a different vowel sound. Participants learn to change how they produce the vowel in a direction that compensates for the altered feedback.

The adjustment also carries over to different consonant contexts and to other vowels. That transfer matters because the learned response extends beyond the particular sound context used during exposure. The findings show that speech production can adapt to changes in auditory feedback and that this adaptation can influence a broader set of speech movements.
summary.tldr: Speakers compensate for altered auditory feedback, and the resulting speech adaptation transfers across consonant contexts and vowels.

title: Adaptation in Speech Motor Control

abstract: Exact inference in densely connected Bayesian networks is computation(cid:173) ally intractable, and so there is considerable interest in developing effec(cid:173) tive approximation schemes. One approach which has been adopted is to bound the log likelihood using a mean-field approximating distribution. While this leads to a tractable algorithm, the mean field distribution is as(cid:173) sumed to be factorial and hence unimodal. In this paper we demonstrate the feasibility of using a richer class of approximating distributions based on mixtures of mean field distributions. We derive an efficient algorithm for updating the mixture parameters and apply it to the problem of learn(cid:173) ing in sigmoid belief networks. Our results demonstrate a systematic improvement over simple mean field theory as the number of mixture components is increased.

One approach which has been adopted is to bound the log likelihood using a mean-field approximating distribution. While this leads to a tractable algorithm, the mean field distribution is as(cid:173) sumed to be factorial and hence unimodal. In this paper we demonstrate the feasibility of using a richer class of approximating distributions based on mixtures of mean field distributions. We derive an efficient algorithm for updating the mixture parameters and apply it to the problem of learn(cid:173) ing in sigmoid belief networks. paragraphs: Densely connected Bayesian networks make exact inference computationally difficult. One practical alternative is mean-field approximation, which replaces a complicated distribution with a simpler one and supports a bound on the log likelihood. The paper focuses on the representational restriction imposed by using a single factorized approximation.

The authors propose mixing several mean-field distributions. Each component retains a simple form, while their combination provides a richer approximation than any one component alone. This matters when uncertainty cannot be adequately represented by the unimodal form assumed in the basic approach. The paper also derives an efficient algorithm for updating the mixture parameters, making the richer representation usable for learning.

The method is applied to sigmoid belief networks. The reported results improve systematically over simple mean-field theory as more mixture components are included. This connects the added expressive capacity to observed benefits: increasing the number of components gives the approximation more flexibility while preserving an efficient parameter-update procedure.
summary.tldr: Mixtures of mean-field distributions provide richer posterior approximations that improve as additional components are introduced.

title: Approximating Posterior Distributions in Belief Networks Using Mixtures

abstract: The Bayesian paradigm apparently only sometimes gives rise to Occam's Razor; at other times very large models perform well. We give simple examples of both kinds of behaviour. The two views are reconciled when measuring complexity of functions, rather than of the machinery used to implement them. We analyze the complexity of functions for some linear in the parameter models that are equivalent to Gaussian Processes, and always find Occam's Razor at work.
originalAbstract: The Bayesian paradigm apparently only sometimes gives rise to Occam's Razor; at other times very large models perform well. We give simple examples of both kinds of behaviour. The two views are reconciled when measuring complexity of functions, rather than of the machinery used to implement them. We analyze the complexity of functions for some linear in the parameter models that are equivalent to Gaussian Processes, and always find Occam's Razor at work.

paragraphs: Bayesian modeling can appear inconsistent with Occam's Razor, the preference for simpler explanations. Sometimes it seems to favor smaller models, yet very large models can also perform well. The paper presents simple examples of both behaviors and asks how they can fit within a coherent understanding of complexity.

The proposed resolution is to measure the complexity of the functions represented, rather than the machinery used to implement them. These are different objects of comparison: the size of a representation does not by itself settle the complexity of its resulting function. This distinction explains how successful large models can remain compatible with a preference for simple explanations.

The authors analyze function complexity for some models that are linear in their parameters and equivalent to Gaussian processes. Within those analyses, they consistently find Occam's Razor operating. The stated conclusion is grounded in that family of models. Its significance is a change in what should be counted as complexity when interpreting Bayesian behavior and comparing apparently simple or elaborate model implementations.
summary.tldr: Measuring function complexity explains how large Bayesian models can succeed while remaining consistent with Occam's Razor.

title: Occam's Razor

abstract: The problem of reinforcement learning in large factored Markov decision processes is explored. The Q-value of a state-action pair is approximated by the free energy of a product of experts network. Network parameters are learned on-line using a modified SARSA algorithm which minimizes the inconsistency of the Q-values of consecutive state-action pairs. Ac(cid:173) tions are chosen based on the current value estimates by fixing the current state and sampling actions from the network using Gibbs sampling. The algorithm is tested on a co-operative multi-agent task. The product of experts model is found to perform comparably to table-based Q-Iearning for small instances of the task, and continues to perform well when the problem becomes too large for a table-based representation.

The Q-value of a state-action pair is approximated by the free energy of a product of experts network. Network parameters are learned on-line using a modified SARSA algorithm which minimizes the inconsistency of the Q-values of consecutive state-action pairs. Ac(cid:173) tions are chosen based on the current value estimates by fixing the current state and sampling actions from the network using Gibbs sampling. The algorithm is tested on a co-operative multi-agent task. The product of experts model is found to perform comparably to table-based Q-Iearning for small instances of the task, and continues to perform well when the problem becomes too large for a table-based representation.

paragraphs: The paper explores reinforcement learning in large factored Markov decision processes, where representing every state-action value in a table can become impractical. It approximates each Q-value with the free energy of a product of experts network. This gives the learner a parameterized representation of action values that can be used when an explicit table grows too large.

Network parameters are updated online through a modified SARSA algorithm. The updates reduce inconsistency between the values of consecutive state-action pairs. To choose an action, the method fixes the current state and uses Gibbs sampling to sample actions from the network according to its current value estimates. The network thus participates in both value representation and action selection.

Tests use a cooperative multi-agent task. For small instances, the product of experts approach performs comparably to table-based Q-learning. It also continues to perform well on instances too large for the table representation. The findings support this representation on the studied task, linking its practical value to the growth of the state-action space.
summary.tldr: A product of experts network represents Q-values through free energy and performs well on a cooperative task beyond practical table sizes.

title: Using Free Energies to Represent Q-values in a Multiagent Reinforcement Learning Task

abstract: In this paper, we extend the Rao-Blackwellised particle filtering method to more complex hybrid models consisting of Gaussian latent variables and discrete observations. This is accomplished by augmenting the models with artificial variables that enable us to apply Rao-Blackwellisation. Other improvements include the design of an optimal importance proposal distribution and being able to swap the sampling an selection steps to handle outliers. We focus on sequential binary classifiers that consist of linear combinations of basis functions , whose coefficients evolve according to a Gaussian smoothness prior. Our results show significant improvements.
originalAbstract: In this paper, we extend the Rao-Blackwellised particle filtering method to more complex hybrid models consisting of Gaussian latent variables and discrete observations. This is accomplished by augmenting the models with artificial variables that enable us to apply Rao-Blackwellisation. Other improvements include the design of an optimal importance proposal distribution and being able to swap the sampling an selection steps to handle outliers. We focus on sequential binary classifiers that consist of linear combinations of basis functions , whose coefficients evolve according to a Gaussian smoothness prior. Our results show significant improvements.

paragraphs: The paper extends Rao-Blackwellised particle filtering to hybrid models with Gaussian hidden variables and discrete observations. The central technique is data augmentation: adding artificial variables to the model so that Rao-Blackwellisation becomes applicable. This changes the computational representation of the inference problem and makes the filtering method usable for the more complex model class.

The authors add two further improvements. They design an optimal importance proposal distribution, which governs the candidate samples used in the filtering calculation. They also make it possible to exchange the order of sampling and selection to handle outliers. These changes address how the filtering procedure constructs and processes its candidate explanations of incoming observations.

The main application is sequential binary classification. Classifiers are built from linear combinations of basis functions, with coefficients that evolve under a Gaussian smoothness prior. The reported results show significant improvements for the proposed approach. The contribution combines a way to enable Rao-Blackwellisation with changes to the sampling procedure, demonstrated in classifiers whose parameters change over time.
summary.tldr: Artificial auxiliary variables extend Rao-Blackwellised particle filtering to Gaussian latent models with discrete observations.

title: Rao-Blackwellised Particle Filtering via Data Augmentation

abstract: In previous work on transformed mixtures of Gaussians'' and transformed hidden Markov models'', we showed how the EM al- gorithm in a discrete latent variable model can be used to jointly normalize data (e.g., center images, pitch-normalize spectrograms) and learn a mixture model of the normalized data. The only input to the algorithm is the data, a list of possible transformations, and the number of clusters to find. The main criticism of this work was that the exhaustive computation of the posterior probabili- ties over transformations would make scaling up to large feature vectors and large sets of transformations intractable. Here, we de- scribe how a tremendous speed-up is acheived through the use of a variational technique for decoupling transformations, and a fast Fourier transform method for computing posterior probabilities. For NN images, learning C clusters under N rotations, N scales, N x-translations and N y-translations takes only (C + 2 log N)N 2 scalar operations per iteration. In contrast, the original algorithm takes CN 6 operations to account for these transformations. We give results on learning a 4-component mixture model from a video sequence with frames of size 320240. The model accounts for 360 rotations and 76,800 translations. Each iteration of EM takes only 10 seconds per frame in MATLAB, which is over 5 million times faster than the original algorithm.

The only input to the algorithm is the data, a list of possible transformations, and the number of clusters to find. The main criticism of this work was that the exhaustive computation of the posterior probabili- ties over transformations would make scaling up to large feature vectors and large sets of transformations intractable. For NN images, learning C clusters under N rotations, N scales, N x-translations and N y-translations takes only (C + 2 log N)N 2 scalar operations per iteration. In contrast, the original algorithm takes CN 6 operations to account for these transformations. We give results on learning a 4-component mixture model from a video sequence with frames of size 320240. The model accounts for 360 rotations and 76,800 translations. paragraphs: The paper addresses clustering data whose appearance changes under transformations such as rotation, scaling, or translation. Earlier transformed mixture models jointly learned clusters and normalized observations through EM. Their inputs were the data, a list of allowable transformations, and the desired number of clusters, but exhaustive transformation calculations limited scalability.

The new approach combines a variational method that decouples transformations with a fast Fourier transform method for posterior calculations. For square images with side length N and N choices for each of four transformations, the stated per-iteration cost falls from C times N to the sixth power to N squared times the quantity C plus twice log N, for C clusters.

The authors demonstrate a four-component mixture on video frames measuring 320 by 240 pixels, accounting for 360 rotations and 76,800 translations. Each EM iteration takes ten seconds per frame in MATLAB, reported as over five million times faster than the original algorithm. This demonstrates a substantial computational improvement for the specified example, making a previously expensive transformation search more practical.
summary.tldr: Variational decoupling and Fourier-transform calculations dramatically reduce the cost of jointly clustering images and accounting for transformations.

title: Fast, Large-Scale Transformation-Invariant Clustering

abstract: According to a series of inﬂuential models, dopamine (DA) neurons sig- nal reward prediction error using a temporal-difference (TD) algorithm. We address a problem not convincingly solved in these accounts: how to maintain a representation of cues that predict delayed consequences. Our new model uses a TD rule grounded in partially observable semi-Markov processes, a formalism that captures two largely neglected features of DA experiments: hidden state and temporal variability. Previous models pre- dicted rewards using a tapped delay line representation of sensory inputs; we replace this with a more active process of inference about the under- lying state of the world. The DA system can then learn to map these inferred states to reward predictions using TD. The new model can ex- plain previously vexing data on the responses of DA neurons in the face of temporal variability. By combining statistical model-based learning with a physiologically grounded TD theory, it also brings into contact with physiology some insights about behavior that had previously been conﬁned to more abstract psychological models.

paragraphs: Models of dopamine activity often interpret neuronal responses as reward prediction errors learned through temporal differences. This paper addresses how such models can retain useful information about cues whose consequences arrive later. The authors focus on two features of dopamine experiments: relevant states can be hidden, and the timing of events can vary.

Their model grounds temporal-difference learning in partially observable semi-Markov processes. Instead of representing sensory history through a tapped delay line, it infers the underlying state of the world. The dopamine system then learns reward predictions associated with those inferred states, combining uncertainty about the situation with learning about its expected consequences.

The authors report that this formulation can explain previously difficult observations of dopamine responses under temporal variability. Its significance is the connection between a process of state inference and a physiologically grounded reward-learning account. The model also brings ideas from more abstract psychological theories of behavior into contact with physiological observations, through a shared account of hidden state and timing.
summary.tldr: A dopamine model combines hidden-state inference with temporal-difference learning to explain reward responses when event timing varies.

title: Timing and Partial Observability in the Dopamine System

abstract: We address in this paper the question of how the knowledge of the marginal distribution P (x) can be incorporated in a learning algorithm. We suggest three theoretical methods for taking into account this distribution for regularization and provide links to existing graph-based semi-supervised learning algorithms. We also propose practical implementations.

We suggest three theoretical methods for taking into account this distribution for regularization and provide links to existing graph-based semi-supervised learning algorithms. We also propose practical implementations.

paragraphs: The paper asks how a learning algorithm can use knowledge of the input distribution, written as P(x). This distribution describes how inputs are distributed independently of their labels. The central idea is to incorporate that knowledge through regularization, so the preferences guiding learning take account of the data distribution.

The authors suggest three theoretical methods for doing this. Their shared purpose is to connect distributional knowledge to the constraints or preferences imposed on a learned function. Framed this way, the distribution becomes part of the learning procedure’s regularizing structure, giving a formal role to information about inputs beyond the labeled examples themselves.

The paper also connects these methods to existing graph-based semi-supervised learning algorithms and proposes practical implementations. Those links matter because they place distribution-aware regularization alongside established ways of using unlabeled data. The stated contribution spans theoretical formulations, relationships to existing approaches, and implementation proposals, providing several routes for incorporating P(x) into learning rather than presenting a single universal prescription.
summary.tldr: The paper proposes three ways to incorporate the input distribution into regularization and links them to graph-based semi-supervised learning.

title: Measure Based Regularization

abstract: Linear Discriminant Analysis (LDA) is a well-known method for feature extraction and dimension reduction. It has been used widely in many applications such as face recognition. Recently, a novel LDA algorithm based on QR Decomposition, namely LDA/QR, has been proposed, which is competitive in terms of classification accuracy with other LDA algorithms, but it has much lower costs in time and space. However, LDA/QR is based on linear projection, which may not be suitable for data with nonlinear structure. This paper first proposes an algorithm called KDA/QR, which extends the LDA/QR algorithm to deal with nonlinear data by using the kernel operator. Then an efficient approximation of KDA/QR called AKDA/QR is proposed. Experiments on face image data show that the classification accuracy of both KDA/QR and AKDA/QR are competitive with Generalized Discriminant Analysis (GDA), a general kernel discriminant analysis algorithm, while AKDA/QR has much lower time and space costs.

A version based on QR decomposition, LDA/QR, offers competitive classification accuracy with substantially lower time and storage costs than other LDA methods. Its linear projection, however, may be unsuitable when the data have nonlinear structure.

The paper introduces KDA/QR, which extends the QR-based approach using a kernel operator to handle nonlinear data. It then develops AKDA/QR, an efficient approximation of that extension. The two steps address related needs: broadening the structures the method can represent and making the resulting computation more economical.

The approximate version also has much lower time and space costs. These findings support the practical value of approximation in the tested setting: it retains competitive classification performance while reducing the computational burden of nonlinear feature extraction.
summary.tldr: A kernel extension of QR-based discriminant analysis, together with an efficient approximation, delivers competitive face classification accuracy at reduced computational cost.

title: Efficient Kernel Discriminant Analysis via QR Decomposition

abstract: If language users are rational, they might choose to structure their utterances so as to optimize communicative properties. In particular, information-theoretic and psycholinguistic considerations suggest that this may include maximizing the uniformity of information density in an utterance. We investigate this possibility in the context of syntactic reduction, where the speaker has the option of either marking a higher-order unit (a phrase) with an extra word, or leaving it unmarked. We demonstrate that speakers are more likely to reduce less information-dense phrases. In a second step, we combine a stochastic model of structured utterance production with a logistic-regression model of syntactic reduction to study which types of cues speakers employ when estimating the predictability of upcoming elements. We demonstrate that the trend toward predictability-sensitive syntactic reduction (Jaeger, 2006) is robust in the face of a wide variety of control variables, and present evidence that speakers use both surface and structural cues for predictability estimation.

paragraphs: Speakers sometimes have a choice between marking a phrase with an extra word and leaving that marker out. This paper uses such syntactic reduction to investigate whether language production tends to spread information more evenly across an utterance. The motivating hypothesis is that speakers may structure language to improve its communicative properties.

The authors find that less information-dense phrases are more likely to be reduced. This pattern fits the idea that optional wording is less useful where the upcoming content is already predictable. They then combine a stochastic model of structured utterance production with logistic regression to examine what information speakers use when judging that predictability.

The tendency toward predictability-sensitive reduction remains robust across a wide variety of control variables. The analysis also provides evidence that speakers use both surface cues and structural cues when estimating what comes next. Together, the findings connect optional grammatical choices to information distribution. They support a tendency compatible with more uniform information density, rather than establishing that every utterance is globally optimized.
summary.tldr: Speakers reduce less information-dense phrases more often, using both surface and structural cues to estimate predictability.

title: Speakers optimize information density through syntactic reduction

abstract: We propose a multiplicative approximation scheme (MAS) for inference problems in graphical models, which can be applied to various inference algorithms. The method uses $\epsilon$-decompositions which decompose functions used throughout the inference procedure into functions over smaller sets of variables with a known error $\epsilon$. MAS translates these local approximations into bounds on the accuracy of the results. We show how to optimize $\epsilon$-decompositions and provide a fast closed-form solution for an $L_2$ approximation. Applying MAS to the Variable Elimination inference algorithm, we introduce an algorithm we call DynaDecomp which is extremely fast in practice and provides guaranteed error bounds on the result. The superior accuracy and efficiency of DynaDecomp is demonstrated.

paragraphs: Probabilistic inference in graphical models can involve functions of many variables, making intermediate calculations costly. The paper introduces a multiplicative approximation scheme, MAS, that can be used with different inference algorithms. Its purpose is to simplify those calculations while keeping track of how approximation affects the final answer.

The method uses epsilon-decompositions: a function is replaced by functions involving smaller sets of variables, with a known approximation error. MAS translates these local errors into bounds on the accuracy of the inference result. The authors also study how to optimize the decompositions and give a fast closed-form solution for an L2 approximation.

Applying the scheme to Variable Elimination produces an algorithm called DynaDecomp. The paper reports that it is extremely fast in practice, demonstrates superior accuracy and efficiency, and provides guaranteed error bounds. The central value is the connection between computational simplification and explicit accuracy control: smaller intermediate functions come with a way to assess their effect on the result.
summary.tldr: MAS simplifies graphical-model inference through smaller-function approximations while bounding their effect on final accuracy.

title: MAS: a multiplicative approximation scheme for probabilistic inference

abstract: We propose an efficient sequential Monte Carlo inference scheme for the recently proposed coalescent clustering model (Teh et al, 2008). Our algorithm has a quadratic runtime while those in (Teh et al, 2008) is cubic. In experiments, we were surprised to find that in addition to being more efficient, it is also a better sequential Monte Carlo sampler than the best in (Teh et al, 2008), when measured in terms of variance of estimated likelihood and effective sample size.

paragraphs: This paper improves the computation used to perform inference in an existing coalescent clustering model. Its contribution is a sequential Monte Carlo inference scheme: the focus is on how to approximate the model's probabilistic calculations efficiently. The clustering model provides the target, while the new algorithm changes how inference is carried out.

The stated computational improvement is from cubic runtime for the earlier algorithms to quadratic runtime for the proposed method. This changes how quickly computational work grows as the problem becomes larger. The result therefore concerns scalability as well as the time needed for any particular experiment.

The experiments also report better sampling performance than the strongest earlier sequential Monte Carlo method considered. The authors assess this through the variance of estimated likelihood and effective sample size. These findings mean that the computational improvement was accompanied by improvements in those sampling measures in the reported experiments. The evidence supports a useful combination of lower runtime growth and stronger empirical inference quality.
summary.tldr: A new coalescent clustering sampler reduces runtime from cubic to quadratic and improves two sampling-quality measures in experiments.

title: An Efficient Sequential Monte Carlo Algorithm for Coalescent Clustering

abstract: In this paper we consider the problem of learning from data the support of a probability distribution when the distribution {\em does not} have a density (with respect to some reference measure). We propose a new class of regularized spectral estimators based on a new notion of reproducing kernel Hilbert space, which we call {\em ``completely regular''}. Completely regular kernels allow to capture the relevant geometric and topological properties of an arbitrary probability space. In particular, they are the key ingredient to prove the universal consistency of the spectral estimators and in this respect they are the analogue of universal kernels for supervised problems. Numerical experiments show that spectral estimators compare favorably to state of the art machine learning algorithms for density support estimation.

Completely regular kernels allow to capture the relevant geometric and topological properties of an arbitrary probability space. paragraphs: The paper studies how to learn a probability distribution's support, the region where its probability mass resides, directly from data. The setting specifically allows the distribution to lack a density relative to a reference measure. This makes it important to estimate support without requiring a density-based description.

The authors propose regularized spectral estimators built around a new property of reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces, called complete regularity. Completely regular kernels capture relevant geometric and topological properties of a probability space. Their role is to give the estimation method access to the structure needed to distinguish the support.

These kernels are the key ingredient in the proof of universal consistency for the proposed estimators. The authors compare their role with that of universal kernels in supervised learning. Numerical experiments also show favorable comparisons with leading density-support estimation algorithms. The contribution therefore combines a consistency argument for the density-free setting with empirical evidence that the spectral approach can perform competitively.
summary.tldr: Completely regular kernels enable universally consistent spectral support estimation for distributions that need not have a density.

title: Spectral Regularization for Support Estimation

abstract: Conventional dynamic Bayesian networks (DBNs) are based on the homogeneous Markov assumption, which is too restrictive in many practical applications. Various approaches to relax the homogeneity assumption have therefore been proposed in the last few years. The present paper aims to improve the flexibility of two recent versions of non-homogeneous DBNs, which either (i) suffer from the need for data discretization, or (ii) assume a time-invariant network structure. Allowing the network structure to be fully flexible leads to the risk of overfitting and inflated inference uncertainty though, especially in the highly topical field of systems biology, where independent measurements tend to be sparse. In the present paper we investigate three conceptually different regularization schemes based on inter-segment information sharing. We assess the performance in a comparative evaluation study based on simulated data. We compare the predicted segmentation of gene expression time series obtained during embryogenesis in Drosophila melanogaster with other state-of-the-art techniques. We conclude our evaluation with an application to synthetic biology, where the objective is to predict a known regulatory network of five genes in Saccharomyces cerevisiae.

paragraphs: Dynamic Bayesian networks often assume that the process governing a time series stays the same over time. This paper seeks more flexible models, addressing earlier approaches that either require discretized data or keep the network structure fixed. The objective is to accommodate changing relationships across time segments.

Greater flexibility also increases the risk of overfitting and uncertain inference, particularly when independent measurements are scarce. The authors investigate three different regularization schemes that share information across segments. The common idea is to support changing structure while allowing evidence from one segment to inform estimation in another.

The evaluation includes comparisons on simulated data and segmentation of gene-expression time series during fruit-fly embryogenesis. It also includes predicting a known five-gene regulatory network in yeast. These settings connect the methodological question to biological processes where relationships can vary over time and measurements may be limited. The stated contribution is the investigation and comparative evaluation of information-sharing schemes for this balance between flexibility and estimation stability.
summary.tldr: The paper investigates three ways to share information across time segments when estimating dynamic Bayesian networks with changing structure.

title: Inter-time segment information sharing for non-homogeneous dynamic Bayesian networks

abstract: The human vision system is able to effortlessly perceive both short-range and long-range motion patterns in complex dynamic scenes. Previous work has assumed that two different mechanisms are involved in processing these two types of motion. In this paper, we propose a hierarchical model as a unified framework for modeling both short-range and long-range motion perception. Our model consists of two key components: a data likelihood that proposes multiple motion hypotheses using nonlinear matching, and a hierarchical prior that imposes slowness and spatial smoothness constraints on the motion field at multiple scales. We tested our model on two types of stimuli, random dot kinematograms and multiple-aperture stimuli, both commonly used in human vision research. We demonstrate that the hierarchical model adequately accounts for human performance in psychophysical experiments.

paragraphs: People perceive movement over both short and long distances in complex scenes. Earlier explanations assumed that these forms of motion perception required separate mechanisms. This paper proposes a hierarchical model that handles both within one framework, asking whether a shared set of computational principles can account for the observed human responses.

The model combines two sources of information. A data likelihood uses nonlinear matching to propose several possible interpretations of motion. A hierarchical prior then constrains those interpretations through preferences for slowness and spatial smoothness at multiple scales. This lets the model consider ambiguous movement evidence while favoring motion fields that satisfy these organizing constraints.

The authors test the framework using random dot kinematograms and multiple-aperture stimuli, two stimulus types used in human vision research. They report that the model adequately accounts for human performance in the psychophysical experiments. These findings support the proposed framework as a unified explanation of the tested behaviors, without establishing that it is the actual mechanism implemented by human vision.
summary.tldr: A hierarchical motion model accounts for tested human responses to both short-range and long-range movement.

title: A unified model of short-range and long-range motion perception

abstract: Bayesian model-based reinforcement learning is a formally elegant approach to learning optimal behaviour under model uncertainty, trading off exploration and exploitation in an ideal way. Unfortunately, finding the resulting Bayes-optimal policies is notoriously taxing, since the search space becomes enormous. In this paper we introduce a tractable, sample-based method for approximate Bayes-optimal planning which exploits Monte-Carlo tree search. Our approach outperformed prior Bayesian model-based RL algorithms by a significant margin on several well-known benchmark problems -- because it avoids expensive applications of Bayes rule within the search tree by lazily sampling models from the current beliefs. We illustrate the advantages of our approach by showing it working in an infinite state space domain which is qualitatively out of reach of almost all previous work in Bayesian exploration.

Our approach outperformed prior Bayesian model-based RL algorithms by a significant margin on several well-known benchmark problems -- because it avoids expensive applications of Bayes rule within the search tree by lazily sampling models from the current beliefs. We illustrate the advantages of our approach by showing it working in an infinite state space domain which is qualitatively out of reach of almost all previous work in Bayesian exploration.

paragraphs: Bayesian model-based reinforcement learning represents uncertainty about the environment while deciding how to act. In principle, this supports an ideal trade-off between learning more about the world and exploiting what is already known. Computing the corresponding Bayes-optimal policy is difficult, however, because planning must account for an enormous space of possibilities.

The paper introduces an approximate planning method based on Monte Carlo tree search. Its key computational choice is to sample models lazily from the learner's current beliefs. This avoids expensive applications of Bayes' rule inside the search tree, reducing the work needed to explore possible future action sequences while still drawing on uncertainty about the environment.

The approach significantly outperforms prior Bayesian model-based reinforcement learning algorithms on several established benchmark problems. The authors also demonstrate it in an infinite-state domain described as beyond the qualitative reach of almost all earlier work in Bayesian exploration. These results support sampling as a practical route to approximate Bayes-optimal planning, expanding the range of problems on which that objective can be pursued.
summary.tldr: Lazy model sampling within Monte Carlo tree search makes approximate Bayesian planning more tractable and improves performance on reported benchmarks.

title: Efficient Bayes-Adaptive Reinforcement Learning using Sample-Based Search

abstract: Multi-task learning (MTL) aims to improve generalization performance by learning multiple related tasks simultaneously and identifying the shared information among tasks. Most of existing MTL methods focus on learning linear models under the supervised setting. We propose a novel semi-supervised and nonlinear approach for MTL using vector fields. A vector field is a smooth mapping from the manifold to the tangent spaces which can be viewed as a directional derivative of functions on the manifold. We argue that vector fields provide a natural way to exploit the geometric structure of data as well as the shared differential structure of tasks, both are crucial for semi-supervised multi-task learning. In this paper, we develop multi-task vector field learning (MTVFL) which learns the prediction functions and the vector fields simultaneously. MTVFL has the following key properties: (1) the vector fields we learned are close to the gradient fields of the prediction functions; (2) within each task, the vector field is required to be as parallel as possible which is expected to span a low dimensional subspace; (3) the vector fields from all tasks share a low dimensional subspace. We formalize our idea in a regularization framework and also provide a convex relaxation method to solve the original non-convex problem. The experimental results on synthetic and real data demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed approach.

paragraphs: The paper proposes semi-supervised, nonlinear multi-task learning through vector fields. A vector field assigns directions along the manifold describing the data, providing a way to express how a prediction function changes locally. The authors use this structure to connect data geometry with information shared among related tasks.

Their method learns prediction functions and vector fields together. The fields are encouraged to remain close to the gradients of the prediction functions. Within each task, they are made as parallel as possible, which is expected to produce low-dimensional structure. Across tasks, the fields share a low-dimensional subspace, expressing common patterns in how predictions vary.

The authors formulate these requirements through regularization and provide a convex relaxation of the original nonconvex optimization problem. Experiments on synthetic and real datasets demonstrate effectiveness. The contribution is a form of sharing based on local changes in predictions, combined with the geometry of the data, rather than a formulation restricted to supervised linear models.
summary.tldr: Multi-task vector field learning shares low-dimensional patterns of prediction changes across nonlinear, semi-supervised tasks.

title: Multi-task Vector Field Learning

abstract: Automatic music recommendation has become an increasingly relevant problem in recent years, since a lot of music is now sold and consumed digitally. Most recommender systems rely on collaborative filtering. However, this approach suffers from the cold start problem: it fails when no usage data is available, so it is not effective for recommending new and unpopular songs. In this paper, we propose to use a latent factor model for recommendation, and predict the latent factors from music audio when they cannot be obtained from usage data. We compare a traditional approach using a bag-of-words representation of the audio signals with deep convolutional neural networks, and evaluate the predictions quantitatively and qualitatively on the Million Song Dataset. We show that using predicted latent factors produces sensible recommendations, despite the fact that there is a large semantic gap between the characteristics of a song that affect user preference and the corresponding audio signal. We also show that recent advances in deep learning translate very well to the music recommendation setting, with deep convolutional neural networks significantly outperforming the traditional approach.

paragraphs: Music recommenders often learn from listening or other usage patterns. That creates a cold-start problem for songs with no usage history: the system lacks the behavioral evidence it normally uses. This paper investigates whether a song's audio can supply the representation needed to recommend it.

The approach uses a latent factor recommendation model, where songs have learned representations that support recommendations. When usage data cannot provide those factors, a model predicts them from audio. The authors compare a traditional bag-of-words audio representation with deep convolutional neural networks. Both approaches address the same task of translating sound into factors relevant to listener preferences.

Evaluation on the Million Song Dataset includes quantitative and qualitative assessments. Predicted factors yield sensible recommendations, despite the substantial gap between an audio signal and the musical characteristics that influence preference. Deep convolutional networks significantly outperform the traditional approach in the reported comparison. The findings support audio-based factor prediction as a way to extend a usage-based recommendation framework to songs lacking the usual behavioral information.
summary.tldr: Predicting recommendation factors from audio helps address song cold starts, with deep convolutional networks outperforming a traditional audio representation.

title: Deep content-based music recommendation

abstract: We provide several applications of Optimistic Mirror Descent, an online learning algorithm based on the idea of predictable sequences. First, we recover the Mirror-Prox algorithm, prove an extension to Holder-smooth functions, and apply the results to saddle-point type problems. Second, we prove that a version of Optimistic Mirror Descent (which has a close relation to the Exponential Weights algorithm) can be used by two strongly-uncoupled players in a finite zero-sum matrix game to converge to the minimax equilibrium at the rate of O(log T / T). This addresses a question of Daskalakis et al, 2011. Further, we consider a partial information version of the problem. We then apply the results to approximate convex programming and show a simple algorithm for the approximate Max-Flow problem.

The shared idea is to use predictability within an iterative process to guide updates. The authors connect this approach to numerical optimization, strategic interaction between players, and approximate solutions to constrained computational problems.

For optimization, they recover the Mirror-Prox algorithm, establish an extension to Hölder-smooth functions, and apply the results to saddle-point problems. summary.tldr: Optimistic Mirror Descent connects predictable sequences to optimization and games, including an O(log T / T) equilibrium rate for strongly uncoupled zero-sum players.

title: Optimization, Learning, and Games with Predictable Sequences

abstract: Discriminative dictionary learning (DL) has been widely studied in various pattern classification problems. Most of the existing DL methods aim to learn a synthesis dictionary to represent the input signal while enforcing the representation coefficients and/or representation residual to be discriminative. However, the $\ell_0$ or $\ell_1$-norm sparsity constraint on the representation coefficients adopted in many DL methods makes the training and testing phases time consuming. We propose a new discriminative DL framework, namely projective dictionary pair learning (DPL), which learns a synthesis dictionary and an analysis dictionary jointly to achieve the goal of signal representation and discrimination. Compared with conventional DL methods, the proposed DPL method can not only greatly reduce the time complexity in the training and testing phases, but also lead to very competitive accuracies in a variety of visual classification tasks.

paragraphs: Dictionary-learning classifiers represent an input using learned building blocks and try to make that representation useful for distinguishing classes. Many approaches impose l0 or l1 sparsity constraints on the representation coefficients. Solving for those coefficients can make both model training and classification computationally expensive.

This paper proposes projective dictionary pair learning, or DPL. It jointly learns a synthesis dictionary for representing signals and an analysis dictionary, organizing the representation and discrimination objectives within one framework. The paired construction changes how representations are obtained rather than simply adding another discriminative penalty to an existing sparse-coding pipeline.

The reported experiments cover a variety of visual classification tasks. The authors find substantially lower training and testing complexity alongside competitive classification accuracy. The abstract does not name the benchmarks or quantify those improvements, so it supports a speed-and-accuracy tradeoff within the evaluated tasks rather than a universal superiority claim over dictionary learning.
summary.tldr: Learning analysis and synthesis dictionaries together makes discriminative dictionary learning faster.

title: Projective dictionary pair learning for pattern classification

abstract: We introduce a new neural architecture to learn the conditional probability of an output sequence with elements that arediscrete tokens corresponding to positions in an input sequence.Such problems cannot be trivially addressed by existent approaches such as sequence-to-sequence and Neural Turing Machines,because the number of target classes in eachstep of the output depends on the length of the input, which is variable.Problems such as sorting variable sized sequences, and various combinatorialoptimization problems belong to this class. Our model solvesthe problem of variable size output dictionaries using a recently proposedmechanism of neural attention. It differs from the previous attentionattempts in that, instead of using attention to blend hidden units of anencoder to a context vector at each decoder step, it uses attention asa pointer to select a member of the input sequence as the output. paragraphs: Some sequence problems require outputs that identify positions in the input. Their available output choices therefore change with input length, creating a difficulty for models with a fixed output dictionary. Pointer Networks address this by learning output sequences whose discrete elements refer directly to members of the input sequence.

The architecture repurposes neural attention. Instead of using attention only to combine encoder representations into a context vector, it uses attention to select an input position as the output. This makes the available choices automatically follow the input's size and provides a neural mechanism for problems such as variable-length sorting and combinatorial optimization.

The models improve over sequence-to-sequence models with input attention and generalize beyond the maximum training lengths in the reported experiments. These findings support learning discrete geometric procedures with variable output dictionaries, while the optimization solutions remain approximate.
summary.tldr: Pointer Networks use attention to select input positions, learning approximate geometric solutions with output choices that vary with input length.

title: Pointer Networks

abstract: We show that there is a largely unexplored class of functions (positive polymatroids) that can define proper discrete metrics over pairs of binary vectors and that are fairly tractable to optimize over. By exploiting submodularity, we are able to give hardness results and approximation algorithms for optimizing over such metrics. Additionally, we demonstrate empirically the effectiveness of these metrics and associated algorithms on both a metric minimization task (a form of clustering) and also a metric maximization task (generating diverse k-best lists).

paragraphs: The paper studies distances between binary vectors, which represent objects through collections of yes-or-no attributes. It identifies positive polymatroids as a largely unexplored class of functions that can define proper discrete metrics. Establishing the metric property gives these functions a sound role as measures of difference between such objects.

The authors exploit submodularity to study optimization involving these distances. They provide both hardness results and approximation algorithms, addressing where computation is difficult and how useful approximate solutions can still be obtained. The resulting picture is qualified tractability: the metric family supports algorithmic treatment, without a claim that every associated optimization problem is easy to solve exactly.

Experiments examine two complementary uses. A clustering task minimizes a metric-based objective, while generating diverse k-best lists involves maximization. The reported effectiveness in both settings supports the usefulness of the metrics and their algorithms. The contribution links a class of discrete distances to theoretical optimization results and practical tasks with different goals.
summary.tldr: Positive polymatroids define useful distances on binary vectors, with approximation algorithms for clustering and diverse-list generation.

title: Submodular Hamming Metrics

abstract: We study the problem of reducing test-time acquisition costs in classification systems. Our goal is to learn decision rules that adaptively select sensors for each example as necessary to make a confident prediction. We model our system as a directed acyclic graph (DAG) where internal nodes correspond to sensor subsets and decision functions at each node choose whether to acquire a new sensor or classify using the available measurements. This problem can be naturally posed as an empirical risk minimization over training data. Rather than jointly optimizing such a highly coupled and non-convex problem over all decision nodes, we propose an efficient algorithm motivated by dynamic programming. We learn node policies in the DAG by reducing the global objective to a series of cost sensitive learning problems. Our approach is computationally efficient and has proven guarantees of convergence to the optimal system for a fixed architecture. In addition, we present an extension to map other budgeted learning problems with large number of sensors to our DAG architecture and demonstrate empirical performance exceeding state-of-the-art algorithms for data composed of both few and many sensors.

paragraphs: The paper studies classification systems in which obtaining sensor measurements has a cost. Instead of acquiring every measurement for every example, the system learns when to request another sensor and when available information is sufficient for a confident prediction. The objective is to reduce acquisition costs at prediction time.

The system is represented as a directed acyclic graph. Internal nodes correspond to sensor subsets, and their decision rules choose between acquiring more information and classifying. Jointly optimizing all these rules creates a tightly coupled, nonconvex problem. The authors use an approach motivated by dynamic programming that reduces the overall learning objective to a sequence of cost-sensitive learning problems.

The resulting algorithm is computationally efficient and has convergence guarantees to the optimal system for a fixed architecture. That qualification ties the guarantee to the chosen graph structure. An extension maps other budgeted problems with many sensors into the architecture, and experiments report performance exceeding leading methods on datasets with both few and many sensors.
summary.tldr: A learned decision graph reduces prediction-time sensor costs by adaptively choosing whether to acquire measurements or classify.

title: Efficient Learning by Directed Acyclic Graph For Resource Constrained Prediction

abstract: Word embeddings are a powerful approach to capturing semantic similarity among terms in a vocabulary. In this paper, we develop exponential family embeddings, which extends the idea of word embeddings to other types of high-dimensional data. As examples, we studied several types of data: neural data with real-valued observations, count data from a market basket analysis, and ratings data from a movie recommendation system. The main idea is that each observation is modeled conditioned on a set of latent embeddings and other observations, called the context, where the way the context is defined depends on the problem. In language the context is the surrounding words; in neuroscience the context is close-by neurons; in market basket data the context is other items in the shopping cart. Each instance of an embedding defines the context, the exponential family of conditional distributions, and how the embedding vectors are shared across data. We infer the embeddings with stochastic gradient descent, with an algorithm that connects closely to generalized linear models. On all three of our applications—neural activity of zebrafish, users’ shopping behavior, and movie ratings—we found that exponential family embedding models are more effective than other dimension reduction methods. They better reconstruct held-out data and find interesting qualitative structure.

The framework models each observation using latent embeddings together with a context made up of other relevant observations.

Each model specifies that context, an exponential-family conditional distribution, and how embedding vectors are shared across the data. Stochastic gradient descent fits the embeddings through an algorithm closely connected to generalized linear models.

The authors evaluate the framework on zebrafish neural activity, shopping behavior, and movie ratings. The contribution is a reusable modelling recipe that adapts both the observation distribution and the meaning of context to the data.
summary.tldr: Exponential family embeddings generalize context-based word representations to neural, shopping, and ratings data, improving held-out reconstruction in the three evaluated applications.

title: Exponential Family Embeddings

abstract: Probabilistic graphical models have been widely used to model complex systems and aid scientific discoveries. As a result, there is a large body of literature focused on consistent model selection. However, scientists are often interested in understanding uncertainty associated with the estimated parameters, which current literature has not addressed thoroughly. In this paper, we propose a novel estimator for edge parameters for pairwise graphical models based on Hyv\"arinen scoring rule. Hyv\"arinen scoring rule is especially useful in cases where the normalizing constant cannot be obtained efficiently in a closed form. We prove that the estimator is $\sqrt{n}$-consistent and asymptotically Normal. This result allows us to construct confidence intervals for edge parameters, as well as, hypothesis tests. We establish our results under conditions that are typically assumed in the literature for consistent estimation. However, we do not require that the estimator consistently recovers the graph structure. In particular, we prove that the asymptotic distribution of the estimator is robust to model selection mistakes and uniformly valid for a large number of data-generating processes. We illustrate validity of our estimator through extensive simulation studies.

This paper develops an estimator for edge parameters in pairwise graphical models using the Hyvärinen scoring rule, which is useful when the normalizing constant is difficult to obtain efficiently.

The authors prove square-root-sample-size consistency and asymptotic normality. These properties support confidence intervals and hypothesis tests for edge parameters. The results hold under conditions commonly used for consistent estimation, giving a theoretical route from estimated relationships to statements about their statistical uncertainty.

A central feature is that the estimator does not require consistent recovery of the entire graph structure. This separates uncertainty estimation for edge parameters from the stronger requirement of perfectly selecting the graph. Extensive simulations illustrate the estimator’s validity, complementing the theoretical results about its large-sample behavior.
summary.tldr: A score-matching estimator supports uncertainty estimates for graphical-model edges without requiring consistent recovery of the full graph.

title: Statistical Inference for Pairwise Graphical Models Using Score Matching

abstract: We introduce the Multiple Quantile Graphical Model (MQGM), which extends the neighborhood selection approach of Meinshausen and Buhlmann for learning sparse graphical models. The latter is defined by the basic subproblem of modeling the conditional mean of one variable as a sparse function of all others. Our approach models a set of conditional quantiles of one variable as a sparse function of all others, and hence offers a much richer, more expressive class of conditional distribution estimates. We establish that, under suitable regularity conditions, the MQGM identifies the exact conditional independencies with probability tending to one as the problem size grows, even outside of the usual homoskedastic Gaussian data model. We develop an efficient algorithm for fitting the MQGM using the alternating direction method of multipliers. We also describe a strategy for sampling from the joint distribution that underlies the MQGM estimate. Lastly, we present detailed experiments that demonstrate the flexibility and effectiveness of the MQGM in modeling hetereoskedastic non-Gaussian data.
