paragraphs: Sparse graphical modeling seeks to identify conditional relationships among variables. A neighborhood-selection approach models each variable’s conditional mean using a sparse function of the others. The Multiple Quantile Graphical Model extends this idea by modeling several conditional quantiles, describing multiple parts of the conditional distribution instead of only its mean.

This gives the model a richer way to represent distributions whose variability changes with other variables or whose shape is non-Gaussian. Under suitable regularity conditions, the authors prove that the probability of identifying the exact conditional independencies tends to one as problem size grows. The guarantee extends beyond the usual constant-variance Gaussian setting while retaining explicit conditions.

The paper provides an efficient fitting algorithm based on the alternating direction method of multipliers. It also describes how to sample from the joint distribution underlying the estimate. Experiments demonstrate flexibility and effectiveness on heteroskedastic, non-Gaussian data. Together, the theory, fitting procedure, and sampling strategy support a broader approach to estimating sparse conditional relationships.
summary.tldr: Modeling multiple conditional quantiles enables richer sparse graphical models, with conditional-independence recovery guarantees under suitable regularity conditions.

title: The Multiple Quantile Graphical Model

abstract: Computing the partition function is a key inference task in many graphical models. In this paper, we propose a dynamic importance sampling scheme that provides anytime finite-sample bounds for the partition function. Our algorithm balances the advantages of the three major inference strategies, heuristic search, variational bounds, and Monte Carlo methods, blending sampling with search to refine a variationally defined proposal. Our algorithm combines and generalizes recent work on anytime search and probabilistic bounds of the partition function. By using an intelligently chosen weighted average over the samples, we construct an unbiased estimator of the partition function with strong finite-sample confidence intervals that inherit both the rapid early improvement rate of sampling and the long-term benefits of an improved proposal from search. This gives significantly improved anytime behavior, and more flexible trade-offs between memory, time, and solution quality. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach empirically on real-world problem instances taken from recent UAI competitions.

paragraphs: This paper addresses estimation of the partition function, a key inference quantity in graphical models. It seeks an anytime method: the computation should provide useful estimates and bounds as it runs, with quality improving as more resources become available. The approach combines heuristic search, variational bounds, and Monte Carlo sampling within one dynamic importance sampling scheme.

Sampling uses a proposal defined through a variational method, while search progressively refines that proposal. An intelligently weighted average of the resulting samples gives an unbiased partition-function estimator with finite-sample confidence intervals. This weighting is central to obtaining the stated statistical properties while combining samples within the evolving procedure.

The resulting method brings together sampling’s rapid early improvement and the longer-term benefits of search improving the proposal. The authors report significantly better anytime behavior and greater flexibility in trading memory and computation time against solution quality. Experiments on real-world instances from UAI competitions demonstrate its effectiveness. The contribution therefore concerns both the estimate itself and useful uncertainty bounds during ongoing computation.
summary.tldr: Dynamic importance sampling combines search and sampling to produce unbiased partition-function estimates with useful finite-sample bounds throughout computation.

title: Dynamic Importance Sampling for Anytime Bounds of the Partition Function

abstract: Given a full rank matrix X with more columns than rows consider the task of estimating the pseudo inverse $X^+$ based on the pseudo inverse of a sampled subset of columns (of size at least the number of rows). We show that this is possible if the subset of columns is chosen proportional to the squared volume spanned by the rows of the chosen submatrix (ie, volume sampling). The resulting estimator is unbiased and surprisingly the covariance of the estimator also has a closed form: It equals a specific factor times $X^+X^{+\top}$. Pseudo inverse plays an important part in solving the linear least squares problem, where we try to predict a label for each column of $X$. We assume labels are expensive and we are only given the labels for the small subset of columns we sample from $X$. Using our methods we show that the weight vector of the solution for the sub problem is an unbiased estimator of the optimal solution for the whole problem based on all column labels. We believe that these new formulas establish a fundamental connection between linear least squares and volume sampling. We use our methods to obtain an algorithm for volume sampling that is faster than state-of-the-art and for obtaining bounds for the total loss of the estimated least-squares solution on all labeled columns.

paragraphs: When labels are expensive, linear regression may need to learn from only a subset of available examples. This paper studies how to select that subset so that its solution is unbiased for the solution using every label. The setup uses a full-rank matrix with more columns than rows and samples at least as many columns as there are rows.

The sampling rule assigns probability in proportion to the squared volume spanned by the selected submatrix's rows. Under this volume-sampling rule, the authors construct an unbiased estimator of the full matrix's pseudoinverse from the sampled subset. They also derive a closed-form covariance, providing an exact characterization of the estimator's variability.

For least-squares regression, the subset's fitted weight vector is consequently an unbiased estimator of the full-data optimum. This means agreement on average over sampled subsets, while individual estimates can vary. The authors also derive total-loss bounds and use their results to develop a volume-sampling algorithm faster than the state of the art.
summary.tldr: Volume sampling yields unbiased pseudoinverse and least-squares estimates from subsets, together with covariance formulas and loss bounds.

title: Unbiased estimates for linear regression via volume sampling

abstract: In this paper, we introduce and analyze Discriminative State-Space Models for forecasting non-stationary time series. We provide data-dependent generalization guarantees for learning these models based on the recently introduced notion of discrepancy. We provide an in-depth analysis of the complexity of such models. Finally, we also study the generalization guarantees for several structural risk minimization approaches to this problem and provide an efficient implementation for one of them which is based on a convex objective.

Finally, we also study the generalization guarantees for several structural risk minimization approaches to this problem and provide an efficient implementation for one of them which is based on a convex objective.

paragraphs: This paper introduces discriminative state-space models for forecasting time series whose statistical behavior changes over time. The focus is on learning forecasts in a non-stationary setting, where performance on previously observed data does not by itself settle how well a model will predict later observations.

The authors derive data-dependent generalization guarantees using a notion called discrepancy. These guarantees connect the analysis to properties of the data, rather than treating forecasting performance solely as a property of the model class. They also examine model complexity in depth, making the capacity of the proposed models an explicit part of the learning analysis.

The paper then studies several structural risk minimization approaches, which organize model selection around the balance between fitting data and controlling complexity. It establishes generalization guarantees for these approaches and provides an efficient implementation of one based on a convex objective. The contribution brings together a forecasting model family, a theory of generalization under changing data, and a tractable learning procedure.
summary.tldr: Discriminative state-space models pair non-stationary forecasting with data-dependent generalization analysis and a convex learning implementation.

title: Discriminative State Space Models

abstract: Large-scale Gaussian process inference has long faced practical challenges due to time and space complexity that is superlinear in dataset size. While sparse variational Gaussian process models are capable of learning from large-scale data, standard strategies for sparsifying the model can prevent the approximation of complex functions. In this work, we propose a novel variational Gaussian process model that decouples the representation of mean and covariance functions in reproducing kernel Hilbert space. We show that this new parametrization generalizes previous models. Furthermore, it yields a variational inference problem that can be solved by stochastic gradient ascent with time and space complexity that is only linear in the number of mean function parameters, regardless of the choice of kernels, likelihoods, and inducing points. This strategy makes the adoption of large-scale expressive Gaussian process models possible. We run several experiments on regression tasks and show that this decoupled approach greatly outperforms previous sparse variational Gaussian process inference procedures.

Sparse variational methods help, but standard sparsification can restrict the complexity of functions they approximate. This paper seeks a more expressive approximation without imposing the same computational burden on every part of the model.

The proposed model decouples the representations of the mean and covariance functions in a reproducing kernel Hilbert space. This new parameterization generalizes earlier models and supports stochastic gradient ascent. Its time and space complexity are linear in the number of mean-function parameters, regardless of the chosen kernels, likelihoods, and inducing points.

The linearity claim concerns the mean representation’s parameter count, making it possible to expand that representation more affordably. This is the route by which the authors argue for expressive Gaussian process models at larger scales. Regression experiments report substantial improvements over previous sparse variational inference procedures, supporting the usefulness of separating the mean and covariance representations.
summary.tldr: Decoupling Gaussian process mean and covariance representations enables inference that scales linearly with mean parameters and improves reported regression performance.

title: Variational Inference for Gaussian Process Models with Linear Complexity

abstract: Deep latent variable models (DLVMs) combine the approximation abilities of deep neural networks and the statistical foundations of generative models. Variational methods are commonly used for inference; however, the exact likelihood of these models has been largely overlooked. The purpose of this work is to study the general properties of this quantity and to show how they can be leveraged in practice. We focus on important inferential problems that rely on the likelihood: estimation and missing data imputation. First, we investigate maximum likelihood estimation for DLVMs: in particular, we show that most unconstrained models used for continuous data have an unbounded likelihood function. This problematic behaviour is demonstrated to be a source of mode collapse. We also show how to ensure the existence of maximum likelihood estimates, and draw useful connections with nonparametric mixture models. Finally, we describe an algorithm for missing data imputation using the exact conditional likelihood of a DLVM. On several data sets, our algorithm consistently and significantly outperforms the usual imputation scheme used for DLVMs.

paragraphs: Deep latent variable models combine neural networks with probabilistic generative modeling. Although variational methods commonly handle inference, this paper investigates the models' exact likelihood and its practical consequences. It focuses on two tasks where likelihood is central: estimating model parameters and filling in missing data.

The authors show that most unconstrained models used for continuous data have an unbounded likelihood. This means the likelihood can increase without reaching a finite maximum, making maximum likelihood estimation problematic. They demonstrate that this behavior can cause mode collapse. They also show how to ensure that maximum likelihood estimates exist and connect the analysis to nonparametric mixture models.

For missing-data imputation, the paper introduces an algorithm based on a model's exact conditional likelihood. Across several datasets, it consistently and significantly outperforms the usual imputation procedure used for these models. The findings give exact likelihood two practical roles: diagnosing a source of failure in parameter estimation and supporting improved reconstruction of missing values. The unboundedness result specifically concerns the unconstrained continuous-data models described by the authors.
summary.tldr: Studying exact likelihood reveals a source of mode collapse in deep latent models and yields an improved missing-data imputation method.

title: Leveraging the Exact Likelihood of Deep Latent Variable Models

abstract: We consider a game-theoretical multi-agent learning problem where the feedback information can be lost during the learning process and rewards are given by a broad class of games known as variationally stable games. We propose a simple variant of the classical online gradient descent algorithm, called reweighted online gradient descent (ROGD) and show that in variationally stable games, if each agent adopts ROGD, then almost sure convergence to the set of Nash equilibria is guaranteed, even when the feedback loss is asynchronous and arbitrarily corrrelated among agents. We then extend the framework to deal with unknown feedback loss probabilities by using an estimator (constructed from past data) in its replacement. Finally, we further extend the framework to accomodate both asynchronous loss and stochastic rewards and establish that multi-agent ROGD learning still converges to the set of Nash equilibria in such settings. Together, these results contribute to the broad lanscape of multi-agent online learning by significantly relaxing the feedback information that is required to achieve desirable outcomes.

paragraphs: In multi-agent learning, agents may lose some of the feedback they need to update their decisions. This paper studies whether learning can still reach equilibrium under such losses. It focuses on variationally stable games and proposes reweighted online gradient descent, a modification of the classical online gradient descent algorithm.

The authors prove that if every agent uses the proposed method in this class of games, learning converges almost surely to the set of Nash equilibria. Feedback losses may occur asynchronously and may be arbitrarily correlated across agents. The result therefore accommodates irregular and interdependent missing feedback within the stated game setting.

The framework is extended to situations where feedback-loss probabilities are unknown, using estimates constructed from past observations. Another extension combines asynchronous loss with stochastic rewards and still establishes convergence to the equilibrium set. These results broaden the feedback conditions under which multi-agent learning has a convergence guarantee, while retaining variational stability and adoption of the proposed learning rule as key parts of the setting.
summary.tldr: Reweighted online gradient descent converges to Nash equilibria in variationally stable games despite asynchronous and correlated feedback loss.

title: Learning in Games with Lossy Feedback

abstract: To convert the input into binary code, hashing algorithm has been widely used for approximate nearest neighbor search on large-scale image sets due to its computation and storage efficiency. Deep hashing further improves the retrieval quality by combining the hash coding with deep neural network. However, a major difficulty in deep hashing lies in the discrete constraints imposed on the network output, which generally makes the optimization NP hard. In this work, we adopt the greedy principle to tackle this NP hard problem by iteratively updating the network toward the probable optimal discrete solution in each iteration. A hash coding layer is designed to implement our approach which strictly uses the sign function in forward propagation to maintain the discrete constraints, while in back propagation the gradients are transmitted intactly to the front layer to avoid the vanishing gradients. In addition to the theoretical derivation, we provide a new perspective to visualize and understand the effectiveness and efficiency of our algorithm. Experiments on benchmark datasets show that our scheme outperforms state-of-the-art hashing methods in both supervised and unsupervised tasks.

Deep hashing learns these codes with neural networks, but requiring binary outputs makes optimization difficult. The paper describes the resulting discrete optimization problem as generally NP-hard and proposes a greedy approach to updating the network.

Its hash-coding layer treats forward and backward computation differently. During the forward pass, a sign function produces genuinely discrete codes. During backpropagation, gradients pass unchanged to the preceding layer to avoid vanishing gradients at this step. Each update aims toward a plausible optimal discrete solution, without claiming to solve the NP-hard problem exactly.

The authors provide a theoretical derivation and a visualization perspective for understanding the method's effectiveness and efficiency. Benchmark experiments show better performance than the compared state-of-the-art hashing methods in both supervised and unsupervised tasks. The practical contribution is a training mechanism that preserves binary outputs while still supplying useful gradients to the network.
summary.tldr: Greedy Hash trains binary image codes using a sign function forward pass and unchanged gradient transmission backward.

title: Greedy Hash: Towards Fast Optimization for Accurate Hash Coding in CNN

abstract: We derive an online learning algorithm with improved regret guarantees for ``easy'' loss sequences. We consider two types of ``easiness'': (a) stochastic loss sequences and (b) adversarial loss sequences with small effective range of the losses. While a number of algorithms have been proposed for exploiting small effective range in the full information setting, Gerchinovitz and Lattimore [2016] have shown the impossibility of regret scaling with the effective range of the losses in the bandit setting. We show that just one additional observation per round is sufficient to circumvent the impossibility result. The proposed Second Order Difference Adjustments (SODA) algorithm requires no prior knowledge of the effective range of the losses, $\varepsilon$, and achieves an $O(\varepsilon \sqrt{KT \ln K}) + \tilde{O}(\varepsilon K \sqrt[4]{T})$ expected regret guarantee, where $T$ is the time horizon and $K$ is the number of actions. The scaling with the effective loss range is achieved under significantly weaker assumptions than those made by Cesa-Bianchi and Shamir [2018] in an earlier attempt to circumvent the impossibility result. We also provide a regret lower bound of $\Omega(\varepsilon\sqrt{T K})$, which almost matches the upper bound. In addition, we show that in the stochastic setting SODA achieves an $O\left(\sum_{a:\Delta_a>0} \frac{K\varepsilon^2}{\Delta_a}\right)$ pseudo-regret bound that holds simultaneously with the adversarial regret guarantee. In other words, SODA is safe against an unrestricted oblivious adversary and provides improved regret guarantees for at least two different types of ``easiness'' simultaneously.

paragraphs: Online learning involves choosing actions repeatedly while learning from their losses. Some sequences are easier to learn from than others: losses may follow a stable stochastic process, or the differences between available actions may remain small. This paper asks how a learner with limited observations can benefit from both kinds of favorable structure.

The authors introduce Second Order Difference Adjustments, or SODA. Its key resource is one additional observation per round beyond standard bandit feedback. They prove that this extra observation is sufficient to overcome an impossibility result that prevents ordinary bandit algorithms from obtaining regret proportional to the effective loss range. SODA does not need that range supplied beforehand.

The resulting guarantees combine protection against an unrestricted oblivious adversary with improved bounds for stochastic losses and adversarial losses with small effective range. A lower bound almost matches the adversarial upper bound. Together, these results show that a modest increase in feedback can enable adaptation to easier data without requiring the learner to choose between the two guarantees.
summary.tldr: SODA uses one extra observation per round to improve regret on two kinds of easy data while retaining an adversarial guarantee.

title: Adaptation to Easy Data in Prediction with Limited Advice

abstract: We present a new approach to the problems of evaluating and learning personalized decision policies from observational data of past contexts, decisions, and outcomes. Only the outcome of the enacted decision is available and the historical policy is unknown. These problems arise in personalized medicine using electronic health records and in internet advertising. Existing approaches use inverse propensity weighting (or, doubly robust versions) to make historical outcome (or, residual) data look like it were generated by a new policy being evaluated or learned. But this relies on a plug-in approach that rejects data points with a decision that disagrees with the new policy, leading to high variance estimates and ineffective learning. We propose a new, balance-based approach that too makes the data look like the new policy but does so directly by finding weights that optimize for balance between the weighted data and the target policy in the given, finite sample, which is equivalent to minimizing worst-case or posterior conditional mean square error. Our policy learner proceeds as a two-level optimization problem over policies and weights. We demonstrate that this approach markedly outperforms existing ones both in evaluation and learning, which is unsurprising given the wider support of balance-based weights. We establish extensive theoretical consistency guarantees and regret bounds that support this empirical success.

paragraphs: Learning personalized decisions from historical records is difficult because each record reveals only the outcome of the action actually taken. The historical decision policy may also be unknown. This paper studies both estimating how a proposed policy would perform and learning a policy from such observational data.

Existing weighting approaches attempt to make past observations resemble data generated by the proposed policy, but the paper identifies high variance associated with rejecting observations whose actions disagree with it. The proposed method instead chooses weights directly to balance the available finite sample against the target policy. The authors connect this balancing objective to minimizing worst-case or posterior conditional mean squared error.

Policy learning then becomes a two-level optimization over decision policies and data weights. The authors report substantial empirical improvements in both evaluation and learning, and provide consistency guarantees and regret bounds. The central contribution is to optimize the usefulness of the observed sample directly: balance becomes the mechanism for estimating policy outcomes and guiding which policy to choose.
summary.tldr: Directly optimizing data-balancing weights improves the evaluation and learning of personalized policies from observational records.

title: Balanced Policy Evaluation and Learning

abstract: We present a novel and unified deep learning framework which is capable of learning domain-invariant representation from data across multiple domains. Realized by adversarial training with additional ability to exploit domain-specific information, the proposed network is able to perform continuous cross-domain image translation and manipulation, and produces desirable output images accordingly. In addition, the resulting feature representation exhibits superior performance of unsupervised domain adaptation, which also verifies the effectiveness of the proposed model in learning disentangled features for describing cross-domain data.

Realized by adversarial training with additional ability to exploit domain-specific information, the proposed network is able to perform continuous cross-domain image translation and manipulation, and produces desirable output images accordingly. In addition, the resulting feature representation exhibits superior performance of unsupervised domain adaptation, which also verifies the effectiveness of the proposed model in learning disentangled features for describing cross-domain data.

paragraphs: Images from different domains contain both shared information and domain-specific variation. This paper aims to learn a representation that captures what remains consistent across domains while still using information unique to each domain. The intended payoff is one framework that supports several cross-domain image tasks.

The proposed deep network uses adversarial training to learn domain-invariant representations and includes a mechanism for exploiting domain-specific information. It can perform continuous image translation and manipulation across multiple domains, producing outputs that reflect the requested changes.

The authors also evaluate the learned features for unsupervised domain adaptation and report superior performance, which they interpret as evidence of effective feature disentanglement. The abstract does not name datasets, metrics, or comparison methods, so the strength of that evidence cannot be quantified here. The work’s scope is a unified representation-learning approach evaluated through both image generation and transfer of learned features.
summary.tldr: A shared disentangled representation supports image translation, manipulation, and domain adaptation.

title: A Unified Feature Disentangler for Multi-Domain Image Translation and Manipulation

abstract: We present the very first robust Bayesian Online Changepoint Detection algorithm through General Bayesian Inference (GBI) with $\beta$-divergences. The resulting inference procedure is doubly robust for both the predictive and the changepoint (CP) posterior, with linear time and constant space complexity. We provide a construction for exponential models and demonstrate it on the Bayesian Linear Regression model. In so doing, we make two additional contributions: Firstly, we make GBI scalable using Structural Variational approximations that are exact as $\beta \to 0$. Secondly, we give a principled way of choosing the divergence parameter $\beta$ by minimizing expected predictive loss on-line. Reducing False Discovery Rates of \CPs from up to 99\% to 0\% on real world data, this offers the state of the art.

paragraphs: Streaming inference must update predictions as observations arrive and identify when the process generating them changes. This paper introduces a robust Bayesian online changepoint detector using General Bayesian Inference with beta-divergences. Its robustness covers both the predictive distribution and the posterior over changepoints, which is the sense in which the procedure is doubly robust.

The authors provide a construction for exponential models and demonstrate it with Bayesian linear regression. To make the inference scalable, they use structural variational approximations that become exact as beta approaches zero. They also choose beta online by minimizing expected predictive loss, giving the divergence parameter a data-guided selection principle.

The resulting procedure has linear time and constant space complexity. On the reported real-world data, changepoint false discovery rates fall from values as high as 99% to 0%. This empirical result concerns avoiding false declarations of change in those evaluations. Alongside the computational properties, it supports robust treatment of both predictions and change decisions within a single streaming inference procedure.
summary.tldr: Beta-divergence Bayesian inference robustifies streaming predictions and changepoint detection, sharply reducing false changepoint discoveries in reported data.

title: Doubly Robust Bayesian Inference for Non-Stationary Streaming Data with $\beta$-Divergences

abstract: The determinantal point process (DPP) is an elegant probabilistic model of repulsion with applications in various machine learning tasks including summarization and search. However, the maximum a posteriori (MAP) inference for DPP which plays an important role in many applications is NP-hard, and even the popular greedy algorithm can still be too computationally expensive to be used in large-scale real-time scenarios. To overcome the computational challenge, in this paper, we propose a novel algorithm to greatly accelerate the greedy MAP inference for DPP. In addition, our algorithm also adapts to scenarios where the repulsion is only required among nearby few items in the result sequence. We apply the proposed algorithm to generate relevant and diverse recommendations. Experimental results show that our proposed algorithm is significantly faster than state-of-the-art competitors, and provides a better relevance-diversity trade-off on several public datasets, which is also confirmed in an online A/B test.

paragraphs: A determinantal point process models repulsion among selected items, making it useful when a result set should contain variety. In recommendation, that means balancing relevant items with a desire to avoid excessive similarity. Finding the most probable set under this model is NP-hard, and even the commonly used greedy procedure can be too slow for large-scale, real-time applications.

The authors introduce an algorithm that substantially accelerates greedy MAP inference. The contribution speeds up this approximate selection procedure; it does not establish an efficient exact solution to the NP-hard problem. The algorithm also accommodates sequences where repulsion is needed only among a few nearby items, allowing diversity requirements to be applied locally within the output.

Applied to recommendation, the method is significantly faster than the compared state-of-the-art competitors and produces a better relevance-diversity trade-off on several public datasets. An online A/B test also supports the reported benefits. The findings connect a computational improvement in probabilistic selection with the practical quality of the recommendations it produces.
summary.tldr: An accelerated greedy DPP inference algorithm produces relevant, diverse recommendations faster, with benefits supported by public datasets and an online A/B test.

title: Fast Greedy MAP Inference for Determinantal Point Process to Improve Recommendation Diversity

abstract: Differential privacy has emerged as the main definition for private data analysis and machine learning. The global model of differential privacy, which assumes that users trust the data collector, provides strong privacy guarantees and introduces small errors in the output. In contrast, applications of differential privacy in commercial systems by Apple, Google, and Microsoft, use the local model. Here, users do not trust the data collector, and hence randomize their data before sending it to the data collector. Unfortunately, local model is too strong for several important applications and hence is limited in its applicability. In this work, we propose a framework based on trusted processors and a new definition of differential privacy called Oblivious Differential Privacy, which combines the best of both local and global models. The algorithms we design in this framework show interesting interplay of ideas from the streaming algorithms, oblivious algorithms, and differential privacy.

paragraphs: Private data analysis faces a practical question: who must users trust with their information? In the global model of differential privacy, users trust the collector, allowing strong privacy guarantees with relatively small output errors. In the local model, users randomize their information before sharing it because they do not trust that collector.

The paper argues that the local model's requirements restrict its usefulness for several important applications. It proposes a framework based on trusted processors and introduces a privacy definition called Oblivious Differential Privacy. The intended benefit is to combine desirable properties of the global and local models by making trusted processing part of the design.

The contribution also includes algorithms that bring together ideas from streaming computation, oblivious algorithms, and differential privacy. This makes the work an algorithmic framework as well as a proposed privacy definition. Its central significance is a different arrangement of trust for private analysis: the stated framework relies on trusted processors to pursue the benefits of both established models.
summary.tldr: The paper introduces Oblivious Differential Privacy and a trusted-processor framework intended to combine benefits of global and local privacy models.

title: An Algorithmic Framework For Differentially Private Data Analysis on Trusted Processors

abstract: Mode connectivity is a surprising phenomenon in the loss landscape of deep nets. Optima---at least those discovered by gradient-based optimization---turn out to be connected by simple paths on which the loss function is almost constant. Often, these paths can be chosen to be piece-wise linear, with as few as two segments. We give mathematical explanations for this phenomenon, assuming generic properties (such as dropout stability and noise stability) of well-trained deep nets, which have previously been identified as part of understanding the generalization properties of deep nets. Our explanation holds for realistic multilayer nets, and experiments are presented to verify the theory.

Often, these paths can be chosen to be piece-wise linear, with as few as two segments. paragraphs: Training a deep network can produce different parameter settings with similarly low loss. Mode connectivity describes the observation that these solutions, at least those found by gradient-based training, can often be joined by simple paths along which loss barely changes. Sometimes a path needs only two straight segments, despite the complexity of the network.

This paper develops mathematical explanations for that behavior in realistic multilayer networks. The explanation assumes properties of well-trained networks such as dropout stability and noise stability. These properties describe forms of robustness to perturbations and had also been identified in work on why trained networks generalize beyond their training examples.

The resulting account connects the geometry of low-loss solutions with stability properties of the networks themselves. It explains how different successful parameter settings can belong to connected regions without requiring a large increase in loss along the connecting route. Experiments are presented to check the theory. The explanation remains conditional on the stated stability assumptions; it is not a claim that every pair of network optima admits such a path.
summary.tldr: The paper explains low-loss paths between trained multilayer networks under stability assumptions and presents experiments checking the theory.

title: Explaining Landscape Connectivity of Low-cost Solutions for Multilayer Nets

abstract: Many recent studies have employed task-based modeling with recurrent neural networks (RNNs) to infer the computational function of different brain regions. These models are often assessed by quantitatively comparing the low-dimensional neural dynamics of the model and the brain, for example using canonical correlation analysis (CCA). However, the nature of the detailed neurobiological inferences one can draw from such efforts remains elusive. For example, to what extent does training neural networks to solve simple tasks, prevalent in neuroscientific studies, uniquely determine the low-dimensional dynamics independent of neural architectures? Or alternatively, are the learned dynamics highly sensitive to different neural architectures? Knowing the answer to these questions has strong implications on whether and how to use task-based RNN modeling to understand brain dynamics. To address these foundational questions, we study populations of thousands of networks of commonly used RNN architectures trained to solve neuroscientifically motivated tasks and characterize their low-dimensional dynamics via CCA and nonlinear dynamical systems analysis. We find the geometry of the dynamics can be highly sensitive to different network architectures, and further find striking dissociations between geometric similarity as measured by CCA and network function, yielding a cautionary tale. Moreover, we find that while the geometry of neural dynamics can vary greatly across architectures, the underlying computational scaffold: the topological structure of fixed points, transitions between them, limit cycles, and linearized dynamics, often appears {\it universal} across all architectures. Overall, this analysis of universality and individuality across large populations of RNNs provides a much needed foundation for interpreting quantitative measures of dynamical similarity between RNN and brain dynamics.

paragraphs: Recurrent networks trained on neuroscience-inspired tasks are often compared with brain activity to infer how brain regions compute. This paper asks what such comparisons can establish. In particular, it examines whether learning the same task produces similar low-dimensional dynamics across network architectures, or whether architecture strongly shapes the resulting patterns.

The authors train thousands of recurrent networks and analyze their dynamics using canonical correlation analysis and nonlinear dynamical systems methods. They find that the geometry of the dynamics can depend strongly on architecture. They also observe substantial mismatches between geometric similarity measured by canonical correlation analysis and similarity of network function, making that comparison an uncertain guide to computation.

At the same time, a more structural description often appears shared across architectures. Fixed points, transitions, limit cycles, and local linearized dynamics can form a common computational scaffold despite differing geometry. The findings support distinguishing geometric resemblance from underlying dynamical organization when interpreting model-to-brain comparisons, with the observed commonality described as frequent rather than an unconditional property of all networks.
summary.tldr: Recurrent networks can share underlying computational structure despite architecture-dependent dynamics and misleading geometric similarity measures.

title: Universality and individuality in neural dynamics across large populations of recurrent networks

abstract: We give a complete characterization of the sampling complexity of best Markovian arm identification in one-parameter Markovian bandit models. We derive instance specific nonasymptotic and asymptotic lower bounds which generalize those of the IID setting. We analyze the Track-and-Stop strategy, initially proposed for the IID setting, and we prove that asymptotically it is at most a factor of four apart from the lower bound. Our one-parameter Markovian bandit model is based on the notion of an exponential family of stochastic matrices for which we establish many useful properties. For the analysis of the Track-and-Stop strategy we derive a novel and optimal concentration inequality for Markov chains that may be of interest in its own right.

paragraphs: Best-arm identification asks how many observations are needed to select the best option at a specified confidence level. This paper studies a Markovian version, where observations have temporal dependence, within a one-parameter family of bandit models. Its goal is to characterize sampling complexity in that structured setting.

The authors derive lower bounds tailored to individual problem instances, both for finite samples and asymptotically. These extend corresponding bounds from independent, identically distributed observations. They also analyze Track-and-Stop, a strategy originally developed for that independent setting, and prove that its asymptotic sampling complexity is within a factor of four of the lower bound.

The analysis builds on exponential families of stochastic matrices and establishes properties of those families. It additionally produces a new optimal concentration inequality for Markov chains. The results connect an unavoidable sampling requirement with an achievable strategy, while the factor-four statement makes clear that the analyzed strategy is not shown to match the lower bound exactly.
summary.tldr: For one-parameter Markovian bandits, the paper derives sampling lower bounds and places Track-and-Stop within a factor of four asymptotically.

title: Optimal Best Markovian Arm Identification with Fixed Confidence

abstract: We present VILLA, the first known effort on large-scale adversarial training for vision-and-language (V+L) representation learning. VILLA consists of two training stages: (i) task-agnostic adversarial pre-training; followed by (ii) task-specific adversarial finetuning. Instead of adding adversarial perturbations on image pixels and textual tokens, we propose to perform adversarial training in the embedding space of each modality. To enable large-scale training, we adopt the ``free'' adversarial training strategy, and combine it with KL-divergence-based regularization to promote higher invariance in the embedding space. We apply VILLA to current best-performing V+L models, and achieve new state of the art on a wide range of tasks, including Visual Question Answering, Visual Commonsense Reasoning, Image-Text Retrieval, Referring Expression Comprehension, Visual Entailment, and NLVR2.

paragraphs: Vision-and-language models learn representations that connect images with text. This paper introduces VILLA, a large-scale adversarial training approach for those representations. Training has two stages: task-agnostic adversarial pretraining, followed by adversarial finetuning for a specific task. This brings the same broad training idea into both general representation learning and downstream adaptation.

VILLA applies adversarial perturbations to the embedding space of each modality. The modifications therefore act on internal representations of images and text. To make the approach practical at scale, the authors adopt a strategy called free adversarial training and combine it with KL-divergence regularization, which encourages greater invariance in the embedding space.

The authors apply VILLA to strong existing vision-and-language models and report new state-of-the-art results across several tasks. These include visual question answering, visual commonsense reasoning, image-text retrieval, referring expression comprehension, visual entailment, and NLVR2. The breadth of the reported improvements supports the usefulness of embedding-space adversarial training across multiple forms of combined visual and textual understanding.
summary.tldr: VILLA applies adversarial training to image and text embeddings during pretraining and finetuning, improving results across vision-and-language tasks.

title: Large-Scale Adversarial Training for Vision-and-Language Representation Learning

abstract: Adversarial training (AT) is among the most effective techniques to improve model robustness by augmenting training data with adversarial examples. However, most existing AT methods adopt a specific attack to craft adversarial examples, leading to the unreliable robustness against other unseen attacks. Besides, a single attack algorithm could be insufficient to explore the space of perturbations. In this paper, we introduce adversarial distributional training (ADT), a novel framework for learning robust models. ADT is formulated as a minimax optimization problem, where the inner maximization aims to learn an adversarial distribution to characterize the potential adversarial examples around a natural one under an entropic regularizer, and the outer minimization aims to train robust models by minimizing the expected loss over the worst-case adversarial distributions. Through a theoretical analysis, we develop a general algorithm for solving ADT, and present three approaches for parameterizing the adversarial distributions, ranging from the typical Gaussian distributions to the flexible implicit ones. Empirical results on several benchmarks validate the effectiveness of ADT compared with the state-of-the-art AT methods.

Besides, a single attack algorithm could be insufficient to explore the space of perturbations. In this paper, we introduce adversarial distributional training (ADT), a novel framework for learning robust models. ADT is formulated as a minimax optimization problem, where the inner maximization aims to learn an adversarial distribution to characterize the potential adversarial examples around a natural one under an entropic regularizer, and the outer minimization aims to train robust models by minimizing the expected loss over the worst-case adversarial distributions. Through a theoretical analysis, we develop a general algorithm for solving ADT, and present three approaches for parameterizing the adversarial distributions, ranging from the typical Gaussian distributions to the flexible implicit ones. Empirical results on several benchmarks validate the effectiveness of ADT compared with the state-of-the-art AT methods.

paragraphs: Adversarial training strengthens a model by training it on deliberately altered examples. The paper identifies a weakness in approaches that generate these examples with one particular attack: they may explore too little of the possible perturbation space, leaving robustness against unfamiliar attacks unreliable. Its proposed alternative learns distributions of adversarial examples around each natural input.

Adversarial distributional training organizes learning as a minimax problem. An inner optimization searches for a distribution of challenging perturbations, subject to an entropy regularizer. An outer optimization updates the model to reduce its expected loss under the worst distributions found. This makes a distribution of possible adversarial inputs the object of training, broadening the approach beyond individual examples crafted by a particular attack.

The authors develop a general solution algorithm through theoretical analysis and describe three ways to represent the adversarial distributions, from Gaussian distributions to flexible implicit representations. Experiments across several benchmarks support the framework's effectiveness relative to leading adversarial training methods. These findings provide empirical support for learning adversarial distributions as a route to stronger robustness.
summary.tldr: Adversarial distributional training learns distributions of challenging perturbations and trains models against their expected loss.

title: Adversarial Distributional Training for Robust Deep Learning

abstract: We explore the phase diagram of approximation rates for deep neural networks and prove several new theoretical results. In particular, we generalize the existing result on the existence of deep discontinuous phase in ReLU networks to functional classes of arbitrary positive smoothness, and identify the boundary between the feasible and infeasible rates. Moreover, we show that all networks with a piecewise polynomial activation function have the same phase diagram. Next, we demonstrate that standard fully-connected architectures with a fixed width independent of smoothness can adapt to smoothness and achieve almost optimal rates. Finally, we consider deep networks with periodic activations ("deep Fourier expansion") and prove that they have very fast, nearly exponential approximation rates, thanks to the emerging capability of the network to implement efficient lookup operations.

paragraphs: This paper studies theoretical approximation rates: how effectively deep neural networks can represent functions as their resources change. Its phase diagram organizes which rates are achievable and which are impossible. The analysis considers how these possibilities relate to function smoothness, network architecture, and the choice of activation function.

For ReLU networks, the authors extend the previously established deep discontinuous phase to function classes with any positive smoothness and identify the boundary between feasible and infeasible rates. They also show that networks with piecewise polynomial activations share the same phase diagram. Standard fully connected architectures with a fixed width independent of smoothness can adapt to smoothness and obtain almost optimal rates.

The paper then examines networks with periodic activations, described as deep Fourier expansions. These achieve nearly exponential approximation rates through an ability to implement efficient lookup operations. Together, the results characterize representational possibilities for several activation families and show how architectural choices can support strong approximation guarantees across function classes.
summary.tldr: The paper maps achievable neural-network approximation rates and proves nearly exponential rates for deep networks with periodic activations.

title: The phase diagram of approximation rates for deep neural networks

abstract: Physical phenomena in the real world are often described by energy-based modeling theories, such as Hamiltonian mechanics or the Landau theory, which yield various physical laws. Recent developments in neural networks have enabled the mimicking of the energy conservation law by learning the underlying continuous-time differential equations. However, this may not be possible in discrete time, which is often the case in practical learning and computation. Moreover, other physical laws have been overlooked in the previous neural network models. In this study, we propose a deep energy-based physical model that admits a specific differential geometric structure. From this structure, the conservation or dissipation law of energy and the mass conservation law follow naturally. To ensure the energetic behavior in discrete time, we also propose an automatic discrete differentiation algorithm that enables neural networks to employ the discrete gradient method.

paragraphs: Learning physical motion involves more than matching observed changes: the resulting model may also need to respect laws governing energy and mass. Earlier neural approaches learned continuous-time equations that mimic energy conservation. This paper addresses the difficulty that practical computations advance through discrete time steps, where the desired energy behavior may no longer hold.

This makes the physical laws consequences of the model's mathematical construction rather than separate behaviors that it merely attempts to reproduce from observations.

The contribution therefore addresses both what physical relationships the learned model represents and how those relationships are maintained when the model is evaluated computationally.
summary.tldr: A structured neural physics model and discrete differentiation algorithm preserve specified physical laws during discrete-time computation.

title: Deep Energy-based Modeling of Discrete-Time Physics

abstract: We determine statistical and computational limits for estimation of a rank-one matrix (the spike) corrupted by an additive gaussian noise matrix, in a sparse limit, where the underlying hidden vector (that constructs the rank-one matrix) has a number of non-zero components that scales sub-linearly with the total dimension of the vector, and the signal-to-noise ratio tends to infinity at an appropriate speed. We prove explicit low-dimensional variational formulas for the asymptotic mutual information between the spike and the observed noisy matrix and analyze the approximate message passing algorithm in the sparse regime. For Bernoulli and Bernoulli-Rademacher distributed vectors, and when the sparsity and signal strength satisfy an appropriate scaling relation, we find all-or-nothing phase transitions for the asymptotic minimum and algorithmic mean-square-errors. These jump from their maximum possible value to zero, at well defined signal-to-noise thresholds whose asymptotic values we determine exactly. In the asymptotic regime the statistical-to-algorithmic gap diverges indicating that sparse recovery is hard for approximate message passing.

paragraphs: The paper studies recovery of a rank-one signal matrix hidden inside additive Gaussian noise. The signal is constructed from a sparse vector whose nonzero entries grow more slowly in number than its total dimension. The analysis follows an asymptotic regime in which dimension grows and the signal-to-noise ratio also increases at an appropriate rate.

The authors derive explicit low-dimensional variational formulas for the mutual information between the signal and the observed matrix. They also analyze approximate message passing, an algorithm for estimating the hidden signal. For Bernoulli and Bernoulli-Rademacher vectors under suitable sparsity and signal scaling, both optimal and algorithmic mean-square errors exhibit abrupt transitions from their maximum values to zero.

The thresholds for these transitions are determined exactly in the asymptotic regime. The gap between statistically possible recovery and recovery by approximate message passing diverges there. This shows a growing separation between available information and what this algorithm can exploit, establishing difficulty for approximate message passing without making the same claim about every possible algorithm.
summary.tldr: Under specified sparse asymptotic conditions, signal recovery has sharp thresholds and a diverging gap between optimal estimation and approximate message passing.

title: All-or-nothing statistical and computational phase transitions in sparse spiked matrix estimation

abstract: Invariances to translations have imbued convolutional neural networks with powerful generalization properties. However, we often do not know a priori what invariances are present in the data, or to what extent a model should be invariant to a given augmentation. We show how to learn invariances by parameterizing a distribution over augmentations and optimizing the training loss simultaneously with respect to the network parameters and augmentation parameters. With this simple procedure we can recover the correct set and extent of invariances on image classification, regression, segmentation, and molecular property prediction from a large space of augmentations, on training data alone. We show our approach is competitive with methods that are specialized to each task with the appropriate hard-coded invariances, without providing any prior knowledge of which invariance is needed.

paragraphs: An invariance describes a transformation that should leave a model's relevant prediction unchanged. Such structure can help generalization, but the appropriate transformations and their useful extent are not always known beforehand. This paper asks whether that choice can be learned directly from training data alongside the predictor.

The approach parameterizes a probability distribution over augmentations. Training then optimizes the same loss with respect to both the neural network's parameters and the augmentation parameters. This makes the choice and extent of augmentations adjustable during learning, rather than fixing all of those choices before fitting the model.

The authors report recovering the appropriate invariances from a large augmentation space in image classification, regression, segmentation, and molecular property prediction. They also report performance competitive with task-specific methods that have the relevant invariances built in. The findings indicate that, in these evaluated settings, training data can guide which candidate transformations the model should accommodate and by how much, without being told in advance which invariance is needed.
summary.tldr: Jointly learning augmentation distributions and network parameters recovers useful invariances from training data across several evaluated tasks.

title: Learning Invariances in Neural Networks from Training Data

abstract: Learning from label proportions (LLP) is a weakly supervised setting for classification in which unlabeled training instances are grouped into bags, and each bag is annotated with the proportion of each class occurring in that bag. Prior work on LLP has yet to establish a consistent learning procedure, nor does there exist a theoretically justified, general purpose training criterion. In this work we address these two issues by posing LLP in terms of mutual contamination models (MCMs), which have recently been applied successfully to study various other weak supervision settings. In the process, we establish several novel technical results for MCMs, including unbiased losses and generalization error bounds under non-iid sampling plans. We also point out the limitations of a common experimental setting for LLP, and propose a new one based on our MCM framework.

In the process, we establish several novel technical results for MCMs, including unbiased losses and generalization error bounds under non-iid sampling plans. paragraphs: Learning from label proportions concerns classification when individual examples have no labels, but groups of examples come with their class percentages. The challenge is to use these aggregate annotations to learn predictions for individual instances. The paper addresses the lack of a consistent learning procedure and a theoretically justified general-purpose training criterion in prior work.

The authors formulate the problem using mutual contamination models, a framework previously applied to other forms of weak supervision. This formulation supports new theoretical results, including unbiased losses and generalization-error bounds for sampling plans that are not independent and identically distributed. Those results connect the available group-level information to a justified learning objective.

The paper also identifies limitations in a commonly used experimental setting and proposes a replacement grounded in its framework. Its contribution therefore spans both learning theory and evaluation design. The new formulation provides a basis for training classifiers from aggregate labels and for studying them under sampling arrangements explicitly covered by the analysis.
summary.tldr: A mutual contamination formulation gives learning from group-level class proportions a consistent procedure, justified losses, and generalization bounds.

title: Learning from Label Proportions: A Mutual Contamination Framework

abstract: In this paper, we propose a transformer-based procedure for the efficient registration of non-rigid 3D point clouds. The proposed approach is data-driven and adopts for the first time the transformers architecture in the registration task. Our method is general and applies to different settings. Given a fixed template with some desired properties (e.g. skinning weights or other animation cues), we can register raw acquired data to it, thereby transferring all the template properties to the input geometry. Alternatively, given a pair of shapes, our method can register the first onto the second (or vice-versa), obtaining a high-quality dense correspondence between the two.In both contexts, the quality of our results enables us to target real applications such as texture transfer and shape interpolation.Furthermore, we also show that including an estimation of the underlying density of the surface eases the learning process. By exploiting the potential of this architecture, we can train our model requiring only a sparse set of ground truth correspondences ($10\sim20\%$ of the total points). The proposed model and the analysis that we perform pave the way for future exploration of transformer-based architectures for registration and matching applications. Qualitative and quantitative evaluations demonstrate that our pipeline outperforms state-of-the-art methods for deformable and unordered 3D data registration on different datasets and scenarios.

paragraphs: Non-rigid shape registration aligns three-dimensional point clouds even when the shapes deform. This paper proposes a data-driven transformer procedure for that task. It supports registering acquired geometry to a fixed template, allowing template properties such as animation cues to transfer to the input, and registering one shape directly to another.

In the second setting, the method produces dense correspondences between shapes. These matches support applications including texture transfer and shape interpolation. The authors also find that estimating the underlying surface density makes learning easier. Their model can be trained with ground-truth correspondences for only about 10%–20% of the total points, reducing the amount of correspondence supervision required.

Qualitative and quantitative evaluations report better performance than state-of-the-art methods across different datasets and registration scenarios. The findings show how a transformer architecture can support matching deformable, unordered geometric data. They also connect the learned correspondences to practical uses: transferring properties from a template or establishing relationships between two independently supplied shapes.
summary.tldr: The paper uses transformers to register deformable 3D point clouds and learn dense matches with sparse correspondence supervision.

title: Shape Registration in the Time of Transformers

abstract: Robust statistics has traditionally focused on designing estimators tolerant to a minority of contaminated data. {\em List-decodable learning}~\cite{CharikarSV17} studies the more challenging regime where only a minority $\tfrac 1 k$ fraction of the dataset, $k \geq 2$, is drawn from the distribution of interest, and no assumptions are made on the remaining data. We study the fundamental task of list-decodable mean estimation in high dimensions. Our main result is a new algorithm for bounded covariance distributions with optimal sample complexity and near-optimal error guarantee, running in {\em nearly-PCA time}. Assuming the ground truth distribution on $\mathbb{R}^d$ has identity-bounded covariance, our algorithm outputs $O(k)$ candidate means, one of which is within distance $O(\sqrt{k\log k})$ from the truth. Our algorithm runs in time $\widetilde{O}(ndk)$, where $n$ is the dataset size. This runtime nearly matches the cost of performing $k$-PCA on the data, a natural bottleneck of known algorithms for (very) special cases of our problem, such as clustering well-separated mixtures. Prior to our work, the fastest runtimes were $\widetilde{O}(n^2 d k^2)$~\cite{DiakonikolasKK20}, and $\widetilde{O}(nd k^C)$ \cite{CherapanamjeriMY20} for an unspecified constant $C \geq 6$. Our approach builds on a novel soft downweighting method we term SIFT, arguably the simplest known polynomial-time mean estimator in the list-decodable setting. To develop our fast algorithms, we boost the computational cost of SIFT via a careful ``win-win-win'' analysis of an approximate Ky Fan matrix multiplicative weights procedure we develop, which may be of independent interest.

This paper studies the case where only a 1/k fraction of the data comes from the distribution of interest, with k at least two. The goal is to return a short list of candidate means containing at least one accurate estimate.

An approximate Ky Fan matrix multiplicative weights procedure and its analysis enable the faster algorithm. The result substantially improves the dependence on dataset size or contamination level relative to the prior runtimes stated in the abstract, making strong statistical guarantees computationally cheaper.
summary.tldr: The algorithm estimates a short list containing an accurate mean from heavily contaminated data in nearly k-PCA time under a bounded-covariance assumption.

title: List-Decodable Mean Estimation in Nearly-PCA Time

abstract: Approximate inference in Bayesian deep networks exhibits a dilemma of how to yield high fidelity posterior approximations while maintaining computational efficiency and scalability. We tackle this challenge by introducing a novel variational structured approximation inspired by the Bayesian interpretation of Dropout regularization. Concretely, we focus on the inflexibility of the factorized structure in Dropout posterior and then propose an improved method called Variational Structured Dropout (VSD). VSD employs an orthogonal transformation to learn a structured representation on the variational Gaussian noise with plausible complexity, and consequently induces statistical dependencies in the approximate posterior. Theoretically, VSD successfully addresses the pathologies of previous Variational Dropout methods and thus offers a standard Bayesian justification. We further show that VSD induces an adaptive regularization term with several desirable properties which contribute to better generalization. Finally, we conduct extensive experiments on standard benchmarks to demonstrate the effectiveness of VSD over state-of-the-art variational methods on predictive accuracy, uncertainty estimation, and out-of-distribution detection.

This paper addresses the tension between making those approximations expressive and keeping inference computationally manageable. It focuses on the restrictive factorized structure of dropout-based posterior approximations, which limits the statistical dependencies they can represent.

Together, the theory and experiments support adding structure to the approximation as a way to improve both predictions and the uncertainty information accompanying them.
summary.tldr: Variational Structured Dropout learns dependencies in Bayesian posterior approximations, improving prediction and uncertainty-related performance on standard benchmarks.

title: Structured Dropout Variational Inference for Bayesian Neural Networks

abstract: Humans are able to rapidly understand scenes by utilizing concepts extracted from prior experience. Such concepts are diverse, and include global scene descriptors, such as the weather or lighting, as well as local scene descriptors, such as the color or size of a particular object. So far, unsupervised discovery of concepts has focused on either modeling the global scene-level or the local object-level factors of variation, but not both. In this work, we propose COMET, which discovers and represents concepts as separate energy functions, enabling us to represent both global concepts as well as objects under a unified framework. COMET discovers energy functions through recomposing the input image, which we find captures independent factors without additional supervision. Sample generation in COMET is formulated as an optimization process on underlying energy functions, enabling us to generate images with permuted and composed concepts. Finally, discovered visual concepts in COMET generalize well, enabling us to compose concepts between separate modalities of images as well as with other concepts discovered by a separate instance of COMET trained on a different dataset. Code and data available at https://energy-based-model.github.io/comet/.

paragraphs: Images contain both global factors, such as lighting, and local factors, such as an object’s color or size. This paper introduces COMET to discover both kinds of concepts within one unsupervised framework. The motivation is to avoid restricting concept discovery to either whole-scene variation or individual objects.

COMET represents concepts as separate energy functions and learns them by recomposing the input image. The authors find that this process captures independent factors without additional supervision. Image generation is then formulated as optimization over the learned energy functions, allowing discovered concepts to be rearranged and combined when producing samples.

The learned concepts also generalize across the settings studied. The authors demonstrate composition between separate image modalities and with concepts learned by another COMET instance trained on a different dataset. These findings support energy functions as a common representation for diverse visual factors. The contribution combines concept discovery with a generation procedure that makes the discovered pieces usable in new compositions, including combinations across independently trained models.
summary.tldr: COMET discovers global and local visual concepts as energy functions that can be recombined to generate images across studied modalities and datasets.

title: Unsupervised Learning of Compositional Energy Concepts

abstract: We present PDLP, a practical first-order method for linear programming (LP) that can solve to the high levels of accuracy that are expected in traditional LP applications. In addition, it can scale to very large problems because its core operation is matrix-vector multiplications. PDLP is derived by applying the primal-dual hybrid gradient (PDHG) method, popularized by Chambolle and Pock (2011), to a saddle-point formulation of LP. PDLP enhances PDHG for LP by combining several new techniques with older tricks from the literature; the enhancements include diagonal preconditioning, presolving, adaptive step sizes, and adaptive restarting. PDLP improves the state of the art for first-order methods applied to LP. We compare PDLP with SCS, an ADMM-based solver, on a set of 383 LP instances derived from MIPLIB 2017. With a target of $10^{-8}$ relative accuracy and 1 hour time limit, PDLP achieves a 6.3x reduction in the geometric mean of solve times and a 4.6x reduction in the number of instances unsolved (from 227 to 49). Furthermore, we highlight standard benchmark instances and a large-scale application (PageRank) where our open-source prototype of PDLP, written in Julia, outperforms a commercial LP solver.

Its central computations are matrix-vector multiplications, providing a basis for scaling to very large instances while pursuing the accuracy expected in traditional linear programming.

title: Practical Large-Scale Linear Programming using Primal-Dual Hybrid Gradient

abstract: The paradigm of differentiable programming has significantly enhanced the scope of machine learning via the judicious use of gradient-based optimization. However, standard differentiable programming methods (such as autodiff) typically require that the machine learning models be differentiable, limiting their applicability. Our goal in this paper is to use a new, principled approach to extend gradient-based optimization to functions well modeled by splines, which encompass a large family of piecewise polynomial models. We derive the form of the (weak) Jacobian of such functions and show that it exhibits a block-sparse structure that can be computed implicitly and efficiently. Overall, we show that leveraging this redesigned Jacobian in the form of a differentiable "layer'' in predictive models leads to improved performance in diverse applications such as image segmentation, 3D point cloud reconstruction, and finite element analysis. We also open-source the code at \url{https://github.com/idealab-isu/DSA}.

Our goal in this paper is to use a new, principled approach to extend gradient-based optimization to functions well modeled by splines, which encompass a large family of piecewise polynomial models. We derive the form of the (weak) Jacobian of such functions and show that it exhibits a block-sparse structure that can be computed implicitly and efficiently. Overall, we show that leveraging this redesigned Jacobian in the form of a differentiable "layer'' in predictive models leads to improved performance in diverse applications such as image segmentation, 3D point cloud reconstruction, and finite element analysis. We also open-source the code at \url{https://github.com/idealab-isu/DSA}.

paragraphs: Differentiable programming makes it possible to train models by following gradients through their computations. Standard tools typically require differentiable model components, which limits their use with some piecewise-defined functions. This paper develops a principled way to extend gradient-based optimization to functions well represented by splines, a broad family built from polynomial pieces.

The key step is deriving a weak Jacobian, a generalized form of the derivative information needed to propagate changes through the model. The authors show that this Jacobian has a block-sparse structure. That structure allows it to be computed implicitly and efficiently, making the proposed derivative treatment usable as part of a predictive model.

The redesigned Jacobian is incorporated into a differentiable layer. The authors report improved performance in image segmentation, three-dimensional point-cloud reconstruction, and finite element analysis, and release their code. The significance is the connection between the mathematics of spline functions and a practical learning component: models can use spline-based structure while obtaining derivative information suitable for gradient-based optimization.
summary.tldr: An efficiently computed weak Jacobian turns spline approximations into useful differentiable layers for several prediction and reconstruction tasks.

title: Differentiable Spline Approximations

abstract: Generalization to out-of-distribution (OOD) data is one of the central problems in modern machine learning. Recently, there is a surge of attempts to propose algorithms that mainly build upon the idea of extracting invariant features. Although intuitively reasonable, theoretical understanding of what kind of invariance can guarantee OOD generalization is still limited, and generalization to arbitrary out-of-distribution is clearly impossible. In this work, we take the first step towards rigorous and quantitative definitions of 1) what is OOD; and 2) what does it mean by saying an OOD problem is learnable. We also introduce a new concept of expansion function, which characterizes to what extent the variance is amplified in the test domains over the training domains, and therefore give a quantitative meaning of invariant features. Based on these, we prove an OOD generalization error bound. It turns out that OOD generalization largely depends on the expansion function. As recently pointed out by Gulrajani & Lopez-Paz (2020), any OOD learning algorithm without a model selection module is incomplete. Our theory naturally induces a model selection criterion. Extensive experiments on benchmark OOD datasets demonstrate that our model selection criterion has a significant advantage over baselines.

This paper asks what kind of stability can actually support a guarantee, recognizing that generalization to arbitrary distribution shifts is impossible. It introduces quantitative definitions of an out-of-distribution problem and of when such a problem is learnable.

Experiments on benchmark out-of-distribution datasets show a significant advantage over baseline selection methods. The contribution therefore links formal definitions and an error bound to a concrete selection rule, making the theory relevant to a decision required by practical learning systems.
summary.tldr: An expansion function quantifies how feature variation changes across domains, supporting an OOD error bound and an empirically effective model-selection criterion.

title: Towards a Theoretical Framework of Out-of-Distribution Generalization

abstract: Driven by the considerable profits, the crime of drug trafficking (a.k.a. illicit drug trading) has co-evolved with modern technologies, e.g., social media such as Instagram has become a popular platform for marketing and selling illicit drugs. The activities of online drug trafficking are nimble and resilient, which call for novel techniques to effectively detect, disrupt, and dismantle illicit drug trades. In this paper, we propose a holistic framework named MetaHG to automatically detect illicit drug traffickers on social media (i.e., Instagram), by tackling the following two new challenges: (1) different from existing works which merely focus on analyzing post content, MetaHG is capable of jointly modeling multi-modal content and relational structured information on social media for illicit drug trafficker detection; (2) in addition, through the proposed meta-learning technique, MetaHG addresses the issue of requiring sufficient data for model training. More specifically, in our proposed MetaHG, we first build a heterogeneous graph (HG) to comprehensively characterize the complex ecosystem of drug trafficking on social media. Then, we employ a relation-based graph convolutional neural network to learn node (i.e., user) representations over the built HG, in which we introduce graph structure refinement to compensate the sparse connection among entities in the HG for more robust node representation learning. Afterwards, we propose a meta-learning algorithm for model optimization. A self-supervised module and a knowledge distillation module are further designed to exploit unlabeled data for improving the model. Extensive experiments based on the real-world data collected from Instagram demonstrate that the proposed MetaHG outperforms state-of-the-art methods.
