paragraphs: Crowdsourced datasets often need methods that combine conflicting labels or correct noisy ones. Improving those labels does not always produce a comparable improvement in the model trained on them. This paper attributes part of that gap to intractable instances whose difficulty continues to affect learning even after label processing.

IWBVT addresses the quality of the trained model through instance weighting and a bias-variance trade-off. Its weighting method uses a complementary set and entropy to reduce the influence of difficult instances. The intended effect is to bring estimates of model bias and variance closer to their unknown true values. It then performs probabilistic loss regressions based on the bias-variance decomposition to reduce generalization error.

The experiments indicate that IWBVT can serve as a broadly applicable post-processing step for existing state-of-the-art label-integration and noise-correction algorithms, significantly improving model quality. The contribution shifts attention from label accuracy alone to how individual training instances affect downstream learning. Its two stages connect the treatment of difficult examples with the balance between bias and variance.
summary.tldr: IWBVT reweights difficult crowdsourced examples and balances bias and variance to improve models after label integration or correction.

title: IWBVT: Instance Weighting-based Bias-Variance Trade-off for Crowdsourcing

abstract: In the present study, we introduce an innovative structure for 3D medical image segmentation that effectively integrates 2D U-Net-derived skip connections into the architecture of 3D convolutional neural networks (3D CNNs). Conventional 3D segmentation techniques predominantly depend on isotropic 3D convolutions for the extraction of volumetric features, which frequently engenders inefficiencies due to the varying information density across the three orthogonal axes in medical imaging modalities such as computed tomography (CT) and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). This disparity leads to a decline in axial-slice plane feature extraction efficiency, with slice plane features being comparatively underutilized relative to features in the time-axial. To address this issue, we introduce the U-shaped Connection (uC), utilizing simplified 2D U-Net in place of standard skip connections to augment the extraction of the axial-slice plane features while concurrently preserving the volumetric context afforded by 3D convolutions. Based on uC, we further present uC 3DU-Net, an enhanced 3D U-Net backbone that integrates the uC approach to facilitate optimal axial-slice plane feature utilization. Through rigorous experimental validation on five publicly accessible datasets—FLARE2021, OIMHS, FeTA2021, AbdomenCT-1K, and BTCV, the proposed method surpasses contemporary state-of-the-art models. Notably, this performance is achieved while reducing the number of parameters and computational complexity. This investigation underscores the efficacy of incorporating 2D convolutions within the framework of 3D CNNs to overcome the intrinsic limitations of volumetric segmentation, thereby potentially expanding the frontiers of medical image analysis. Our implementation is available at https://github.com/IMOP-lab/U-Shaped-Connection.

paragraphs: Three-dimensional medical image segmentation must use both details within individual slices and context across the full volume. Conventional methods often rely on isotropic 3D convolutions, despite differences in information density across imaging axes. The paper argues that this can leave useful features within axial slices insufficiently exploited.

The proposed U-shaped Connection, or uC, replaces standard skip connections with simplified 2D U-Nets. These connections strengthen extraction of features within the slice plane while the surrounding 3D convolutions retain volumetric context. The authors integrate this design into an enhanced 3D U-Net backbone called uC 3DU-Net.

Evaluation covers FLARE2021, OIMHS, FeTA2021, AbdomenCT-1K, and BTCV. Across the reported experiments, the method surpasses contemporary state-of-the-art models while reducing parameter count and computational complexity. The result supports a targeted combination of two-dimensional and three-dimensional processing: the added slice-level structure improves feature use without requiring a larger or more computationally expensive model in these comparisons.
summary.tldr: Replacing 3D U-Net skip connections with simplified 2D U-Nets improves reported segmentation while reducing model size and computation.

title: Upping the Game: How 2D U-Net Skip Connections Flip 3D Segmentation

abstract: With the rapid advancement of Natural Language Processing in recent years, numerous studies have shown that generic summaries generated by Large Language Models (LLMs) can sometimes surpass those annotated by experts, such as journalists, according to human evaluations. However, there is limited research on whether these generic summaries meet the individual needs of ordinary people. The biggest obstacle is the lack of human-annotated datasets from the general public. Existing work on personalized summarization often relies on pseudo datasets created from generic summarization datasets or controllable tasks that focus on specific named entities or other aspects, such as the length and specificity of generated summaries, collected from hypothetical tasks without the annotators' initiative. To bridge this gap, we propose a high-quality, personalized, manually annotated summarization dataset called PersonalSum. This dataset is the first to investigate whether the focus of public readers differs from the generic summaries generated by LLMs. It includes user profiles, personalized summaries accompanied by source sentences from given articles, and machine-generated generic summaries along with their sources. We investigate several personal signals — entities/topics, plot, and structure of articles—that may affect the generation of personalized summaries using LLMs in a few-shot in-context learning scenario. Our preliminary results and analysis indicate that entities/topics are merely one of the key factors that impact the diverse preferences of users, and personalized summarization remains a significant challenge for existing LLMs.

paragraphs: A summary can be well written and broadly useful without emphasizing what a particular reader cares about. PersonalSum investigates this difference between generic summarization and individual preferences. The paper identifies a shortage of datasets based on the public's own summary choices, rather than preferences inferred from generic datasets or imposed through hypothetical tasks.

The authors introduce a manually annotated dataset containing user profiles, personalized summaries, and the article sentences supporting those summaries. It also includes machine-generated generic summaries and their source sentences. This structure supports examining how readers' selections differ from generic model outputs while retaining a connection between each summary and the original article.

The paper studies entities and topics, plot, and article structure as possible signals for personalization in a few-shot in-context learning setting. Preliminary findings suggest that entities and topics explain only part of the variation in user preferences. Personalized summarization remains challenging for the evaluated language models. The dataset therefore supports studying personalization as a richer problem than simply choosing which named entities or topics a summary should mention.
summary.tldr: PersonalSum provides human-authored personalized summaries and finds that reader preferences extend beyond topic selection, remaining challenging for existing language models.

title: PersonalSum: A User-Subjective Guided Personalized Summarization Dataset for Large Language Models

abstract: In the field of 3D Human Pose Estimation (HPE), scalability and generalization across diverse real-world scenarios remain significant challenges. This paper addresses two key bottlenecks to scalability: limited data diversity caused by 'popularity bias' and increased 'one-to-many' depth ambiguity arising from greater pose diversity. We introduce the Biomechanical Pose Generator (BPG), which leverages biomechanical principles, specifically the normal range of motion, to autonomously generate a wide array of plausible 3D poses without relying on a source dataset, thus overcoming the restrictions of popularity bias. To address depth ambiguity, we propose the Binary Depth Coordinates (BDC), which simplifies depth estimation into a binary classification of joint positions (front or back). This method decomposes a 3D pose into three core elements—2D pose, bone length, and binary depth decision—substantially reducing depth ambiguity and enhancing model robustness and accuracy, particularly in complex poses. Our results demonstrate that these approaches increase the diversity and volume of pose data while consistently achieving performance gains, even amid the complexities introduced by increased pose diversity.

paragraphs: Scaling 3D human pose estimation involves two connected problems. Available data can overrepresent popular poses, limiting diversity. Expanding pose diversity also increases depth ambiguity, because a two-dimensional configuration can correspond to multiple three-dimensional poses. This paper addresses both the supply of plausible training poses and the representation used to infer their depth.

The Biomechanical Pose Generator uses normal ranges of motion to generate diverse plausible 3D poses without a source dataset. Binary Depth Coordinates then represent a pose through three elements: its two-dimensional configuration, bone lengths, and binary front-or-back decisions for joint positions. This turns part of depth estimation into a classification problem and substantially reduces ambiguity.

The authors report increased pose-data volume and diversity together with consistent performance gains, including under the added complexity of more varied poses. Their results connect data generation with a representation designed to handle that diversity. The two components work on complementary bottlenecks: obtaining a broader set of plausible poses and making their three-dimensional interpretation more manageable.
summary.tldr: Biomechanical pose generation and binary depth decisions jointly expand pose diversity and improve 3D pose estimation.

title: Toward Approaches to Scalability in 3D Human Pose Estimation

abstract: Promptable segmentation typically requires instance-specific manual prompts to guide the segmentation of each desired object. To minimize such a need, task-generic promptable segmentation has been introduced, which employs a single task-generic prompt to segment various images of different objects in the same task. Current methods use Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) to reason detailed instance-specific prompts from a task-generic prompt for improving segmentation accuracy. The effectiveness of this segmentation heavily depends on the precision of these derived prompts. However, MLLMs often suffer hallucinations during reasoning, resulting in inaccurate prompting. While existing methods focus on eliminating hallucinations to improve a model, we argue that MLLM hallucinations can reveal valuable contextual insights when leveraged correctly, as they represent pre-trained large-scale knowledge beyond individual images. In this paper, we first utilize hallucinations to mine task-related information from images and verify its accuracy to enhance precision of the generated prompts. Specifically, we introduce an iterative \textbf{Pro}mpt-\textbf{Ma}sk \textbf{C}ycle generation framework (ProMaC) with a prompt generator and a mask generator. The prompt generator uses a multi-scale chain of thought prompting, initially leveraging hallucinations to extract extended contextual prompts on a test image. These hallucinations are then minimized to formulate precise instance-specific prompts, directing the mask generator to produce masks that are consistent with task semantics by mask semantic alignment. Iteratively the generated masks induce the prompt generator to focus more on task-relevant image areas and reduce irrelevant hallucinations, resulting jointly in better prompts and masks. Experiments on 5 benchmarks demonstrate the effectiveness of ProMaC. Code is in https://lwpyh.github.io/ProMaC/.

paragraphs: Promptable segmentation usually needs a separate manual prompt for each object. Task-generic prompting instead starts with one instruction that applies across images, using a multimodal language model to derive object-specific guidance. The difficulty is that the derived prompts can contain hallucinations, making them unreliable instructions for the segmentation model.

ProMaC treats those hallucinations as potential sources of contextual information that must subsequently be checked and refined. Its prompt generator uses multiscale chain-of-thought prompting to produce extended contextual prompts, then reduces inaccuracies to obtain more precise instance-specific instructions. A mask generator uses these instructions and semantic alignment to produce regions consistent with the task.

The two generators operate in an iterative cycle. Generated masks direct subsequent prompting toward task-relevant image regions, helping reduce irrelevant hallucinations and improve both prompts and masks. Experiments across five benchmarks demonstrate the framework's effectiveness. The central idea is a staged use of broader pretrained knowledge: initially expand the contextual information considered, then use verification and segmentation feedback to focus that information on the image and task.
summary.tldr: ProMaC iteratively checks and refines hallucination-derived context through prompt and mask generation to reduce reliance on object-specific manual prompts.

title: Leveraging Hallucinations to Reduce Manual Prompt Dependency in Promptable Segmentation

abstract: We study the problem of private online learning, specifically, online prediction from experts (OPE) and online convex optimization (OCO). We propose a new transformation that transforms lazy online learning algorithms into private algorithms. We apply our transformation for differentially private OPE and OCO using existing lazy algorithms for these problems. Our final algorithms obtain regret which significantly improves the regret in the high privacy regime $\varepsilon \ll 1$, obtaining $\sqrt{T \log d} + T^{1/3} \log(d)/\varepsilon^{2/3}$ for DP-OPE and $\sqrt{T} + T^{1/3} \sqrt{d}/\varepsilon^{2/3}$ for DP-OCO. We also complement our results with a lower bound for DP-OPE, showing that these rates are optimal for a natural family of low-switching private algorithms.

We propose a new transformation that transforms lazy online learning algorithms into private algorithms. We apply our transformation for differentially private OPE and OCO using existing lazy algorithms for these problems. Our final algorithms obtain regret which significantly improves the regret in the high privacy regime $\varepsilon \ll 1$, obtaining $\sqrt{T \log d} + T^{1/3} \log(d)/\varepsilon^{2/3}$ for DP-OPE and $\sqrt{T} + T^{1/3} \sqrt{d}/\varepsilon^{2/3}$ for DP-OCO. paragraphs: Online learning makes predictions or decisions sequentially as information arrives. Performance is measured through regret, which captures accumulated loss relative to a comparison choice. This paper studies how to obtain low regret while providing differential privacy, focusing on prediction from experts and online convex optimization. Its main tool is a transformation of lazy algorithms, which switch decisions infrequently.

Applying this transformation to existing algorithms gives private methods with improved regret when the privacy parameter epsilon is much smaller than one. The reported bounds are sqrt(T log d) + T^(1/3) log(d)/epsilon^(2/3) for prediction from experts and sqrt(T) + T^(1/3) sqrt(d)/epsilon^(2/3) for convex optimization. These expressions quantify the privacy-related contribution alongside the other regret term.

The paper also proves a lower bound for private prediction from experts. It establishes optimality within a natural family of private algorithms that switch infrequently. This scope is central to the result: the optimality statement applies to that low-switching family. Together, the transformation and bound clarify the usefulness of laziness for private sequential learning.
summary.tldr: A transformation of low-switching online algorithms improves regret under strong privacy and achieves family-specific optimality for prediction from experts.

title: Private Online Learning via Lazy Algorithms

abstract: Sequential recommendation systems predict the next interaction item based on users' past interactions, aligning recommendations with individual preferences. Leveraging the strengths of Large Language Models (LLMs) in knowledge comprehension and reasoning, recent approaches are eager to apply LLMs to sequential recommendation. A common paradigm is converting user behavior sequences into instruction data, and fine-tuning the LLM with parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) methods like Low-Rank Adaption (LoRA). However, the uniform application of LoRA across diverse user behaviors is insufficient to capture individual variability, resulting in negative transfer between disparate sequences.To address these challenges, we propose Instance-wise LoRA (iLoRA). We innovatively treat the sequential recommendation task as a form of multi-task learning, integrating LoRA with the Mixture of Experts (MoE) framework. This approach encourages different experts to capture various aspects of user behavior. Additionally, we introduce a sequence representation guided gate function that generates customized expert participation weights for each user sequence, which allows dynamic parameter adjustment for instance-wise recommendations. In sequential recommendation, iLoRA achieves an average relative improvement of 11.4\% over basic LoRA in the hit ratio metric, with less than a 1\% relative increase in trainable parameters.Extensive experiments on three benchmark datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of iLoRA, highlighting its superior performance compared to existing methods in mitigating negative transfer and improving recommendation accuracy.Our data and code are available at https://github.com/AkaliKong/iLoRA.
originalAbstract: Sequential recommendation systems predict the next interaction item based on users' past interactions, aligning recommendations with individual preferences. Leveraging the strengths of Large Language Models (LLMs) in knowledge comprehension and reasoning, recent approaches are eager to apply LLMs to sequential recommendation. A common paradigm is converting user behavior sequences into instruction data, and fine-tuning the LLM with parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) methods like Low-Rank Adaption (LoRA). However, the uniform application of LoRA across diverse user behaviors is insufficient to capture individual variability, resulting in negative transfer between disparate sequences.To address these challenges, we propose Instance-wise LoRA (iLoRA). We innovatively treat the sequential recommendation task as a form of multi-task learning, integrating LoRA with the Mixture of Experts (MoE) framework. This approach encourages different experts to capture various aspects of user behavior. Additionally, we introduce a sequence representation guided gate function that generates customized expert participation weights for each user sequence, which allows dynamic parameter adjustment for instance-wise recommendations. In sequential recommendation, iLoRA achieves an average relative improvement of 11.4\% over basic LoRA in the hit ratio metric, with less than a 1\% relative increase in trainable parameters.Extensive experiments on three benchmark datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of iLoRA, highlighting its superior performance compared to existing methods in mitigating negative transfer and improving recommendation accuracy.Our data and code are available at https://github.com/AkaliKong/iLoRA.

paragraphs: Sequential recommendation predicts a user's next interaction from their previous interactions. One approach turns these histories into instructions and adapts a language model using LoRA, a method that trains a limited set of additional parameters. The paper identifies a problem with sharing the same adaptation across very different histories: learning from one sequence can interfere with learning from another.

Instance-wise LoRA, or iLoRA, treats recommendation as a multi-task problem and combines LoRA with a mixture of experts. Different experts are encouraged to represent different aspects of user behavior. A gate uses a representation of each interaction sequence to decide how strongly each expert participates, making the adaptation depend on the particular sequence.

Experiments on three benchmark datasets support improved recommendation accuracy and reduced negative transfer. Compared with basic LoRA, iLoRA reports an average relative improvement of 11.4% in hit ratio with less than a 1% relative increase in trainable parameters. The result shows that customizing how adaptation parameters are used can provide gains without substantially expanding their number.
summary.tldr: iLoRA combines adaptation experts differently for each user sequence to improve recommendations with little additional parameter cost.

title: Customizing Language Models with Instance-wise LoRA for Sequential Recommendation

abstract: We study the problems of differentially private federated online prediction from experts against both *stochastic adversaries* and *oblivious adversaries*. We aim to minimize the average regret on $m$ clients working in parallel over time horizon $T$ with explicit differential privacy (DP) guarantees. With stochastic adversaries, we propose a **Fed-DP-OPE-Stoch** algorithm that achieves $\sqrt{m}$-fold speed-up of the per-client regret compared to the single-player counterparts under both pure DP and approximate DP constraints, while maintaining logarithmic communication costs. With oblivious adversaries, we establish non-trivial lower bounds indicating that *collaboration among clients does not lead to regret speed-up with general oblivious adversaries*. We then consider a special case of the oblivious adversaries setting, where there exists a low-loss expert. We design a new algorithm **Fed-SVT** and show that it achieves an $m$-fold regret speed-up under both pure DP and approximate DP constraints over the single-player counterparts. Our lower bound indicates that Fed-SVT is nearly optimal up to logarithmic factors. Experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed algorithms. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first work examining the differentially private online prediction from experts in the federated setting.

paragraphs: The paper asks when multiple clients can improve online prediction by collaborating while preserving differential privacy. Its objective is to reduce average regret across m clients operating over T rounds. The central finding is that the benefit of collaboration depends strongly on the kind of prediction environment.

For stochastic adversaries, the proposed Fed-DP-OPE-Stoch algorithm improves per-client regret by a factor of square root of m over single-player counterparts. This holds under both pure and approximate differential privacy, with logarithmic communication costs. For general oblivious adversaries, however, the authors establish lower bounds showing that collaboration does not yield a regret speed-up.

A more favorable result becomes possible within the oblivious setting when a low-loss expert exists. Under that condition, Fed-SVT achieves an m-fold regret speed-up under both privacy definitions. A lower bound places its performance near optimality up to logarithmic factors, and experiments support the algorithms’ effectiveness. The results separate settings where private collaboration helps from one where its regret benefit is fundamentally limited.
summary.tldr: Private federated prediction gains depend on the adversary: collaboration helps in stochastic and low-loss settings but not against general oblivious adversaries.

title: Federated Online Prediction from Experts with Differential Privacy: Separations and Regret Speed-ups

abstract: Membership Inference Attacks (MIA) aim to infer whether a target data record has been utilized for model training or not. Existing MIAs designed for large language models (LLMs) can be bifurcated into two types: reference-free and reference-based attacks. Although reference-based attacks appear promising performance by calibrating the probability measured on the target model with reference models, this illusion of privacy risk heavily depends on a reference dataset that closely resembles the training set. Both two types of attacks are predicated on the hypothesis that training records consistently maintain a higher probability of being sampled. However, this hypothesis heavily relies on the overfitting of target models, which will be mitigated by multiple regularization methods and the generalization of LLMs. Thus, these reasons lead to high false-positive rates of MIAs in practical scenarios.We propose a Membership Inference Attack based on Self-calibrated Probabilistic Variation (SPV-MIA). Specifically, we introduce a self-prompt approach, which constructs the dataset to fine-tune the reference model by prompting the target LLM itself. In this manner, the adversary can collect a dataset with a similar distribution from public APIs.Furthermore, we introduce probabilistic variation, a more reliable membership signal based on LLM memorization rather than overfitting, from which we rediscover the neighbour attack with theoretical grounding. Comprehensive evaluation conducted on three datasets and four exemplary LLMs shows that SPV-MIA raises the AUC of MIAs from 0.7 to a significantly high level of 0.9. Our code and dataset are available at: https://github.com/tsinghua-fib-lab/NeurIPS2024_SPV-MIA

paragraphs: Membership inference asks whether a particular record was used to train a model. The paper identifies two weaknesses in existing attacks on language models: reference-based calibration depends on suitably matched reference data, and probability-based membership signals depend heavily on overfitting. Regularization and generalization can weaken that signal and contribute to false positives.

SPV-MIA addresses both issues. Its self-prompt procedure queries the target language model to collect data for fine-tuning a reference model, helping align the reference data distribution through public API access. It also introduces probabilistic variation as a membership signal grounded in memorization rather than relying on high sampling probability alone.

The authors provide theoretical grounding that reconnects this signal with the neighbour attack. Evaluations across three datasets and four language models report an increase in attack AUC from 0.7 to 0.9. This is evidence of stronger membership discrimination in those experiments, highlighting how reference-data construction and the choice of signal affect estimates of privacy exposure.
summary.tldr: SPV-MIA combines self-prompted reference data with a memorization-based signal, raising membership-inference AUC from 0.7 to 0.9 in the reported evaluations.

title: Membership Inference Attacks against Fine-tuned Large Language Models via Self-prompt Calibration

abstract: In the Lasry--Lions framework, Mean-Field Games (MFGs) model interactions among an infinite number of agents. However, existing algorithms either require strict monotonicity or only guarantee the convergence of averaged iterates, as in Fictitious Play in continuous time. We address this gap with the following theoretical result. First, we prove that the last-iterated policy of a proximal-point (PP) update with KL regularization converges to an MFG equilibrium under non-strict monotonicity. Second, we see that each PP update is equivalent to finding the equilibria of a KL-regularized MFG. We then prove that this equilibrium can be found using mirror descent with an exponential last-iterate convergence rate. Building on these insights, we propose the Approximate Proximal-Point ($\mathtt{APP}$) algorithm, which approximately implements the PP update via a small number of Mirror Descent steps. Numerical experiments on standard benchmarks confirm that the $\mathtt{APP}$ algorithm reliably converges to the unregularized mean-field equilibrium without time-averaging.

paragraphs: Mean-field games describe interactions among an infinite population of agents. Finding an equilibrium means finding policies consistent with that population's behavior. Existing algorithms can require strict monotonicity or guarantee convergence only after averaging many successive policies. This paper studies whether the latest policy itself can converge under the weaker condition of non-strict monotonicity.

The authors prove that a proximal-point update with KL regularization has this last-iterate convergence property. They then show that each update amounts to solving a KL-regularized mean-field game. Mirror descent can find the equilibrium of that regularized problem with an exponential last-iterate convergence rate, providing a way to implement the update through an inner optimization procedure.

Their Approximate Proximal-Point algorithm, APP, uses a small number of mirror descent steps to approximate each proximal update. Benchmark experiments show reliable convergence to the original, unregularized equilibrium without time averaging. The exponential rate concerns the regularized inner problem; the broader contribution is convergence of the current policy under non-strict monotonicity and a practical approximation supported by numerical results.
summary.tldr: KL-regularized proximal updates achieve last-policy convergence under non-strict monotonicity, and APP approximates them using a few mirror descent steps.

title: Last Iterate Convergence in Monotone Mean Field Games

abstract: Preference-based data often appear complex and noisy but may conceal underlying homogeneous structures. This paper introduces a novel framework of ranking structure recognition for preference-based data. We first develop an approach to identify dynamic ranking groups by incorporating temporal penalties into a spectral estimation for the celebrated Bradley-Terry model. To detect structural changes, we introduce an innovative objective function and present a practicable algorithm based on dynamic programming. Theoretically, we establish the consistency of ranking group recognition by exploiting properties of a random 'design matrix' induced by a reversible Markov chain. We also tailor a group inverse technique to quantify the uncertainty in item ability estimates. Additionally, we prove the consistency of structure change recognition, ensuring the robustness of the proposed framework. Experiments on both synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate the practical utility and interpretability of our approach.

paragraphs: Preference observations can be noisy while still reflecting groups with shared ranking structure. This paper develops a framework for recognizing those groups as they evolve over time and identifying when the structure changes. It treats grouping and change detection as related parts of understanding dynamic preference data.

The method adds temporal penalties to spectral estimation for the Bradley-Terry model, allowing ranking-group recognition to account for time. A separate objective and a dynamic-programming algorithm identify structural changes. Together, these components aim to recover an interpretable organization from preferences instead of reducing the data to a single static ordering.

The theoretical analysis establishes consistency for both group recognition and change recognition. It uses a random design matrix arising from a reversible Markov chain, while a tailored group-inverse technique quantifies uncertainty in estimated item abilities. Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate practical usefulness and interpretability. The uncertainty analysis complements the recovered structure by addressing how precisely the underlying item abilities have been estimated.
summary.tldr: The framework identifies evolving ranking groups and structural changes in preference data, with consistency results and uncertainty estimates.

title: Preference-Based Dynamic Ranking Structure Recognition

abstract: Test-time adaptation (TTA) aims to adapt a source model to a target domain using only test data. Existing methods predominantly rely on unsupervised entropy minimization or its variants, which suffer from degeneration, leading to trivial solutions with low-entropy but inaccurate predictions. In this work, we identify *entropy-deceptive* (ED) samples, instances where the model makes highly confident yet incorrect predictions, as the underlying cause of degeneration. Further, we reveal that the gradients of entropy minimization in TTA have an intrinsic low-dimensional structure, driven primarily by *entropy-truthful* (ET) samples whose gradients are highly correlated. In contrast, ED samples have scattered, less correlated gradients. Leveraging this observation, we show that the detrimental impact of ED samples can be suppressed by constraining model updates within the principal subspace of backward gradients. Building on this insight, we propose LCoTTA, a lifelong continual TTA method that tracks the principal subspace of gradients online and utilizes their projections onto this subspace for adaptation. Further, we provide theoretical analysis to show that the proposed subspace-based method can enhance the robustness against detrimental ED samples. Extensive experiments demonstrate that LCoTTA effectively overcomes degeneration and significantly outperforms existing methods in long-term continual adaptation scenarios. Code is available online.

paragraphs: Test-time adaptation updates a model using the data it encounters after deployment. A common objective reduces prediction entropy, encouraging confidence without requiring labels. This paper identifies confidently incorrect predictions, called entropy-deceptive samples, as a cause of degeneration: the adaptation objective can favor confident answers even when those answers are wrong.

The authors find that adaptation gradients have a useful geometric structure. Gradients from entropy-truthful samples are strongly correlated and primarily occupy a low-dimensional subspace, whereas entropy-deceptive gradients are more scattered. Restricting updates to the principal gradient subspace can therefore suppress the harmful influence of the deceptive samples while retaining shared adaptation directions.

LCoTTA tracks this subspace online and projects gradients into it before updating the model. Its theoretical analysis shows that this strategy can improve robustness to detrimental samples. Experiments report that it overcomes degeneration and substantially outperforms existing methods in long-term continual adaptation. The central insight is that the direction shared across gradients can help distinguish useful adaptation signals from misleading confidence.
summary.tldr: LCoTTA projects test-time updates into an online-tracked gradient subspace to reduce harm from confident but incorrect predictions.

title: Lifelong Test-Time Adaptation via Online Learning in Tracked Low-Dimensional Subspace

abstract: Split Federated Learning (SFL) enables scalable training on edge devices by combining the parallelism of Federated Learning (FL) with the computational offloading of Split Learning (SL). Despite its great success, SFL suffers significantly from the well-known straggler issue in distributed learning systems. This problem is exacerbated by the dependency between Split Server and clients: the Split Server side model update relies on receiving activations from clients. Such synchronization requirement introduces significant time latency, making straggler a critical bottleneck to the scalability and efficiency of the system. To mitigate this problem, we propose *MU-SplitFed*, a straggler-resilient SFL algorithm that decouples training progress from straggler delays via a simple yet effective unbalanced update mechanism. By enabling the server to perform $\tau$ local updates per client round, *MU-SplitFed* achieves convergence rate $\mathcal{O}(\sqrt{d/(\tau T)})$, showing a linear reduction in communication round by a factor of $\tau$. Experiments demonstrate that *MU-SplitFed* consistently outperforms baseline methods with the presence of stragglers and effectively mitigates their impact through adaptive tuning of $\tau$.

paragraphs: Split federated learning combines parallel training across clients with offloading part of a model's computation to a server. Slow clients create a particular bottleneck because server updates depend on receiving client activations. The resulting synchronization can leave training progress tied to delayed participants, increasing latency and limiting the system's efficiency.

MU-SplitFed introduces an unbalanced update schedule in which the server performs tau local updates for each client round. This changes the relationship between server-side optimization and client communication, allowing more server progress per round. The authors derive a convergence rate of order square root of d divided by tau times T, and describe the result as a factor-of-tau reduction in communication rounds.

Experiments show that MU-SplitFed consistently outperforms the evaluated baselines when stragglers are present. Adjusting tau adaptively further mitigates their impact. The findings support update scheduling as a useful way to reduce the cost of client-server synchronization: the method changes how much optimization occurs between communication rounds to make training less dependent on slow-client delays.
summary.tldr: MU-SplitFed performs multiple server updates per client round to reduce communication needs and mitigate slow-client delays.

title: Towards Straggler-Resilient Split Federated Learning: An Unbalanced Update Approach

abstract: We propose SCONE (**S**calable, **C**ontextualized, **O**ffloaded, **N**-gram **E**mbedding), a new method for extending input embedding layers to enhance language model performance. To avoid increased decoding costs, SCONE retains the original vocabulary while introducing embeddings for a set of frequent $n$-grams. These embeddings provide contextualized representation for each input token and are learned with a separate model during training. After training, embeddings are precomputed and stored in off-accelerator memory; during inference, querying them has minimal impact on latency due to the low complexity of embedding lookups. SCONE enables two new scaling strategies: increasing the number of $n$-gram embeddings and scaling the model used to learn them, both while maintaining fixed accelerator usage during inference (in terms of FLOPS and memory). We show that scaling both aspects enables a model with 1B accelerator-resident parameters to outperform a 1.9B-parameter baseline across diverse corpora, while using only about half the FLOPS and accelerator memory during inference.

paragraphs: SCONE expands a language model’s input representations using embeddings for frequent sequences of tokens, or n-grams. It keeps the original vocabulary, avoiding an increase in decoding costs from vocabulary expansion. The additional embeddings provide each input token with a representation informed by its surrounding token sequence.

A separate model learns these contextualized embeddings during training. Afterward, they are precomputed and stored outside accelerator memory. Inference retrieves them through low-complexity lookups, which the authors report have minimal latency impact. This allows scaling either the number of stored n-gram embeddings or the model that learns them while keeping inference accelerator FLOPS and memory fixed.

The authors show that scaling both components lets a model with one billion accelerator-resident parameters outperform a 1.9-billion-parameter baseline across diverse corpora. It uses about half the inference FLOPS and accelerator memory. The result demonstrates a way to improve language-model performance by moving representational capacity into precomputed, externally stored embeddings rather than requiring all additional capacity to occupy the accelerator during inference.
summary.tldr: SCONE scales contextual n-gram embeddings stored off accelerator to improve language-model performance while keeping inference accelerator usage fixed.

title: Scaling Embedding Layers in Language Models

abstract: Large Reasoning Models (LRMs) have shown promising accuracy improvements on complex problem-solving tasks. While these models have attained high accuracy by leveraging additional computation at test time, they need to generate long chain-of-thought reasoning in order to think before answering, which requires generating thousands of tokens. While sparse attention methods can help reduce the KV cache pressure induced by this long autoregressive reasoning, these methods can introduce errors which disrupt the reasoning process. Our work addresses these challenges by introducing Multipole Attention, which accelerates autoregressive reasoning by only computing exact attention for the most important tokens, while maintaining approximate representations for the remaining tokens. Our method first performs clustering to group together semantically similar key vectors, and then uses the cluster centroids both to identify important key vectors and to approximate the remaining key vectors in order to retain high accuracy. Additionally, in order to accelerate long generation tasks, we design a fast cluster update process to quickly re-cluster the input and previously generated tokens, thereby allowing for accelerating attention to the previous output tokens. We evaluate our method using emerging LRMs such as Qwen-8B and Deepseek-R1-Distil-Qwen2.5-14B, demonstrating that our approach can maintain accuracy on complex reasoning tasks even with aggressive attention sparsity settings. We also provide kernel implementations to demonstrate the practical efficiency gains from our method, achieving up to 4.5$\times$ speedup for attention in long-context reasoning applications.

paragraphs: Reasoning models can generate thousands of tokens before answering, increasing the cost of attending to earlier context and outputs. Sparse attention reduces this pressure, but discarding information can introduce errors that derail reasoning. Multipole Attention addresses the tradeoff by retaining approximate representations of tokens that do not receive exact attention.

The method clusters semantically similar key vectors. Cluster centroids help identify the most important vectors for exact attention and provide approximations for the others. A fast update procedure re-clusters both the input and previously generated tokens, allowing the same approach to support attention over a growing reasoning sequence as generation proceeds.

Evaluations using Qwen-8B and Deepseek-R1-Distil-Qwen2.5-14B show that the method can preserve accuracy on complex reasoning tasks under aggressive attention sparsity. Kernel implementations achieve attention speedups of up to 4.5 times in long-context reasoning applications. That figure applies to attention, while the accuracy results support keeping a coarse representation of less-important context instead of dropping its contribution entirely.
summary.tldr: Multipole Attention combines exact attention for important tokens with clustered approximations, achieving up to 4.5-fold attention speedups.

title: Multipole Attention for Efficient Long Context Reasoning

abstract: We study the complexity of online stochastic gradient descent (SGD) for learning a two-layer neural network with $P$ neurons on isotropic Gaussian data: $f_*(\boldsymbol{x}) = \sum_{p=1}^P a_p\cdot \sigma(\langle\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{v_p}^{\star}\rangle)$, $\boldsymbol{x} \sim \mathcal{N}(0,\boldsymbol{I_d})$, where the activation $\sigma:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$ is an even function with information exponent $k>2$ (defined as the lowest degree in the Hermite expansion), $\lbrace\boldsymbol{v_p}^\star\rbrace_{p\in[P]}\subset \mathbb{R}^d$ are orthonormal signal directions, and the non-negative second-layer coefficients satisfy $\sum_{p} a_p^2=1$. We focus on the challenging extensive-width regime $P\gg 1$ and permit diverging condition number in the second-layer, covering as a special case the power-law scaling $a_p\asymp p^{-\beta}$ where $\beta\in\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}$. We provide a precise analysis of SGD dynamics for the training of a student two-layer network to minimize the mean squared error (MSE) objective, and explicitly identify sharp transition times to recover each signal direction. In the power-law setting, we characterize scaling law exponents for the MSE loss with respect to the number of training samples and SGD steps, as well as the number of parameters in the student neural network. Our analysis entails that while the learning of individual teacher neurons exhibits abrupt transitions, the juxtaposition of $P\gg 1$ emergent learning curves at different timescales leads to a smooth scaling law in the cumulative objective.

paragraphs: This paper connects abrupt learning events with smooth overall scaling laws in a theoretical study of shallow neural networks. A student network learns a two-layer teacher through online stochastic gradient descent. The analysis focuses on teachers with many neurons, allowing the strengths of their contributions to differ substantially.

The results rely on a specified setting: isotropic Gaussian inputs, orthonormal signal directions, nonnegative normalized output coefficients, and an even activation whose first informative Hermite degree exceeds two. Within this setting, the authors analyze training dynamics and identify sharp transition times at which individual signal directions are recovered. They also cover teacher coefficients that follow a power law.

For that power-law case, the paper characterizes how mean squared error scales with training samples, optimization steps, and student parameter count. Individual teacher neurons can be learned abruptly, yet their transitions occur at different times. Combining many such learning curves produces a smooth aggregate loss curve, explaining how emergence and gradual scaling can coexist within the studied model.
summary.tldr: A theoretical analysis shows how abrupt recovery of individual features can combine into smooth scaling laws in shallow-network learning.

title: Emergence and scaling laws in SGD learning of shallow neural networks

abstract: Speculative decoding generally dictates having a small, efficient draft model that is either pretrained or distilled offline to a particular target model series, for instance, Llama or Qwen models. However, within online deployment settings, there are two major challenges: 1) usage of a target model that is incompatible with the draft model; 2) expectation of latency improvements over usage and time. In this work, we propose OmniDraft, a unified framework that enables a single draft model to operate with any target model and adapt dynamically to user data. We introduce an online n-gram cache with hybrid distillation fine-tuning to address the cross-vocabulary mismatch across draft and target models; and further improve decoding speed by leveraging adaptive drafting techniques. OmniDraft is particularly suitable for on-device LLM applications where model cost, efficiency and user customization are the major points of contention. This further highlights the need to tackle the above challenges and motivates the “one drafter for all” paradigm. We showcase the proficiency of the OmniDraft framework by performing online learning on math reasoning, coding and text generation tasks. Notably, OmniDraft enables a single Llama-68M model to pair with various target models including Vicuna-7B, Qwen2-7B and Llama3-8B models for speculative decoding; and additionally provides up to 1.5-2x speedup.

OmniDraft addresses that compatibility problem while also adapting the drafter to user data during deployment.

summary.tldr: OmniDraft lets one small draft model adapt online across target models with different vocabularies, reporting speedups of up to 1.5–2 times.

title: OmniDraft: A cross-vocabulary, online adaptive drafter for on-device speculative decoding

abstract: Sample selection is a prevalent approach in learning with noisy labels, aiming to identify confident samples for training. Although existing sample selection methods have achieved decent results by reducing the noise rate of the selected subset, they often overlook that not all mislabeled examples harm the model's performance equally. In this paper, we demonstrate that mislabeled examples correctly predicted by the model early in the training process are particularly harmful to model performance. We refer to these examples as Mislabeled Easy Examples (MEEs). To address this, we propose Early Cutting, which introduces a recalibration step that employs the model's later training state to re-select the confident subset identified early in training, thereby avoiding misleading confidence from early learning and effectively filtering out MEEs. Experiments on the CIFAR, WebVision, and full ImageNet-1k datasets demonstrate that our method effectively improves sample selection and model performance by reducing MEEs.

paragraphs: When training data contain incorrect labels, one common response is to select examples that appear trustworthy and train on that subset. Existing methods often judge success by how much they lower the fraction of incorrect labels. This paper argues that the remaining mistakes deserve closer attention because different mislabeled examples can have different effects on learning.

The authors identify a particularly harmful group: examples with incorrect supplied labels that the model nevertheless predicts correctly early in training. They call these Mislabeled Easy Examples. Their proposed method, Early Cutting, revisits an initially selected confident subset using the model at a later training stage. This recalibration aims to remove misleading early selections and filter out these harmful examples.

Experiments on CIFAR, WebVision, and full ImageNet-1k show improvements in both sample selection and model performance through reducing Mislabeled Easy Examples. The result shifts attention from simply counting label errors toward identifying which errors are especially damaging. It also supports revisiting early confidence judgments instead of treating an initial selection as permanently reliable.
summary.tldr: Early Cutting revisits early sample selections to remove particularly harmful mislabeled examples and improve learning with noisy labels.

title: Enhancing Sample Selection Against Label Noise by Cutting Mislabeled Easy Examples

abstract: Recent progress in speech processing has highlighted that high-quality performance across languages requires substantial training data for each individual language. While existing multilingual datasets cover many languages, they often contain insufficient data for each language, leading to models trained on these datasets to exhibit poor performance on most supported languages. Our work addresses this challenge by introducing a scalable pipeline for constructing speech datasets from parliamentary recordings. The proposed pipeline includes robust components for media retrieval and a two-stage alignment algorithm designed to handle non-verbatim transcripts and long-form audio. Applying this pipeline to recordings from 22 European parliaments, we extract over 61k hours of aligned speech segments, achieving substantial per-language coverage with 19 languages exceeding 1k hours and 22 languages exceeding 500 hours of high-quality speech data. We obtain an average 41.8\% reduction in word error rates over baselines when finetuning an existing ASR model on our dataset, demonstrating the usefulness of our approach.

paragraphs: A speech dataset can cover many languages yet provide too little material for strong performance in each one. EuroSpeech addresses this gap by emphasizing substantial training data per language. The paper introduces a scalable process for turning parliamentary recordings and their accompanying transcripts into aligned speech segments suitable for training speech recognition systems.

The pipeline includes robust media retrieval and a two-stage alignment algorithm. Alignment is particularly important because parliamentary audio can be long and the transcripts may not reproduce every spoken word exactly. Handling those mismatches makes it possible to use recordings whose text and audio are not already neatly paired.

Applied to recordings from 22 European parliaments, the pipeline produces more than 61,000 hours of aligned speech. Nineteen languages exceed 1,000 hours, and 22 exceed 500 hours. Fine-tuning an existing speech recognition model on the dataset yields an average 41.8% reduction in word error rates relative to the evaluated baselines. This provides practical evidence that deeper language coverage can improve recognition performance.
summary.tldr: EuroSpeech converts parliamentary recordings into over 61,000 hours of multilingual speech data and substantially improves evaluated speech recognition performance.

title: EuroSpeech: A Multilingual Speech Corpus

abstract: Tensorized Incomplete Multi-View Clustering (TIMVC) algorithms have attracted growing attention for their ability to capture high-order correlations across multiple views. However, most existing TIMVC methods rely on simplistic noise assumptions using specific norms (e.g., $\ell_1$ or $\ell_{2,1}$), which fail to reflect the complex noise patterns encountered in real-world scenarios. Moreover, they primarily focus on modeling the global Euclidean structure of the tensor representation, while overlooking the preservation of local manifold structures. To address these limitations, we propose a novel approach, GaUssian regressIon-driven TIMVC with dual mAnifold Regularization (GUITAR). Specifically, we employ a Gaussian regression model to characterize complex noise distributions in a more realistic and flexible manner. Meanwhile, a dual manifold regularization is introduced in tensor representation learning, simultaneously modeling manifold information at both the view-specific and cross-view consensus levels, thereby promoting intra-view and inter-view consistency in the tensor representation. Furthermore, to better capture the intrinsic low-rank structure, we propose the high-preservation $\ell_{\delta}$-norm tensor rank constraint, which applies differentiated penalties to the singular values, thereby enhancing the robustness of the tensor representation. In addition, an efficient optimization algorithm is developed to solve the resulting non-convex problem with provable convergence. Extensive experiments on six datasets demonstrate that our method outperforms SOTA approaches.

paragraphs: Incomplete multi-view clustering groups examples described through several information sources, some of which may be missing. Tensor representations help capture relationships across these views. The paper identifies two weaknesses in existing methods: restrictive noise models and an emphasis on global structure that can overlook local relationships within and between views.

GUITAR combines Gaussian regression for more flexible noise modeling with dual manifold regularization. The latter preserves local structure both inside each view and in the shared representation across views, encouraging consistency at both levels. A further tensor-rank constraint applies different penalties to singular values, aiming to preserve useful low-rank structure while improving robustness.

These components produce a non-convex optimization problem, for which the authors develop an efficient algorithm with a convergence proof. Experiments on six datasets show better performance than the compared state-of-the-art methods. The approach matters because it addresses noise, local geometry, and shared structure together, rather than depending solely on a global tensor representation to capture the relationships needed for clustering.
summary.tldr: GUITAR improves incomplete multi-view clustering by combining flexible noise modeling, local-structure preservation, and a differentiated low-rank constraint.

title: Gaussian Regression-Driven Tensorized Incomplete Multi-View Clustering with Dual Manifold Regularization

abstract: In this work, we prove that agents capable of adapting to distribution shifts must have learned the causal model of their environment even in the presence of mediation. This term describes situations where an agent's actions affect its environment, a dynamic common to most real-world settings. For example, a robot in an industrial plant might interact with tools, move through space, and transform products to complete its task. We introduce an algorithm for eliciting causal knowledge from robust agents using optimal policy oracles, with the flexibility to incorporate prior causal knowledge. We further demonstrate its effectiveness in mediated single-agent scenarios and multi-agent environments. We identify conditions under which the presence of a single robust agent is sufficient to recover the full causal model and derive optimal policies for other agents in the same environment. Finally, we show how to apply these results to sequential decision-making tasks modeled as Partially Observable Markov Decision Processes (POMDPs).

We introduce an algorithm for eliciting causal knowledge from robust agents using optimal policy oracles, with the flexibility to incorporate prior causal knowledge. paragraphs: This paper connects an agent's ability to adapt to distribution shifts with its knowledge of environmental causes and effects. The authors prove that robust adaptation requires learning the environment's causal model even when the agent's actions change that environment. They call this action-dependent setting mediation, which includes interactions such as moving tools or transforming products.

The paper also gives an algorithm for extracting this causal knowledge through access to optimal policy oracles. The procedure can incorporate causal information already known beforehand. This turns the theoretical connection into a way of eliciting environmental structure from an agent's policy capabilities, and the authors demonstrate it in mediated single-agent and multi-agent settings.

A further result identifies conditions under which one robust agent provides enough information to recover the full causal model and derive optimal policies for other agents. That sufficiency depends on the stated conditions; it is not an unconditional claim about every robust agent. The authors also extend the results to sequential decisions represented as partially observable Markov decision processes.
summary.tldr: The paper links robust adaptation to causal knowledge and shows how to extract that knowledge even when agents change their environments.

title: Agents Robust to Distribution Shifts Learn Causal World Models Even Under Mediation

abstract: Modern neural recording techniques such as two-photon imaging or Neuropixel probes allow to acquire vast time-series datasets with responses of hundreds or thousands of neurons. Contrastive learning is a powerful self-supervised framework for learning representations of complex datasets. Existing applications for neural time series rely on generic data augmentations and do not exploit the multi-trial data structure inherent in many neural datasets. Here we present TRACE, a new contrastive learning framework that averages across different subsets of trials to generate positive pairs. TRACE allows to directly learn a two-dimensional embedding, combining ideas from contrastive learning and neighbor embeddings. We show that TRACE outperforms other methods, resolving fine response differences in simulated data. Further, using in vivo recordings, we show that the representations learned by TRACE capture both biologically relevant continuous variation, cell-type-related cluster structure, and can assist data quality control.

paragraphs: TRACE learns representations of neural time series by using the repeated-trial structure common in neuroscience recordings. Such datasets can contain responses from hundreds or thousands of neurons. Existing contrastive approaches often create training pairs through generic data transformations, leaving the information provided by repeated trials underused.

The method creates positive pairs by averaging different subsets of trials. These paired averages give the contrastive learning process two related representations constructed from the data’s own trial structure. TRACE combines this approach with ideas from neighbor embeddings to learn a two-dimensional representation directly. The resulting embedding provides a compact space for examining similarities and differences in neural responses.

On simulated data, TRACE outperforms comparison methods in resolving fine response differences. In recordings from living animals, its representations capture both continuous biological variation and clusters associated with cell types. They can also assist data quality control. These findings show that exploiting repeated trials can support a representation that retains several distinct forms of biologically relevant structure.
summary.tldr: TRACE uses averages from different trial subsets to learn two-dimensional neural representations that capture fine response differences and biological structure.

title: TRACE: Contrastive learning for multi-trial time series data in neuroscience

abstract: The ability to recognize patterns from examples and apply them to new ones is a primal ability for general intelligence, and is widely studied by psychology and AI researchers. Many benchmarks have been proposed to measure such ability for Large Language Models (LLMs); however, they focus on few-shot (usually <10) setting and lack evaluation for aggregating many pieces of information from long contexts. On the other hand, the ever-growing context length of LLMs have brought forth the novel paradigm of many-shot In-Context Learning (ICL), which addresses new tasks with hundreds to thousands of examples without expensive and inefficient fine-tuning. However, many-shot evaluations often focus on classification, and popular long-context LLM tasks such as Needle-In-A-Haystack (NIAH) seldom require complicated intelligence for integrating many pieces of information. To fix the issues from both worlds, we propose MIR-Bench, the first many-shot in-context reasoning benchmark for pattern recognition that asks LLM to predict output via input-output examples from underlying functions with diverse data format. Based on MIR-Bench, we study many novel problems for many-shot in-context reasoning, and acquired many insightful findings including scaling effect, robustness, inductive vs. transductive reasoning, retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG), coding for inductive reasoning, cross-domain generalizability, etc. Our dataset is available at https://huggingface.co/datasets/kaiyan289/MIR-Bench.

paragraphs: MIR-Bench evaluates whether language models can infer complicated patterns from many examples placed in their context. The motivation is a gap between short pattern-recognition tests and long-context evaluations: the former usually provide few examples, while many of the latter emphasize classification or finding information rather than integrating evidence into a rule.

The benchmark presents input-output examples generated by underlying functions in diverse data formats, then asks models to predict outputs for new inputs. This setup examines learning within the prompt, without fine-tuning. It makes the relationship among examples central to solving the task, providing a setting for studying reasoning over hundreds or thousands of demonstrations.

The authors use MIR-Bench to investigate scaling, robustness, retrieval augmentation, coding-based induction, and generalization across domains. They also examine inductive reasoning, which seeks a general rule, versus transductive reasoning directed at the requested prediction. The abstract identifies these research directions without stating their individual outcomes. The contribution is an evaluation framework for testing how extended context supports pattern learning and application.
summary.tldr: MIR-Bench tests whether language models can integrate many input-output examples to infer and apply complicated patterns.

title: MIR-Bench: Can Your LLM Recognize Complicated Patterns via Many-Shot In-Context Reasoning?

abstract: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) based on knowledge graphs (KGs) enhances large language models (LLMs) by providing structured and interpretable external knowledge. However, existing KG-based RAG methods struggle to retrieve accurate and diverse information from text-rich KGs for complex real-world queries. Process Reward Models (PRMs) offer a way to align the retrieval process of KG-based RAG with query-specific knowledge requirements, but they heavily rely on process-level supervision signals that are expensive and hard to obtain on KGs. To address this challenge, we propose GraphFlow, a framework that efficiently retrieves accurate and diverse knowledge required for real-world queries from text-rich KGs. GraphFlow employs a transition-based flow matching objective to jointly optimize a retrieval policy and a flow estimator. The flow estimator factorizes the reward of the retrieval outcome into the intermediate retrieval states. Such reward factorization guides the retrieval policy to retrieve candidates from KGs in proportion to their reward. This allows GraphFlow to explore high-quality regions of KGs that yield diverse and relevant results. We evaluate GraphFlow on the STaRK benchmark, which includes real-world queries from multiple domains over text-rich KGs. GraphFlow outperforms strong KG-RAG baselines, including GPT-4o, by 10\% on average in hit rate and recall. It also shows strong generalization to unseen KGs, demonstrating its effectiveness and robustness.

paragraphs: Knowledge graphs can supply language models with structured external information, but complex queries require retrieval that is both relevant and diverse. Supervising every intermediate retrieval decision is expensive. GraphFlow addresses this problem by learning how to navigate text-rich graphs using rewards attached to retrieval outcomes.

Its training objective jointly learns a retrieval policy and a flow estimator. The estimator distributes an outcome's reward across intermediate retrieval states, giving the policy guidance about which choices lead toward useful information. The policy is trained to retrieve candidates in proportion to their reward, encouraging exploration of multiple promising graph regions rather than relying on a single retrieval route.

On STaRK, a benchmark containing real-world queries across several domains, GraphFlow exceeds strong knowledge-graph retrieval baselines, including GPT-4o, by an average of 10% in hit rate and recall. It also shows strong generalization to unseen graphs. These results support the usefulness of learning intermediate retrieval guidance from outcome rewards when the objective is to return varied, relevant knowledge.
summary.tldr: GraphFlow learns reward-guided graph retrieval that improves relevance and diversity without relying on costly supervision for every retrieval step.

title: Can Knowledge-Graph-based Retrieval Augmented Generation Really Retrieve What You Need?

abstract: Clinical risk prediction plays a crucial role in early disease detection and personalized intervention. While recent models increasingly incorporate multimodal data, their development typically assumes access to large-scale, multimodal datasets and substantial computational resources. In practice, however, most clinical sites operate under resource constraints, with access limited to EHR data alone and insufficient capacity to train complicated models. This gap highlights the urgent need to democratize clinical risk prediction by enabling effective deployment in data- and resource-limited local clinical settings. In this work, we propose a cross-cohort cross-modal knowledge transfer framework that leverages the multimodal model trained on a nationwide cohort and adapts it to local cohorts with only EHR data. We focus on EHR and genetic data as representative multimodal inputs and address two key challenges. First, to mitigate the influence of noisy or less informative biological signals, we propose a novel mixture-of-aggregations design to enhance the modeling of informative and relevant genetic features. Second, to support rapid model adaptation in low-resource sites, we develop a lightweight graph-guided fine-tuning method that adapts pretrained phenotypical EHR representations to target cohorts using limited patient data. Extensive experiments on real-world clinical data validate the effectiveness of our proposed model.

paragraphs: Clinical prediction models increasingly combine several kinds of patient information, but many local sites have only electronic health records and limited training resources. This paper proposes transferring knowledge from a multimodal model trained on a nationwide cohort to smaller local cohorts that have EHR data alone. The transfer crosses both patient populations and available data types.

The framework studies EHR and genetic information as its two modalities. To handle noisy or less useful biological signals, it introduces a mixture-of-aggregations design intended to emphasize informative genetic features. For local adaptation, a lightweight graph-guided fine-tuning method adjusts pretrained representations of EHR-based patient characteristics using limited patient data.

Experiments on real-world clinical data support the effectiveness of the proposed model. The practical significance is that a local site can benefit from knowledge learned with richer data without needing the same modalities locally. The work addresses the adaptation burden directly, combining improved modeling of genetic information at the source with a lighter method for transferring useful representations.
summary.tldr: The framework transfers knowledge from nationwide EHR-and-genetics models to local EHR-only cohorts through lightweight adaptation.

title: Democratizing Clinical Risk Prediction with Cross-Cohort Cross-Modal Knowledge Transfer

abstract: Petrography is a branch of geology that analyzes the mineralogical composition of rocks from microscopical thin section samples. It is essential for understanding rock properties across geology, archaeology, engineering, mineral exploration, and the oil industry. However, petrography is a labor-intensive task requiring experts to conduct detailed visual examinations of thin section samples through optical polarization microscopes, thus hampering scalability and highlighting the need for automated techniques. To address this challenge, we introduce the Large-scale Imaging and Thin section Optical-polarization Set (LITHOS), the largest and most diverse publicly available experimental framework for automated petrography. LITHOS includes 211,604 high-resolution RGB patches of polarized light and 105,802 expert-annotated grains across 25 mineral categories. Each annotation consists of the mineral class, spatial coordinates, and expert-defined major and minor axes represented as intersecting vector paths, capturing grain geometry and orientation. We evaluate multiple deep learning techniques for mineral classification in LITHOS and propose a dual-encoder transformer architecture that integrates both polarization modalities as a strong baseline for future reference. Our method consistently outperforms single-polarization models, demonstrating the value of polarization synergy in mineral classification. We have made the LITHOS Benchmark publicly available, comprising our dataset, code, and pretrained models, to foster reproducibility and further research in automated petrographic analysis.

paragraphs: Petrography examines thin sections of rock under polarization microscopes to identify minerals and understand rock properties. Expert visual analysis is labor-intensive, limiting how readily it can scale. This paper introduces LITHOS, a public experimental framework designed to support the development and evaluation of automated petrographic methods.

Each grain annotation includes its mineral class, position, and expert-defined major and minor axes. These intersecting vector paths preserve information about grain geometry and orientation alongside the identification labels.

The authors evaluate multiple deep learning approaches and propose a dual-encoder transformer that combines both polarization modalities. It consistently outperforms models using a single polarization modality, supporting the value of combining the two views for mineral classification. By releasing the dataset, code, and pretrained models together, the paper provides both a substantial evaluation resource and a strong reference model for further research into automated analysis of rock thin sections.
summary.tldr: LITHOS provides expert-annotated rock microscopy data and a dual-polarization transformer that improves mineral classification over single-polarization models.

title: Towards Automated Petrography

abstract: Multimodal hallucination in multimodal large language models (MLLMs) restricts the correctness of MLLMs. However, multimodal hallucinations are multi-sourced and arise from diverse causes. Existing benchmarks fail to adequately distinguish between perception-induced hallucinations and reasoning-induced hallucinations. This failure constitutes a significant issue and hinders the diagnosis of multimodal reasoning failures within MLLMs. To address this, we propose the MIRAGE benchmark, which isolates reasoning hallucinations by constructing questions where input images are correctly perceived by MLLMs yet reasoning errors persist. MIRAGE introduces multi-granular evaluation metrics: accuracy, factuality, and LLMs hallucination score for hallucination quantification. Our analysis reveals strong correlations between question types and specific hallucination patterns, particularly systematic failures of MLLMs in spatial reasoning involving complex relationships (\emph{e.g.}, complex geometric patterns across images). This highlights a critical limitation in the reasoning capabilities of current MLLMs and provides targeted insights for hallucination mitigation on specific types. To address these challenges, we propose Logos, a method that combines curriculum reinforcement fine-tuning to encourage models to generate logic-consistent reasoning chains by stepwise reducing learning difficulty, and collaborative hint inference to reduce reasoning complexity. Logos establishes a baseline on MIRAGE, and reduces the logical hallucinations in original base models. Link: \url{https://bit.ly/25mirage}.

summary.tldr: MIRAGE isolates reasoning hallucinations after correct image perception, while Logos reduces them through curriculum training and collaborative hints.

title: MIRAGE: Assessing Hallucination in Multimodal Reasoning Chains of MLLM

abstract: Large multimodal models (LMMs) have gained impressive performance due to their outstanding capability in various understanding tasks. However, these models still suffer from some fundamental limitations related to robustness and generalization due to the alignment and correlation between visual and textual features. In this paper, we introduce a simple but efficient learning mechanism for improving the robust alignment between visual and textual modalities by solving shuffling problems. In particular, the proposed approach can improve reasoning capability, visual understanding, and cross-modality alignment by introducing two new tasks: reconstructing the image order and the text order into the LMM's pre-training and fine-tuning phases. In addition, we propose a new directed-token approach to capture visual and textual knowledge, enabling the capability to reconstruct the correct order of visual inputs. Then, we introduce a new Image-to-Response Guided loss to further improve the visual understanding of the LMM in its responses. The proposed approach consistently achieves state-of-the-art (SoTA) performance compared with prior LMMs on academic task-oriented and instruction-following LMM benchmarks.

Although these models perform well on many understanding tasks, their alignment between modalities can still limit robustness and generalization. The paper proposes teaching models to recover order from shuffled inputs as a way to improve that connection.

The method adds image-order and text-order reconstruction tasks during both pretraining and fine-tuning. It also introduces directed tokens that capture visual and textual knowledge and support reconstructing the correct order of visual inputs. An additional Image-to-Response Guided loss is intended to improve how the model's responses reflect visual understanding. These components place explicit training pressure on relationships among inputs and their connection to outputs.

The authors report consistent state-of-the-art performance relative to earlier multimodal models on task-oriented and instruction-following benchmarks. The stated findings support order reconstruction as a useful learning mechanism for reasoning, visual understanding, and cross-modal alignment. The approach matters because it adds concrete training tasks for improving these capabilities within the model's existing training phases.
summary.tldr: Directed-Tokens trains multimodal models to reconstruct shuffled image and text order, improving alignment and benchmark performance.

title: Directed-Tokens: A Robust Multi-Modality Alignment Approach to Large Language-Vision Models

abstract: Online advertising platforms use automated auctions to connect advertisers with potential customers, requiring effective bidding strategies to maximize profits. Accurate ad impact estimation requires considering three key factors: delayed and long-term effects, cumulative ad impacts such as reinforcement or fatigue, and customer heterogeneity. However, these effects are often not jointly addressed in previous studies. To capture these factors, we model ad bidding as a Contextual Markov Decision Process (CMDP) with delayed Poisson rewards. For efficient estimation, we propose a two-stage maximum likelihood estimator combined with data-splitting strategies, ensuring controlled estimation error based on the first-stage estimator's (in)accuracy. Building on this, we design a reinforcement learning algorithm to derive efficient personalized bidding strategies. This approach achieves a near-optimal regret bound of $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(dH^2\sqrt{T})$, where $d$ is the contextual dimension, $H$ is the number of rounds, and $T$ is the number of customers. Our theoretical findings are validated by simulation experiments.
