paragraphs: Advertising decisions are difficult to evaluate because an advertisement’s effect may arrive later, depend on earlier exposures, and vary across customers. Repeated exposure can reinforce an advertisement’s influence or produce fatigue. This paper develops a bidding framework that addresses these delayed, cumulative, and personalized effects together.

The authors model bidding as a contextual Markov decision process with delayed Poisson rewards. This supplies a specific statistical structure for learning from delayed outcomes while accounting for customer context and sequential decisions. They propose a two-stage maximum likelihood estimator with data splitting. Its error analysis explicitly tracks how inaccuracies in the first estimation stage affect the overall estimate, providing controlled estimation error within the proposed framework.

A reinforcement learning algorithm then uses these estimates to develop personalized bidding strategies. The authors establish a near-optimal regret bound scaling as dH²√T, up to logarithmic factors, where d is context dimension, H is the number of rounds, and T is the number of customers. Simulation experiments support the theoretical findings under the modeled advertising setting.
summary.tldr: A contextual reinforcement learning framework models delayed and cumulative advertising effects to learn personalized bidding strategies with a near-optimal regret bound.

title: Learning Personalized Ad Impact via Contextual Reinforcement Learning under Delayed Rewards

abstract: Symmetry is pervasive in robotics and has been widely exploited to improve sample efficiency in deep reinforcement learning (DRL). However, existing approaches primarily focus on spatial symmetries—such as reflection, rotation, and translation—while largely neglecting temporal symmetries. To address this gap, we explore time reversal symmetry, a form of temporal symmetry commonly found in robotics tasks such as door opening and closing. We propose Time Reversal symmetry enhanced Deep Reinforcement Learning (TR-DRL), a framework that combines trajectory reversal augmentation and time reversal guided reward shaping to efficiently solve temporally symmetric tasks. Our method generates reversed transitions from fully reversible transitions, identified by a proposed dynamics-consistent filter, to augment the training data. For partially reversible transitions, we apply reward shaping to guide learning, according to successful trajectories from the reversed task. Extensive experiments on the Robosuite and MetaWorld benchmarks demonstrate that TR-DRL is effective in both single-task and multi-task settings, achieving higher sample efficiency and stronger final performance compared to baseline methods.

paragraphs: Some robotic tasks have useful temporal symmetry: opening and closing a door are related through reversal. While reinforcement-learning methods often exploit spatial symmetries, this paper investigates how reversing task experience can improve learning. TR-DRL combines two uses of reversal, depending on how faithfully a transition can be reversed.

A dynamics-consistent filter identifies fully reversible transitions. The method reverses these transitions to create additional training data, extracting more learning material from collected experience. For transitions that are only partially reversible, it instead shapes rewards using successful trajectories from the reversed task. This distinction lets the framework use reverse-task information without treating every observed transition as fully reversible.

Experiments on Robosuite and MetaWorld report improved sample efficiency and stronger final performance relative to baseline methods. The benefits appear in both single-task and multi-task settings. The approach is intended for temporally symmetric tasks, where reverse behavior supplies useful information. Its contribution is a structured way to use that information either as additional transitions or as guidance for learning.
summary.tldr: TR-DRL uses reversible transitions and reverse-task reward guidance to improve learning efficiency and final performance on tested temporally symmetric robotic tasks.

title: Time Reversal Symmetry for Efficient Robotic Manipulations in Deep Reinforcement Learning

abstract: We present Neural Attention Search (NAtS), an end-to-end learnable sparse transformer that automatically evaluates the importance of each token within a sequence and determines if the corresponding token can be dropped after several steps. To this end, we design a search space that contains three token types: (i) Global Tokens will be preserved and queried by all the following tokens. (ii) Local Tokens survive until the next global token appears. (iii) Sliding Window Tokens have an impact on the inference of a fixed size of the next following tokens. Similar to the One-Shot Neural Architecture Search approach, this token-type information can be learned jointly with the architecture weights via a learnable attention mask. Experiments on both training a new transformer from scratch and fine-tuning existing large language models show that NAtS can efficiently reduce the KV cache and the inference costs for the transformer-based models while maintaining the models' performance.

paragraphs: Neural Attention Search asks a transformer to learn how long each token needs to remain available to later tokens. Keeping token information available affects the key–value cache and inference cost. The proposed sparse transformer evaluates token importance and learns whether a token can be dropped after contributing to a limited number of subsequent steps.

Its search space contains three token types. Global tokens remain available to every following token. Local tokens remain until the next global token appears. Sliding-window tokens influence a fixed number of subsequent tokens. A learnable attention mask determines these roles jointly with the model's weights, using an approach similar to one-shot neural architecture search.

The researchers test both training transformers from scratch and fine-tuning existing large language models. They report reduced cache requirements and inference costs while maintaining model performance. The practical idea is that token retention becomes a learned part of the model: different tokens can serve persistent, locally bounded, or fixed-window roles according to the learned attention structure.
summary.tldr: Neural Attention Search learns token-specific attention lifetimes to reduce transformer cache use and inference costs while preserving performance in experiments.

title: Neural Attention Search

abstract: We study the problem of sampling from a distribution under local differential privacy (LDP). Given a private distribution $P \in \mathcal{P}$, the goal is to generate a single sample from a distribution that remains close to $P$ in $f$-divergence while satisfying the constraints of LDP. This task captures the fundamental challenge of producing realistic-looking data under strong privacy guarantees. While prior work by Park et al. (NeurIPS'24) focuses on global minimax-optimality across a class of distributions, we take a local perspective. Specifically, we examine the minimax error in a neighborhood around a fixed distribution $P_0$, and characterize its exact value, which depends on both $P_0$ and the privacy level. Our main result shows that the local minimax error is determined by the global minimax error when the distribution class $\mathcal{P}$ is restricted to a neighborhood around $P_0$. To establish this, we (1) extend previous work from pure LDP to the more general functional LDP framework, and (2) prove that the globally optimal functional LDP sampler yields the optimal local sampler when constrained to distributions near $P_0$. Building on this, we also derive a simple closed-form expression for the locally minimax-optimal samplers which does not depend on the choice of $f$-divergence. We further argue that this local framework naturally models private sampling with public data, where the public data distribution is represented by $P_0$. In this setting, we empirically compare our locally optimal sampler to existing global methods, and demonstrate that it consistently outperforms global minimax samplers.

A globally minimax sampler protects against the worst case across an entire distribution class. This paper instead studies the worst-case error near a fixed reference distribution, allowing the analysis to reflect local knowledge about the target.

The authors characterize the exact local minimax error as a function of the reference distribution and privacy level. They extend prior analysis to functional local differential privacy and show how the globally optimal sampler yields a locally optimal one when restricted to a neighborhood of the reference. They also derive a closed-form optimal sampler that does not depend on which f-divergence measures distributional error.

The reference distribution can represent public data, providing a natural setting in which local information is available without exposing private observations. In experiments motivated by this setting, the local sampler consistently outperforms global minimax samplers. The result shows how restricting the relevant distribution class can improve private sampling while retaining an explicit optimality characterization.
summary.tldr: The paper characterizes optimal private sampling near a reference distribution and shows empirical benefits when that reference represents public data.

title: Locally Optimal Private Sampling: Beyond the Global Minimax

abstract: We propose a new benchmark to measure a language model's linguistic reasoning skills without relying on pre-existing language-specific knowledge. The test covers 894 questions grouped in 160 problems across 75 (mostly) extremely low-resource languages, extracted from the International Linguistic Olympiad corpus. To attain high accuracy on this benchmark, models don't need previous knowledge of the tested language, as all the information needed to solve the linguistic puzzle is presented in the context. We find that, while all analyzed models rank below 25% accuracy, there is a significant gap between open and closed models, with the best-performing proprietary model scoring 24.05% and the best-performing open model 8.84%.

The test covers 894 questions grouped in 160 problems across 75 (mostly) extremely low-resource languages, extracted from the International Linguistic Olympiad corpus. paragraphs: Linguini evaluates whether a language model can solve linguistic puzzles using information provided in the problem itself. Its central aim is to measure reasoning without requiring prior knowledge of the particular language being tested. This makes the benchmark useful for examining how models work out unfamiliar linguistic relationships from the context they receive.

The benchmark draws on the International Linguistic Olympiad corpus and contains 894 questions organized into 160 problems across 75 languages. Most of those languages have extremely limited resources. Each puzzle supplies the information needed for a solution, so familiarity with the language is not a prerequisite for high accuracy under the benchmark’s design.

Every evaluated model scores below 25% accuracy. The strongest proprietary model reaches 24.05%, while the strongest open model reaches 8.84%, revealing a substantial gap between those groups in this evaluation. These results indicate that the supplied linguistic puzzles remain difficult for the tested systems even when the necessary evidence is present. The benchmark therefore exposes a challenging form of contextual reasoning across unfamiliar languages.
summary.tldr: Linguini tests linguistic reasoning from self-contained puzzles across 75 languages, with all evaluated models scoring below 25% accuracy.

title: Linguini: A benchmark for language-agnostic linguistic reasoning

abstract: We consider the generalization ability of algorithms for learning to rank at a query level, a problem also called subset ranking. Existing generalization error bounds necessarily degrade as the size of the document list associated with a query increases. We show that such a degradation is not intrinsic to the problem. For several loss functions, including the cross-entropy loss used in the well known ListNet method, there is no degradation in generalization ability as document lists become longer. We also provide novel generalization error bounds under \ell_1 regularization and faster convergence rates if the loss function is smooth.

paragraphs: Learning to rank at the query level means learning how to order the documents associated with a query. Earlier generalization bounds worsened as those document lists became longer. Such bounds could suggest that list length inherently makes it harder for a learned ranking method to perform well beyond its training data.

This paper shows that the deterioration is not intrinsic to the problem. For several loss functions, including the cross-entropy loss used by ListNet, the authors obtain generalization results without degradation as document lists lengthen. The contribution separates a dependence appearing in earlier analyses from a difficulty that must necessarily occur in learning.

The paper also derives new bounds for learning with ℓ1 regularization and establishes faster convergence rates when the loss is smooth. These are qualified results for the losses and conditions studied, rather than a universal statement about all ranking procedures. Their significance is a sharper account of what controls generalization: longer lists alone need not worsen the theoretical guarantee, and additional loss structure can improve the rates.
summary.tldr: For several ranking losses, generalization bounds need not worsen with document-list length, and smoothness enables faster convergence rates.

title: Generalization error bounds for learning to rank: Does the length of document lists matter?

abstract: Kernel online convex optimization (KOCO) is a framework combining the expressiveness of non-parametric kernel models with the regret guarantees of online learning. First-order KOCO methods such as functional gradient descent require only $O(t)$ time and space per iteration, and, when the only information on the losses is their convexity, achieve a minimax optimal $O(\sqrt{T})$ regret. Nonetheless, many common losses in kernel problems, such as squared loss, logistic loss, and squared hinge loss posses stronger curvature that can be exploited. In this case, second-order KOCO methods achieve $O(\log(\mathrm{Det}(K)))$ regret, which we show scales as $O(deff \log T)$, where $deff$ is the effective dimension of the problem and is usually much smaller than $O(\sqrt{T})$. The main drawback of second-order methods is their much higher $O(t^2)$ space and time complexity. In this paper, we introduce kernel online Newton step (KONS), a new second-order KOCO method that also achieves $O(deff\log T)$ regret. To address the computational complexity of second-order methods, we introduce a new matrix sketching algorithm for the kernel matrix~$K$, and show that for a chosen parameter $\gamma \leq 1$ our Sketched-KONS reduces the space and time complexity by a factor of $\gamma^2$ to $O(t^2\gamma^2)$ space and time per iteration, while incurring only $1/\gamma$ times more regret.

paragraphs: Kernel online learning combines flexible models with regret guarantees for sequential decisions. First-order methods have relatively low computational costs and optimal square-root regret when convexity is the only available property. Many common losses have additional curvature, however, which second-order methods can use to obtain stronger regret bounds.

The paper introduces kernel online Newton step, or KONS, with regret O(d_eff log T), where d_eff measures the problem's effective dimension. The authors also express an existing kernel determinant-based bound in this form. The obstacle is computation: second-order methods require quadratic time and space in the number of rounds processed.

An adaptive matrix sketch addresses that obstacle by approximating the kernel matrix. With a chosen positive parameter gamma at most one, Sketched-KONS uses O(t² gamma²) time and space per iteration while increasing regret by a factor of 1/gamma. This gives an explicit resource–accuracy tradeoff: a smaller sketch saves computation and memory at a quantified cost in the regret guarantee.
summary.tldr: Adaptive kernel sketching reduces the computational cost of second-order online learning with a quantified increase in regret.

title: Second-Order Kernel Online Convex Optimization with Adaptive Sketching

abstract: The generalization properties of Gaussian processes depend heavily on the choice of kernel, and this choice remains a dark art. We present the Neural Kernel Network (NKN), a flexible family of kernels represented by a neural network. The NKN’s architecture is based on the composition rules for kernels, so that each unit of the network corresponds to a valid kernel. It can compactly approximate compositional kernel structures such as those used by the Automatic Statistician (Lloyd et al., 2014), but because the architecture is differentiable, it is end-to-end trainable with gradient- based optimization. We show that the NKN is universal for the class of stationary kernels. Empirically we demonstrate NKN’s pattern discovery and extrapolation abilities on several tasks that depend crucially on identifying the underlying structure, including time series and texture extrapolation, as well as Bayesian optimization.

The NKN’s architecture is based on the composition rules for kernels, so that each unit of the network corresponds to a valid kernel. paragraphs: A Gaussian process depends heavily on its kernel, which encodes the relationships the model uses to generalize from observations. Choosing an effective kernel can be difficult, especially when the data contain several interacting patterns. This paper introduces Neural Kernel Networks as a flexible, trainable representation of kernel structure.

The architecture follows valid kernel-composition rules, so every unit represents a valid kernel. This makes it possible to build complex kernels while preserving the mathematical requirements of the Gaussian-process model. The network can compactly approximate compositional structures of the kind used by the Automatic Statistician. Because the construction is differentiable, its parameters can be trained end to end using gradient-based optimization.

The authors establish universality for the class of stationary kernels, giving the representation a broad but explicitly scoped expressiveness result. Experiments demonstrate pattern discovery and extrapolation in time series and textures, along with applications to Bayesian optimization. These findings show how learning the kernel's composition can help a Gaussian process capture underlying structure that matters for predictions beyond observed data.
summary.tldr: Neural Kernel Networks learn valid compositional Gaussian-process kernels through gradient optimization and are universal within the stationary-kernel class.

title: Differentiable Compositional Kernel Learning for Gaussian Processes

abstract: This paper considers the problem of inverse reinforcement learning in zero-sum stochastic games when expert demonstrations are known to be suboptimal. Compared to previous works that decouple agents in the game by assuming optimality in expert policies, we introduce a new objective function that directly pits experts against Nash Equilibrium policies, and we design an algorithm to solve for the reward function in the context of inverse reinforcement learning with deep neural networks as model approximations. To ?nd Nash Equilibrium in large-scale games, we also propose an adversarial training algorithm for zero-sum stochastic games, and show the theoretical appeal of non-existence of local optima in its objective function. In numerical experiments, we demonstrate that our Nash Equilibrium and inverse reinforcement learning algorithms address games that are not amenable to existing benchmark algorithms. Moreover, our algorithm successfully recovers reward and policy functions regardless of the quality of the sub-optimal expert demonstration set.

This paper studies that problem in zero-sum stochastic games, where agents compete and the demonstrations are known to be imperfect. Assuming that demonstrators already behave optimally would remove an important part of the problem the authors want to address.

Their objective directly compares expert behavior against Nash equilibrium policies, keeping the competitive relationship between agents in the learning problem. They develop an algorithm for recovering rewards using deep neural networks as approximations. To obtain equilibrium policies in large games, they also introduce an adversarial training procedure for zero-sum stochastic games.

The authors identify a theoretical property of the equilibrium objective: the absence of local optima. Their numerical experiments show that the equilibrium and reward-learning algorithms handle games that existing benchmark algorithms cannot address. They also report successful recovery of rewards and policies across the demonstration qualities examined. These experimental findings support learning from imperfect competitors without treating demonstration optimality as a prerequisite.
summary.tldr: The paper learns rewards in competitive zero-sum games by comparing imperfect demonstrations with Nash equilibrium policies.

title: Competitive Multi-agent Inverse Reinforcement Learning with Sub-optimal Demonstrations

abstract: Shallow supervised 1-hidden layer neural networks have a number of favorable properties that make them easier to interpret, analyze, and optimize than their deep counterparts, but lack their representational power. Here we use 1-hidden layer learning problems to sequentially build deep networks layer by layer, which can inherit properties from shallow networks. Contrary to previous approaches using shallow networks, we focus on problems where deep learning is reported as critical for success. We thus study CNNs on image classification tasks using the large-scale ImageNet dataset and the CIFAR-10 dataset. Using a simple set of ideas for architecture and training we find that solving sequential 1-hidden-layer auxiliary problems lead to a CNN that exceeds AlexNet performance on ImageNet. Extending this training methodology to construct individual layers by solving 2-and-3-hidden layer auxiliary problems, we obtain an 11-layer network that exceeds several members of the VGG model family on ImageNet, and can train a VGG-11 model to the same accuracy as end-to-end learning. To our knowledge, this is the first competitive alternative to end-to-end training of CNNs that can scale to ImageNet. We illustrate several interesting properties of these models and conduct a range of experiments to study the properties this training induces on the intermediate layers.

summary.tldr: Sequential shallow learning problems can build competitive ImageNet networks, including a VGG-11 model matching end-to-end training accuracy.

title: Greedy Layerwise Learning Can Scale To ImageNet

abstract: We design and study a Contextual Memory Tree (CMT), a learning memory controller that inserts new memories into an experience store of unbounded size. It operates online and is designed to efficiently query for memories from that store, supporting logarithmic time insertion and retrieval operations. Hence CMT can be integrated into existing statistical learning algorithms as an augmented memory unit without substantially increasing training and inference computation. Furthermore CMT operates as a reduction to classification, allowing it to benefit from advances in representation or architecture. We demonstrate the efficacy of CMT by augmenting existing multi-class and multi-label classification algorithms with CMT and observe statistical improvement. We also test CMT learning on several image-captioning tasks to demonstrate that it performs computationally better than a simple nearest neighbors memory system while benefitting from reward learning.

paragraphs: A learning system that stores past experiences also needs a practical way to retrieve useful memories as its store grows. The Contextual Memory Tree addresses this problem with a learned memory controller. It works online, inserting new memories into an experience store whose size is not fixed in advance.

The tree supports insertion and retrieval in logarithmic time. This makes it suitable as an added memory component for existing statistical learning algorithms without substantially increasing their training and inference computation. Its learning problem is expressed as a reduction to classification, allowing improvements in classification representations or architectures to benefit the memory controller as well.

The authors augment multi-class and multi-label classification algorithms with this memory and observe statistical improvements. They also evaluate it on image-captioning tasks, where it performs better computationally than a simple nearest-neighbor memory system and benefits from reward learning. The findings connect efficient memory access with learned retrieval behavior, showing that the store can contribute to predictions while remaining computationally manageable.
summary.tldr: Contextual Memory Trees add learned, growing experience stores to models with logarithmic-time insertion and retrieval.

title: Contextual Memory Trees

abstract: How can prior knowledge on the transformation invariances of a domain be incorporated into the architecture of a neural network? We propose Equivariant Transformers (ETs), a family of differentiable image-to-image mappings that improve the robustness of models towards pre-defined continuous transformation groups. Through the use of specially-derived canonical coordinate systems, ETs incorporate functions that are equivariant by construction with respect to these transformations. We show empirically that ETs can be flexibly composed to improve model robustness towards more complicated transformation groups in several parameters. On a real-world image classification task, ETs improve the sample efficiency of ResNet classifiers, achieving relative improvements in error rate of up to 15% in the limited data regime while increasing model parameter count by less than 1%.

paragraphs: When a domain has known transformation rules, a network architecture can incorporate that knowledge. This paper introduces Equivariant Transformers, differentiable mappings from images to images that improve robustness to predefined continuous transformation groups. The approach makes those specified transformations part of the model’s construction.

The key mechanism is a specially derived canonical coordinate system. Within these coordinates, the model includes functions whose responses respect the transformations by construction. The authors also show empirically that multiple Equivariant Transformers can be composed to improve robustness to more complicated transformation groups involving several parameters. This connects the basic construction to settings with multiple transformation dimensions.

On a real-world image-classification task, adding these components improves the sample efficiency of ResNet classifiers. In the limited-data setting, the reported relative reduction in error reaches up to 15%, while the parameter count increases by less than 1%. The result indicates that encoding relevant transformation knowledge can help a model learn effectively from fewer examples with a small parameter increase.
summary.tldr: Equivariant Transformers encode predefined image transformations into network structure and improve limited-data classification with few additional parameters.

title: Equivariant Transformer Networks

abstract: Graph Convolutional Networks (GCNs) and their variants have experienced significant attention and have become the de facto methods for learning graph representations. GCNs derive inspiration primarily from recent deep learning approaches, and as a result, may inherit unnecessary complexity and redundant computation. In this paper, we reduce this excess complexity through successively removing nonlinearities and collapsing weight matrices between consecutive layers. We theoretically analyze the resulting linear model and show that it corresponds to a fixed low-pass filter followed by a linear classifier. Notably, our experimental evaluation demonstrates that these simplifications do not negatively impact accuracy in many downstream applications. Moreover, the resulting model scales to larger datasets, is naturally interpretable, and yields up to two orders of magnitude speedup over FastGCN.

paragraphs: Graph convolutional networks combine graph structure with learned transformations to build representations. This paper investigates whether some of their inherited deep-learning complexity is unnecessary. The authors progressively remove nonlinearities and combine the weight matrices between successive layers, producing a substantially simpler linear model.

Their theoretical analysis identifies the resulting computation as a fixed low-pass graph filter followed by a linear classifier. This description separates the graph-based filtering operation from the learned prediction step. It also makes the model easier to interpret, because its behavior can be understood through those two components rather than a sequence of nonlinear layers.

Experiments show that these simplifications preserve accuracy in many downstream applications. The resulting model also handles larger datasets and achieves speedups of up to two orders of magnitude over FastGCN. The evidence supports the usefulness of this simpler architecture across the evaluated settings, showing that graph filtering plus linear classification can retain much of the practical value of more elaborate graph convolutional models.
summary.tldr: Removing nonlinearities yields a graph filter plus linear classifier that preserves accuracy in many applications while substantially accelerating computation.

title: Simplifying Graph Convolutional Networks

abstract: To address the challenge of backpropagating the gradient through categorical variables, we propose the augment-REINFORCE-swap-merge (ARSM) gradient estimator that is unbiased and has low variance. ARSM first uses variable augmentation, REINFORCE, and Rao-Blackwellization to re-express the gradient as an expectation under the Dirichlet distribution, then uses variable swapping to construct differently expressed but equivalent expectations, and finally shares common random numbers between these expectations to achieve significant variance reduction. Experimental results show ARSM closely resembles the performance of the true gradient for optimization in univariate settings; outperforms existing estimators by a large margin when applied to categorical variational auto-encoders; and provides a "try-and-see self-critic" variance reduction method for discrete-action policy gradient, which removes the need of estimating baselines by generating a random number of pseudo actions and estimating their action-value functions.

paragraphs: Training models that make categorical choices requires estimating how those choices affect the objective. ARSM addresses this problem with a gradient estimator that is unbiased and has low variance. Unbiasedness means the estimator targets the correct gradient on average; low variance makes its individual estimates less noisy.

The method constructs several equivalent ways to express the same gradient. It first combines variable augmentation, REINFORCE, and Rao-Blackwellization to write the gradient as an expectation involving a Dirichlet distribution. Swapping variables produces additional equivalent expressions. Sharing random numbers across these expressions then reduces the variance of the combined estimate.

The experiments connect this construction to several uses. In univariate optimization, ARSM behaves similarly to using the true gradient. In categorical variational autoencoders, it substantially outperforms the compared estimators. For policy gradients with discrete actions, it also supplies a self-criticism mechanism: generated pseudo actions and their estimated values replace the need to estimate baselines. These results support the usefulness of coordinating randomness across equivalent gradient expressions.
summary.tldr: ARSM combines equivalent gradient expressions with shared randomness to provide unbiased, low-variance learning signals through categorical choices.

title: ARSM: Augment-REINFORCE-Swap-Merge Estimator for Gradient Backpropagation Through Categorical Variables

abstract: A growing body of research has shown that many classifiers are susceptible to adversarial examples – small strategic modifications to test inputs that lead to misclassification. In this work, we study general non-parametric methods, with a view towards understanding when they are robust to these modifications. We establish general conditions under which non-parametric methods are r-consistent – in the sense that they converge to optimally robust and accurate classifiers in the large sample limit. Concretely, our results show that when data is well-separated, nearest neighbors and kernel classifiers are r-consistent, while histograms are not. For general data distributions, we prove that preprocessing by Adversarial Pruning (Yang et. al., 2019)– that makes data well-separated – followed by nearest neighbors or kernel classifiers also leads to r-consistency.

In this work, we study general non-parametric methods, with a view towards understanding when they are robust to these modifications. paragraphs: This paper asks when nonparametric classifiers become robust to small, strategically chosen changes in test inputs. It studies r-consistency, a large-sample property that combines robustness with accuracy. The goal is to establish conditions under which increasing the amount of data leads to an optimally robust and accurate classifier.

For well-separated data, the authors prove r-consistency for nearest-neighbor and kernel classifiers. Histogram classifiers do not share that guarantee. This distinction shows that nonparametric methods cannot be treated as a single category when reasoning about adversarial robustness: the classification rule matters even within the stated favorable data setting.

For general data distributions, the paper proves that Adversarial Pruning followed by nearest neighbors or a kernel classifier also yields r-consistency. The preprocessing creates the separation needed by the subsequent learning methods. These are asymptotic guarantees about convergence as sample size grows. Their significance is to connect robustness to both data geometry and algorithm choice, while showing how preprocessing can extend the applicable setting.
summary.tldr: Nearest-neighbor and kernel classifiers are asymptotically robust under separation conditions, and Adversarial Pruning extends the guarantee to general distributions.

title: When are Non-Parametric Methods Robust?

abstract: We present Natural Gradient Boosting (NGBoost), an algorithm for generic probabilistic prediction via gradient boosting. Typical regression models return a point estimate, conditional on covariates, but probabilistic regression models output a full probability distribution over the outcome space, conditional on the covariates. This allows for predictive uncertainty estimation - crucial in applications like healthcare and weather forecasting. NGBoost generalizes gradient boosting to probabilistic regression by treating the parameters of the conditional distribution as targets for a multiparameter boosting algorithm. Furthermore, we show how the Natural Gradient is required to correct the training dynamics of our multiparameter boosting approach. NGBoost can be used with any base learner, any family of distributions with continuous parameters, and any scoring rule. NGBoost matches or exceeds the performance of existing methods for probabilistic prediction while offering additional benefits in flexibility, scalability, and usability. An open-source implementation is available at github.com/stanfordmlgroup/ngboost.

paragraphs: A regression model often returns one predicted outcome, but many applications also need information about uncertainty. NGBoost predicts an entire conditional probability distribution instead. This lets the model express a range of possible outcomes given the input features, which motivates its use in settings such as healthcare and weather forecasting.

The method extends gradient boosting by treating the parameters of that distribution as multiple prediction targets. Training must therefore coordinate updates to several parameters that jointly determine one predictive distribution. The authors show that the natural gradient is required to correct the training dynamics of their multiparameter boosting approach, making it a central part of the algorithm.

NGBoost supports any base learner, any distribution family with continuous parameters, and any scoring rule. This flexibility separates choices about the prediction model, uncertainty distribution, and training objective. The authors report performance matching or exceeding existing probabilistic prediction methods, alongside benefits in scalability and usability. The result is a general boosting framework for learning uncertainty-bearing predictions rather than only point estimates.
summary.tldr: NGBoost uses natural-gradient updates to extend boosting from point predictions to flexible conditional probability distributions.

title: NGBoost: Natural Gradient Boosting for Probabilistic Prediction

abstract: A trade-off between accuracy and fairness is almost taken as a given in the existing literature on fairness in machine learning. Yet, it is not preordained that accuracy should decrease with increased fairness. Novel to this work, we examine fair classification through the lens of mismatched hypothesis testing: trying to find a classifier that distinguishes between two ideal distributions when given two mismatched distributions that are biased. Using Chernoff information, a tool in information theory, we theoretically demonstrate that, contrary to popular belief, there always exist ideal distributions such that optimal fairness and accuracy (with respect to the ideal distributions) are achieved simultaneously: there is no trade-off. Moreover, the same classifier yields the lack of a trade-off with respect to ideal distributions while yielding a trade-off when accuracy is measured with respect to the given (possibly biased) dataset. To complement our main result, we formulate an optimization to find ideal distributions and derive fundamental limits to explain why a trade-off exists on the given biased dataset. We also derive conditions under which active data collection can alleviate the fairness-accuracy trade-off in the real world. Our results lead us to contend that it is problematic to measure accuracy with respect to data that reflects bias, and instead, we should be considering accuracy with respect to ideal, unbiased data.

paragraphs: The paper questions whether improving fairness must reduce classification accuracy. Its approach distinguishes the distributions a classifier ideally should distinguish from the possibly biased distributions represented by available data. This becomes a mismatched hypothesis-testing problem: evaluation against the observed data may tell a different story from evaluation against an ideal target.

Using Chernoff information, the authors prove that there always exist ideal distributions for which optimal fairness and accuracy can be achieved together. Crucially, this is an existence result about ideal distributions. The same classifier can exhibit no trade-off relative to those distributions while exhibiting a trade-off when accuracy is measured against the supplied biased dataset.

The authors also formulate an optimization problem for finding ideal distributions and derive limits explaining trade-offs on biased data. They identify conditions under which active data collection can alleviate the trade-off in practice. Their argument makes the evaluation distribution central: an apparent conflict between fairness and accuracy can depend on what the accuracy measure treats as the correct target.
summary.tldr: Fairness–accuracy trade-offs can depend on the evaluation distribution, with ideal distributions existing where both objectives are simultaneously optimal.

title: Is There a Trade-Off Between Fairness and Accuracy? A Perspective Using Mismatched Hypothesis Testing

abstract: The decision-theoretic foundations of classical machine learning models have largely focused on estimating model parameters that minimize the expectation of a given loss function. However, as machine learning models are deployed in varied contexts, such as in high-stakes decision-making and societal settings, it is clear that these models are not just evaluated by their average performances. In this work, we study a novel notion of L-Risk based on the classical idea of rank-weighted learning. These L-Risks, induced by rank-dependent weighting functions with bounded variation, is a unification of popular risk measures such as conditional value-at-risk and those defined by cumulative prospect theory. We give uniform convergence bounds of this broad class of risk measures and study their consequences on a logistic regression example.

However, as machine learning models are deployed in varied contexts, such as in high-stakes decision-making and societal settings, it is clear that these models are not just evaluated by their average performances. In this work, we study a novel notion of L-Risk based on the classical idea of rank-weighted learning. paragraphs: Training objectives often summarize performance using average loss. In some settings, however, how losses are distributed matters as well as their average. This paper studies L-Risk, a framework that assigns importance according to where a loss falls in the ranking of outcomes, allowing evaluation to reflect priorities beyond mean performance.

The framework uses rank-dependent weighting functions with bounded variation. It brings together risk measures including conditional value-at-risk and measures arising from cumulative prospect theory. Treating these objectives as members of one class allows their statistical behavior to be studied through shared mathematical tools rather than separately for each measure.

The authors derive uniform convergence bounds for this broad class and examine their consequences using logistic regression. Such bounds address how reliably data-based risk estimates track their population counterparts across the considered models. The contribution provides a statistical foundation for learning with rank-sensitive objectives, under the stated restriction on weighting functions, and connects that foundation to a concrete prediction model.
summary.tldr: L-Risk unifies rank-weighted performance objectives and supplies uniform convergence guarantees for weighting functions with bounded variation.

title: Uniform Convergence of Rank-weighted Learning

abstract: We present and investigate a novel application domain for deep reinforcement learning (RL): droplet routing on digital microfluidic biochips (DMFBs). A DMFB, composed of a two-dimensional electrode array, manipulates discrete fluid droplets to automatically execute biochemical protocols such as point-of-care clinical diagnosis. However, a major concern associated with the use of DMFBs is that electrodes in a biochip can degrade over time. Droplet-transportation operations associated with the degraded electrodes can fail, thereby compromising the integrity of the bioassay outcome. We show that casting droplet transportation as an RL problem enables the training of deep network policies to capture the underlying health conditions of electrodes and to provide reliable fluidic operations. We propose a new RL-based droplet-routing flow that can be used for various sizes of DMFBs, and demonstrate reliable execution of an epigenetic bioassay with the RL droplet router on a fabricated DMFB. To facilitate further research, we also present a simulation environment based on the OpenAI Gym Interface for RL-guided droplet-routing problems on DMFBs.

paragraphs: Digital microfluidic biochips move tiny fluid droplets across a two-dimensional array of electrodes to carry out biochemical procedures. Reliable movement matters because a failed transport step can compromise the assay. The paper addresses a practical source of failure: electrodes deteriorate over time, so a route that previously worked may become unreliable.

The authors formulate droplet transportation as a reinforcement learning problem and train deep neural network policies for routing. Their aim is for these policies to capture the electrodes’ underlying health conditions and use that information to support reliable fluid movement. This connects the routing decision to the changing condition of the device. The proposed routing workflow also accommodates different chip sizes.

The work includes a demonstration of reliable execution of an epigenetic bioassay on a fabricated chip using the learned router. That provides a physical-device demonstration alongside the learning formulation. The authors also introduce a simulation environment using the OpenAI Gym interface, giving researchers a shared setting for investigating reinforcement learning methods for droplet routing.
summary.tldr: Deep reinforcement learning guides droplet routing around changing electrode conditions, with a successful bioassay demonstration on a fabricated chip.

title: Adaptive Droplet Routing in Digital Microfluidic Biochips Using Deep Reinforcement Learning

abstract: We consider active learning for binary classification in the agnostic pool-based setting. The vast majority of works in active learning in the agnostic setting are inspired by the CAL algorithm where each query is uniformly sampled from the disagreement region of the current version space. The sample complexity of such algorithms is described by a quantity known as the disagreement coefficient which captures both the geometry of the hypothesis space as well as the underlying probability space. To date, the disagreement coefficient has been justified by minimax lower bounds only, leaving the door open for superior instance dependent sample complexities. In this work we propose an algorithm that, in contrast to uniform sampling over the disagreement region, solves an experimental design problem to determine a distribution over examples from which to request labels. We show that the new approach achieves sample complexity bounds that are never worse than the best disagreement coefficient-based bounds, but in specific cases can be dramatically smaller. From a practical perspective, the proposed algorithm requires no hyperparameters to tune (e.g., to control the aggressiveness of sampling), and is computationally efficient by means of assuming access to an empirical risk minimization oracle (without any constraints). Empirically, we demonstrate that our algorithm is superior to state of the art agnostic active learning algorithms on image classification datasets.

paragraphs: Active learning selects which examples to label from an available pool. This paper studies binary classification in the agnostic setting. Many existing approaches sample uniformly from examples where the remaining candidate classifiers disagree. Their label requirements are described using a disagreement coefficient, whose worst-case justification leaves room for improvements on particular instances.

The proposed algorithm instead solves an experimental design problem to choose a distribution over examples to query. This makes label allocation responsive to the instance rather than uniform throughout the disagreement region. The authors prove sample complexity bounds that are never worse than the best disagreement-coefficient-based bounds and can be dramatically smaller in specific cases.

The method requires no hyperparameters to tune and is computationally efficient assuming access to an unconstrained empirical risk minimization oracle. That assumption supplies the optimization capability used by the algorithm. Image classification experiments show better performance than the compared state-of-the-art agnostic active learning methods, supporting the practical value of directing queries through experimental design.
summary.tldr: Experimental design guides label requests, matching established active-learning bounds while substantially improving them for some instances.

title: Improved Algorithms for Agnostic Pool-based Active Classification

abstract: In this paper, we study the hard and soft support vector regression techniques applied to a set of $n$ linear measurements of the form $y_i=\boldsymbol{\beta}_\star^{T}{\bf x}_i +n_i$ where $\boldsymbol{\beta}_\star$ is an unknown vector, $\left\{{\bf x}_i\right\}_{i=1}^n$ are the feature vectors and $\left\{{n}_i\right\}_{i=1}^n$ model the noise. Particularly, under some plausible assumptions on the statistical distribution of the data, we characterize the feasibility condition for the hard support vector regression in the regime of high dimensions and, when feasible, derive an asymptotic approximation for its risk. Similarly, we study the test risk for the soft support vector regression as a function of its parameters. Our results are then used to optimally tune the parameters intervening in the design of hard and soft support vector regression algorithms. Based on our analysis, we illustrate that adding more samples may be harmful to the test performance of support vector regression, while it is always beneficial when the parameters are optimally selected. Such a result reminds a similar phenomenon observed in modern learning architectures according to which optimally tuned architectures present a decreasing test performance curve with respect to the number of samples.
originalAbstract: In this paper, we study the hard and soft support vector regression techniques applied to a set of $n$ linear measurements of the form $y_i=\boldsymbol{\beta}_\star^{T}{\bf x}_i +n_i$ where $\boldsymbol{\beta}_\star$ is an unknown vector, $\left\{{\bf x}_i\right\}_{i=1}^n$ are the feature vectors and $\left\{{n}_i\right\}_{i=1}^n$ model the noise. Particularly, under some plausible assumptions on the statistical distribution of the data, we characterize the feasibility condition for the hard support vector regression in the regime of high dimensions and, when feasible, derive an asymptotic approximation for its risk. Similarly, we study the test risk for the soft support vector regression as a function of its parameters. Our results are then used to optimally tune the parameters intervening in the design of hard and soft support vector regression algorithms. Based on our analysis, we illustrate that adding more samples may be harmful to the test performance of support vector regression, while it is always beneficial when the parameters are optimally selected. Such a result reminds a similar phenomenon observed in modern learning architectures according to which optimally tuned architectures present a decreasing test performance curve with respect to the number of samples.

paragraphs: This paper studies how accurately support vector regression can recover a linear relationship from noisy measurements. It considers both hard and soft versions, asking when the hard formulation has a valid solution and how well either version predicts new data. The analysis focuses on high-dimensional settings under assumptions about the statistical distribution of the data.

For hard support vector regression, the authors characterize feasibility and derive an asymptotic approximation to prediction risk when a solution exists. For the soft version, they describe how test risk depends on the algorithm’s parameters. These results turn parameter selection into a problem informed by predicted performance rather than treating the settings as fixed.

A central finding is that adding training examples can hurt test performance when parameters are not appropriately chosen. Within the analyzed setting, optimally selecting those parameters makes additional samples beneficial. The implication is that the relationship between dataset size and accuracy depends on tuning: more data and unchanged settings need not produce the same trend as more data with optimal settings.
summary.tldr: A high-dimensional analysis of support vector regression explains its prediction risk and why optimal tuning matters when adding data.

title: A Precise Performance Analysis of Support Vector Regression

abstract: Two central problems in Stochastic Optimization are Min-Sum Set Cover and Pandora’s Box. In Pandora’s Box, we are presented with n boxes, each containing an unknown value and the goal is to open the boxes in some order to minimize the sum of the search cost and the smallest value found. Given a distribution of value vectors, we are asked to identify a near-optimal search order. Min-Sum Set Cover corresponds to the case where values are either 0 or infinity. In this work, we study the case where the value vectors are not drawn from a distribution but are presented to a learner in an online fashion. We present a computationally efficient algorithm that is constant-competitive against the cost of the optimal search order. We extend our results to a bandit setting where only the values of the boxes opened are revealed to the learner after every round. We also generalize our results to other commonly studied variants of Pandora’s Box and Min-Sum Set Cover that involve selecting more than a single value subject to a matroid constraint.

Min-Sum Set Cover is a special case in which values are either zero or infinity. This paper studies these problems when value vectors arrive online rather than being sampled from a given distribution.

The authors provide a computationally efficient algorithm whose cost is constant-competitive with the optimal search order. This gives a bounded-factor performance comparison for learning the order in the online setting. The result addresses the challenge of making search decisions while the sequence of values is being presented to the learner.

The paper extends the approach to bandit feedback, where each round reveals only the values in boxes that were actually opened. It also treats variants involving the selection of multiple values under a matroid constraint. These extensions broaden the framework to search problems with limited observations and structured restrictions on the selections that are allowed.
summary.tldr: An efficient online search algorithm achieves constant competitiveness, with extensions to partial feedback and constrained multiple selections.

title: Online Learning for Min Sum Set Cover and Pandora’s Box

abstract: Neural population activity relating to behaviour is assumed to be inherently low-dimensional despite the observed high dimensionality of data recorded using multi-electrode arrays. Therefore, predicting behaviour from neural population recordings has been shown to be most effective when using latent variable models. Over time however, the activity of single neurons can drift, and different neurons will be recorded due to movement of implanted neural probes. This means that a decoder trained to predict behaviour on one day performs worse when tested on a different day. On the other hand, evidence suggests that the latent dynamics underlying behaviour may be stable even over months and years. Based on this idea, we introduce a model capable of inferring behaviourally relevant latent dynamics from previously unseen data recorded from the same animal, without any need for decoder recalibration. We show that unsupervised domain adaptation combined with a sequential variational autoencoder, trained on several sessions, can achieve good generalisation to unseen data and correctly predict behaviour where conventional methods fail. Our results further support the hypothesis that behaviour-related neural dynamics are low-dimensional and stable over time, and will enable more effective and flexible use of brain computer interface technologies.

The proposed model combines unsupervised domain adaptation with a sequential variational autoencoder trained across several sessions. This shared latent description supports behavior prediction without requiring the decoder to be recalibrated for each new recording session.

The work points toward more flexible brain-computer interfaces by addressing changes in recording conditions while preserving access to the underlying behavioral information.
summary.tldr: Combining unsupervised domain adaptation with a sequential latent-variable model enables behavior prediction across unseen recording sessions from the same animal.

title: Robust alignment of cross-session recordings of neural population activity by behaviour via unsupervised domain adaptation

abstract: Negative sampling (NS) loss plays an important role in learning knowledge graph embedding (KGE) to handle a huge number of entities. However, the performance of KGE degrades without hyperparameters such as the margin term and number of negative samples in NS loss being appropriately selected. Currently, empirical hyperparameter tuning addresses this problem at the cost of computational time. To solve this problem, we theoretically analyzed NS loss to assist hyperparameter tuning and understand the better use of the NS loss in KGE learning. Our theoretical analysis showed that scoring methods with restricted value ranges, such as TransE and RotatE, require appropriate adjustment of the margin term or the number of negative samples different from those without restricted value ranges, such as RESCAL, ComplEx, and DistMult. We also propose subsampling methods specialized for the NS loss in KGE studied from a theoretical aspect. Our empirical analysis on the FB15k-237, WN18RR, and YAGO3-10 datasets showed that the results of actually trained models agree with our theoretical findings.

paragraphs: Knowledge graph embedding methods learn representations while handling potentially huge collections of entities. Negative sampling is an important part of this training, but performance depends on choices such as the loss margin and the number of negative samples. Finding suitable settings through repeated experiments can consume substantial computation.

This paper analyzes the negative sampling loss to explain how these choices interact with different scoring methods. Its central finding distinguishes methods whose scores have restricted value ranges from those whose scores do not. Restricted-range methods, including TransE and RotatE, require margin or negative-sample adjustments that differ from those appropriate for RESCAL, ComplEx, and DistMult. The scoring function therefore matters when selecting training settings.

The authors also propose subsampling methods designed specifically for this loss and grounded in their theoretical analysis. Experiments on FB15k-237, WN18RR, and YAGO3-10 produce results consistent with the theory. The contribution is a more principled basis for tuning and using negative sampling, connecting practical training behavior to mathematical properties of the embedding model.
summary.tldr: The paper explains how knowledge graph scoring functions affect negative sampling settings and develops theoretically motivated subsampling methods.

title: Comprehensive Analysis of Negative Sampling in Knowledge Graph Representation Learning

abstract: Mini-batch optimal transport (m-OT) has been successfully used in practical applications that involve probability measures with a very high number of supports. The m-OT solves several smaller optimal transport problems and then returns the average of their costs and transportation plans. Despite its scalability advantage, the m-OT does not consider the relationship between mini-batches which leads to undesirable estimation. Moreover, the m-OT does not approximate a proper metric between probability measures since the identity property is not satisfied. To address these problems, we propose a novel mini-batch scheme for optimal transport, named Batch of Mini-batches Optimal Transport (BoMb-OT), that finds the optimal coupling between mini-batches and it can be seen as an approximation to a well-defined distance on the space of probability measures. Furthermore, we show that the m-OT is a limit of the entropic regularized version of the BoMb-OT when the regularized parameter goes to infinity. Finally, we carry out experiments on various applications including deep generative models, deep domain adaptation, approximate Bayesian computation, color transfer, and gradient flow to show that the BoMb-OT can be widely applied and performs well in various applications.

paragraphs: Mini-batch optimal transport scales distribution comparison by solving smaller transport problems and averaging their costs and plans. However, this procedure ignores relationships between the mini-batches themselves. The paper identifies undesirable estimates and a failure of the identity property, which prevents the usual mini-batch construction from approximating a proper metric in the stated sense.

Batch of Mini-batches Optimal Transport, or BoMb-OT, adds a higher-level transport problem that finds an optimal coupling between mini-batches. This makes the relationships among batches part of the calculation. The authors show that the construction can be understood as an approximation to a well-defined distance between probability measures.

They also connect the new method to the previous approach: ordinary mini-batch optimal transport emerges as the entropically regularized BoMb-OT regularization parameter tends to infinity. Experiments cover deep generative models, domain adaptation, approximate Bayesian computation, color transfer, and gradient flow, reporting good performance across these applications. The work thus combines a more structured batch comparison with a theoretical account of how it relates to existing mini-batch transport.
summary.tldr: BoMb-OT optimally couples mini-batches to improve distribution comparison and approximate a well-defined distance between probability measures.

title: On Transportation of Mini-batches: A Hierarchical Approach

abstract: We study the efficiency of Thompson sampling for contextual bandits. Existing Thompson sampling-based algorithms need to construct a Laplace approximation (i.e., a Gaussian distribution) of the posterior distribution, which is inefficient to sample in high dimensional applications for general covariance matrices. Moreover, the Gaussian approximation may not be a good surrogate for the posterior distribution for general reward generating functions. We propose an efficient posterior sampling algorithm, viz., Langevin Monte Carlo Thompson Sampling (LMC-TS), that uses Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) methods to directly sample from the posterior distribution in contextual bandits. Our method is computationally efficient since it only needs to perform noisy gradient descent updates without constructing the Laplace approximation of the posterior distribution. We prove that the proposed algorithm achieves the same sublinear regret bound as the best Thompson sampling algorithms for a special case of contextual bandits, viz., linear contextual bandits. We conduct experiments on both synthetic data and real-world datasets on different contextual bandit models, which demonstrates that directly sampling from the posterior is both computationally efficient and competitive in performance.

paragraphs: Thompson sampling makes contextual-bandit decisions using samples from a posterior distribution. The paper targets the cost and potential inaccuracy of constructing a Gaussian approximation to that posterior. Sampling such an approximation can be inefficient in high dimensions with general covariance matrices, and its shape may poorly represent the posterior for general reward functions.

The proposed Langevin Monte Carlo Thompson Sampling method uses Markov chain Monte Carlo to sample directly from the posterior. Its computation consists of noisy gradient-descent updates, avoiding construction of the Laplace approximation. This changes the sampling mechanism while keeping posterior sampling at the center of the decision procedure.

For linear contextual bandits, the authors prove the same sublinear regret bound as the best Thompson-sampling algorithms. That theoretical guarantee is specifically for the linear case. Experiments cover synthetic and real datasets with different contextual-bandit models, showing computational efficiency and competitive performance. Together, the results provide a formal guarantee in one important setting and empirical evidence for a broader range of reward models.
summary.tldr: Langevin-based posterior sampling makes contextual-bandit Thompson sampling efficient, with a matching regret guarantee for the linear case.

title: Langevin Monte Carlo for Contextual Bandits

abstract: We analyze Elman-type recurrent neural networks (RNNs) and their training in the mean-field regime. Specifically, we show convergence of gradient descent training dynamics of the RNN to the corresponding mean-field formulation in the large width limit. We also show that the fixed points of the limiting infinite-width dynamics are globally optimal, under some assumptions on the initialization of the weights. Our results establish optimality for feature-learning with wide RNNs in the mean-field regime.
originalAbstract: We analyze Elman-type recurrent neural networks (RNNs) and their training in the mean-field regime. Specifically, we show convergence of gradient descent training dynamics of the RNN to the corresponding mean-field formulation in the large width limit. We also show that the fixed points of the limiting infinite-width dynamics are globally optimal, under some assumptions on the initialization of the weights. Our results establish optimality for feature-learning with wide RNNs in the mean-field regime.

paragraphs: Training recurrent networks involves complex interactions among parameters reused across time. This paper studies Elman-type RNNs through a mean-field description that becomes appropriate as network width grows. The aim is to understand feature learning and the quality of the solutions represented by the limiting dynamics.

The authors show that gradient-descent training dynamics converge to the corresponding mean-field formulation in the large-width limit. They then analyze fixed points of those infinite-width dynamics. Under assumptions on weight initialization, every such fixed point is globally optimal, giving a favorable characterization of the limiting optimization landscape.

The result establishes an optimality property for wide RNNs in the mean-field regime. Two distinctions are important for interpreting it: convergence of finite-width dynamics to a limiting description is different from proving every training run reaches a fixed point, and optimality in that limit is not an unrestricted guarantee for finite networks with arbitrary initialization. The abstract reports a theoretical contribution rather than benchmark improvements.
summary.tldr: Elman-type RNN training admits a mean-field limit whose fixed points are globally optimal under initialization assumptions.

title: Global optimality of Elman-type RNNs in the mean-field regime

abstract: Reward design is one of the most critical and challenging aspects when formulating a task as a reinforcement learning (RL) problem. In practice, it often takes several attempts of reward specification and learning with it in order to find one that leads to sample-efficient learning of the desired behavior. Instead, in this work, we study whether directly incorporating multiple alternate reward formulations of the same task in a single agent can lead to faster learning. We analyze multi-reward extensions of action-elimination algorithms and prove more favorable instance-dependent regret bounds compared to their single-reward counterparts, both in multi-armed bandits and in tabular Markov decision processes. Our bounds scale for each state-action pair with the inverse of the largest gap among all reward functions. This suggests that learning with multiple rewards can indeed be more sample-efficient, as long as the rewards agree on an optimal policy. We further prove that when rewards do not agree, multi-reward action elimination in multi-armed bandits still learns a policy that is good across all reward functions.

paragraphs: Reward design often involves trying several formulations before finding one that teaches the desired behavior efficiently. This paper asks whether a single agent can benefit from learning with multiple alternative rewards for the same task at once. It studies this question through multi-reward versions of action-elimination algorithms, which progressively rule out less favorable actions.

For multi-armed bandits and tabular Markov decision processes, the authors prove improved instance-dependent regret bounds relative to single-reward versions. For each state-action pair, the bounds depend on the inverse of the largest gap across reward functions. A reward that distinguishes that action more clearly can therefore contribute to a more favorable bound, even when other rewards offer weaker separation.

The sample-efficiency implication is conditional on the reward functions agreeing on an optimal policy. The authors also analyze disagreement in multi-armed bandits, proving that multi-reward action elimination still learns a policy that is good across all reward functions. These results separate the benefit of aligned alternative rewards from the different objective that remains achievable when the rewards disagree.
summary.tldr: Multiple rewards can improve action-elimination regret bounds when they share an optimal policy, with a separate bandit guarantee when rewards disagree.

title: Reinforcement Learning Can Be More Efficient with Multiple Rewards

abstract: The trade-off between regret and computational cost is a fundamental problem for online kernel regression, and previous algorithms worked on the trade-off can not keep optimal regret bounds at a sublinear computational complexity. In this paper, we propose two new algorithms, AOGD-ALD and NONS-ALD, which can keep nearly optimal regret bounds at a sublinear computational complexity, and give sufficient conditions under which our algorithms work. Both algorithms dynamically maintain a group of nearly orthogonal basis used to approximate the kernel mapping, and keep nearly optimal regret bounds by controlling the approximate error. The number of basis depends on the approximate error and the decay rate of eigenvalues of the kernel matrix. If the eigenvalues decay exponentially, then AOGD-ALD and NONS-ALD separately achieves a regret of $O(\sqrt{L(f)})$ and $O(\mathrm{d}_{\mathrm{eff}}(\mu)\ln{T})$ at a computational complexity in $O(\ln^2{T})$. If the eigenvalues decay polynomially with degree $p\geq 1$, then our algorithms keep the same regret bounds at a computational complexity in $o(T)$ in the case of $p>4$ and $p\geq 10$, respectively. $L(f)$ is the cumulative losses of $f$ and $\mathrm{d}_{\mathrm{eff}}(\mu)$ is the effective dimension of the problem. The two regret bounds are nearly optimal and are not comparable.

paragraphs: Online kernel regression must balance predictive performance against computational cost as data arrives. The paper proposes AOGD-ALD and NONS-ALD, which retain nearly optimal regret bounds with sublinear computational complexity under sufficient conditions. Regret measures accumulated loss relative to a comparison predictor, making this a tradeoff between prediction quality and the work required to maintain it.

Both algorithms maintain a changing collection of nearly orthogonal basis elements to approximate the kernel mapping. Controlling approximation error preserves their regret guarantees. The required basis size depends on the allowed error and how quickly the kernel matrix’s eigenvalues decay, linking computational savings to the structure of the kernel problem.

For polynomial decay, the same respective bounds accompany sublinear computation when p > 4 and p ≥ 10. L(f) is comparator cumulative loss and d_eff is effective dimension. The regret bounds are nearly optimal but not comparable, so neither uniformly dominates the other.
summary.tldr: Two adaptive kernel approximations achieve nearly optimal, distinct regret bounds with sublinear computation under sufficient eigenvalue-decay conditions.

title: Nearly Optimal Algorithms with Sublinear Computational Complexity for Online Kernel Regression

abstract: We present Language-Image Value learning (LIV), a unified objective for vision-language representation and reward learning from action-free videos with text annotations. Exploiting a novel connection between dual reinforcement learning and mutual information contrastive learning, the LIV objective trains a multi-modal representation that implicitly encodes a universal value function for tasks specified as language or image goals. We use LIV to pre-train the first control-centric vision-language representation from large human video datasets such as EpicKitchen. Given only a language or image goal, the pre-trained LIV model can assign dense rewards to each frame in videos of unseen robots or humans attempting that task in unseen environments. Further, when some target domain-specific data is available, the same objective can be used to fine-tune and improve LIV and even other pre-trained representations for robotic control and reward specification in that domain. In our experiments on several simulated and real-world robot environments, LIV models consistently outperform the best prior input state representations for imitation learning, as well as reward specification methods for policy synthesis. Our results validate the advantages of joint vision-language representation and reward learning within the unified, compact LIV framework.

paragraphs: Robotic control needs both useful representations of observations and rewards that indicate progress toward a goal. Language-Image Value learning, or LIV, learns these together from videos with text annotations but no action labels. Tasks can be specified through either language or a goal image.

The objective connects dual reinforcement learning with mutual-information contrastive learning. The resulting multimodal representation implicitly contains a universal value function. After pretraining on large human video datasets, including EpicKitchen, LIV can assign rewards to individual frames of unseen humans or robots attempting a task in unfamiliar environments. These dense rewards provide feedback throughout a video.

Across the reported simulated and real-world robot experiments, LIV consistently outperforms the best prior input representations for imitation learning and reward methods for policy synthesis. The findings support learning representations and task progress together, with a shared objective spanning pretraining and adaptation to a particular robotic setting.
summary.tldr: LIV jointly learns visual-language representations and goal-conditioned rewards from action-free videos for robotic control.

title: LIV: Language-Image Representations and Rewards for Robotic Control

abstract: Self-predictive unsupervised learning methods such as BYOL or SimSIAM have shown impressive results, and counter-intuitively, do not collapse to trivial representations. In this work, we aim at exploring the simplest possible mathematical arguments towards explaining the underlying mechanisms behind self-predictive unsupervised learning. We start with the observation that those methods crucially rely on the presence of a predictor network (and stop-gradient). With simple linear algebra, we show that when using a linear predictor, the optimal predictor is close to an orthogonal projection, and propose a general framework based on orthonormalization that enables to interpret and give intuition on why BYOL works. In addition, this framework demonstrates the crucial role of the exponential moving average and stop-gradient operator in BYOL as an efficient orthonormalization mechanism. We use these insights to propose four new closed-form predictor variants of BYOL to support our analysis. Our closed-form predictors outperform standard linear trainable predictor BYOL at 100 and 300 epochs (top-1 linear accuracy on ImageNet).

paragraphs: Self-predictive learning methods such as BYOL and SimSiam learn useful representations without collapsing to trivial outputs. This paper seeks a simple mathematical explanation for that behavior. It starts from the importance of the predictor network and the stop-gradient operation, asking what role these components play in shaping learned representations.

Using linear algebra, the authors show that an optimal linear predictor is close to an orthogonal projection. They build an interpretation around orthonormalization, which organizes representation directions into an orthogonal structure. Within this framework, BYOL's exponential moving average and stop-gradient operation act as an efficient orthonormalization mechanism, providing an explanation of how these training ingredients work together.

The analysis also motivates four predictor variants with closed-form expressions. In ImageNet evaluations after 100 and 300 training epochs, these variants outperform BYOL with a standard trainable linear predictor on top-1 linear accuracy. This links the proposed interpretation to a concrete design change. The explanation specifically develops from the linear-predictor setting, while the experiments support the usefulness of the resulting predictor constructions.
summary.tldr: An orthonormalization perspective explains key BYOL components and motivates closed-form predictors that improve the reported ImageNet linear-evaluation results.

title: The Edge of Orthogonality: A Simple View of What Makes BYOL Tick

abstract: Despite not being designed for this purpose, the use of variational autoencoders (VAEs) has proven remarkably effective for disentangled representation learning (DRL). Recent research attributes this success to certain characteristics of the loss function that prevent latent space rotation, or hypothesize about the orthogonality properties of the decoder by drawing parallels with principal component analysis (PCA). This hypothesis, however, has only been tested experimentally for linear VAEs, and the theoretical justification still remains an open problem. Moreover, since real-world VAEs are often inherently non-linear due to the use of neural architectures, understanding DRL capabilities of real-world VAEs remains a critical task. Our work takes a step towards understanding disentanglement in real-world VAEs to theoretically establish how the orthogonality properties of the decoder promotes disentanglement in practical applications. Complementary to our theoretical contributions, our experimental results corroborate our analysis. Code is available at https://github.com/criticalml-uw/Disentanglement-in-VAE.
