paragraphs: Variational autoencoders often learn disentangled representations even though that was not their original design goal. This paper investigates why. Earlier explanations focus on loss-function properties that restrict rotations of the latent space, or connect the decoder’s orthogonality properties with ideas from principal component analysis.

The authors identify a gap in that account: the decoder-orthogonality hypothesis had only been tested experimentally for linear VAEs, while practical neural-network VAEs are commonly nonlinear. Understanding the behavior of these real-world models therefore requires theoretical support that goes beyond the evidence from linear cases.

The paper develops theory establishing how decoder orthogonality properties promote disentanglement in practical applications, and experiments corroborate the analysis. This offers a mathematical explanation for a useful behavior observed in VAEs and takes a step toward understanding nonlinear models. The claim is about how these properties encourage disentanglement; the work frames its contribution as progress on explaining that mechanism, rather than a universal guarantee that every VAE learns disentangled representations.
summary.tldr: The paper provides theory and supporting experiments explaining how decoder orthogonality promotes disentanglement in practical variational autoencoders.

title: Why do Variational Autoencoders Really Promote Disentanglement?

abstract: We introduce SPARse fine-grained Contrastive alignment (SPARC), a simple method for pretraining more fine-grained multimodal representations from image-text pairs. Given that multiple image patches often correspond to single words, we propose to learn a grouping of image patches for every token in the caption. To achieve this, we use a sparse similarity metric between image patches and language tokens and compute for each token a language-grouped vision embedding as the weighted average of patches. The token and language-grouped vision embeddings are then contrasted through a fine-grained sequence-wise loss that only depends on individual samples and does not require other batch samples as negatives, i.e., more detailed information is encoded in a computationally inexpensive way. SPARC combines this fine-grained loss with a contrastive loss between global image and text embeddings to learn representations that simultaneously encode global and local information. We thoroughly evaluate SPARC and show improved performance over competing approaches both on image-level tasks relying on coarse-grained information, e.g. classification, as well as region-level tasks relying on fine-grained information, e.g., retrieval, object detection, segmentation while also improving model faithfulness and captioning in foundational vision-language models.

paragraphs: Matching an entire image with a caption does not by itself specify which image regions correspond to individual words. SPARC addresses this finer level of alignment during image-text pretraining. Its starting point is that a single word can correspond to several image patches, so the method learns a patch grouping for each caption token.

SPARC uses sparse similarities between patches and tokens to compute a weighted visual representation for each token. A fine-grained loss then contrasts the token representations with these grouped visual representations within each sample. This loss does not need other batch samples as negatives. A separate global image-text contrastive loss preserves learning at the whole-image and whole-caption level.

The evaluations report improvements on both coarse tasks, such as image classification, and tasks requiring regional detail, including retrieval, detection, and segmentation. SPARC also improves faithfulness and captioning in foundation vision-language models. The approach therefore combines local correspondence learning with global alignment while keeping the fine-grained component computationally inexpensive.
summary.tldr: SPARC aligns caption tokens with learned groups of image patches, improving both global and fine-grained image-text representations.

title: Improving fine-grained understanding in image-text pre-training

abstract: Diffusion models have made significant strides in visual content generation but also raised increasing demands on generated image detection. Existing detection methods have achieved considerable progress, but they usually suffer a significant decline in accuracy when detecting images generated by an unseen diffusion model. In this paper, we seek to address the generalizability of generated image detectors from the perspective of hard sample classification. The basic idea is that if a classifier can distinguish generated images that closely resemble real ones, then it can also effectively detect less similar samples, potentially even those produced by a different diffusion model. Based on this idea, we propose Diffusion Reconstruction Contrastive Learning (DRCT), a universal framework to enhance the generalizability of the existing detectors. DRCT generates hard samples by high-quality diffusion reconstruction and adopts contrastive training to guide the learning of diffusion artifacts. In addition, we have built a million-scale dataset, DRCT-2M, including 16 types diffusion models for the evaluation of generalizability of detection methods. Extensive experimental results show that detectors enhanced with DRCT achieve over a 10% accuracy improvement in cross-set tests. The code, models, and dataset will soon be available at https://github.com/beibuwandeluori/DRCT.

paragraphs: Detectors of diffusion-generated images often lose accuracy when images come from a generator they have not encountered before. DRCT tackles this generalization problem through difficult training examples: generated images that closely resemble real ones. Its motivating idea is that learning to distinguish these subtle cases could also help identify more obvious generated images, potentially including outputs from other diffusion models.

The framework creates hard samples through high-quality diffusion reconstruction. It then uses contrastive training to guide detectors toward learning diffusion artifacts. DRCT is designed to enhance existing detectors, making the training procedure the central intervention rather than requiring a single specialized detector architecture.

The authors also introduce DRCT-2M, a million-scale evaluation dataset covering 16 types of diffusion models. In cross-set tests, detectors enhanced with DRCT achieve accuracy improvements exceeding 10%. These findings support the approach’s ability to improve transfer across evaluated data settings. The proposed connection between difficult examples and unseen generators remains a motivation supported by experiments, rather than a guarantee of detection for every future generator.
summary.tldr: DRCT improves generated-image detector generalization by training on realistic diffusion reconstructions with a contrastive objective.

title: DRCT: Diffusion Reconstruction Contrastive Training towards Universal Detection of Diffusion Generated Images

abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is widely used for compressing a teacher model to a smaller student model, reducing its inference cost and memory footprint while preserving model capabilities. However, current KD methods for auto-regressive sequence models (e.g., large language models) suffer from missing a standardized objective function. Moreover, the recent use of student-generated outputs to address training-inference mismatches has significantly escalated computational costs. To tackle these issues, we introduce DistiLLM, a more effective and efficient KD framework for auto-regressive language models. DistiLLM comprises two components: (1) a novel skew Kullback-Leibler divergence loss, where we unveil and leverage its theoretical properties, and (2) an adaptive off-policy approach designed to enhance the efficiency in utilizing student-generated outputs. Extensive experiments, including instruction-following tasks, demonstrate the effectiveness of DistiLLM in building high-performing student models while achieving up to 4.3$\times$ speedup compared to recent KD methods.

paragraphs: Knowledge distillation trains a smaller student model to retain capabilities of a larger teacher, reducing the cost of using the model. For language models that generate sequences step by step, the paper identifies two challenges: the lack of a standardized training objective and the computational expense of incorporating outputs generated by the student.

DistiLLM addresses both through a two-part framework. First, it introduces a skew Kullback-Leibler divergence loss and uses its theoretical properties to guide distillation. This loss provides a way to compare teacher and student output distributions. Second, an adaptive off-policy approach improves the efficiency with which training uses student-generated outputs.

Student-generated outputs matter because they help address the mismatch between training and the conditions a student encounters when generating its own sequences. DistiLLM aims to retain this benefit with less computation. Extensive experiments, including instruction-following tasks, demonstrate high-performing students and speedups of up to 4.3 times compared with recent distillation methods. The reported gain concerns the evaluated distillation procedures, rather than a universal acceleration for all language-model training.
summary.tldr: DistiLLM combines a skew divergence loss with efficient use of student-generated outputs, achieving distillation speedups of up to 4.3 times.

title: DistiLLM: Towards Streamlined Distillation for Large Language Models

abstract: Recent advances in adversarial robustness rely on an abundant set of training data, where using external or additional datasets has become a common setting. However, in real life, the training data is often kept private for security and privacy issues, while only the pretrained weight is available to the public. In such scenarios, existing methods that assume accessibility to the original data become inapplicable. Thus we investigate the pivotal problem of data-free adversarial robustness, where we try to achieve adversarial robustness without accessing any real data. Through a preliminary study, we highlight the severity of the problem by showing that robustness without the original dataset is difficult to achieve, even with similar domain datasets. To address this issue, we propose DataFreeShield, which tackles the problem from two perspectives: surrogate dataset generation and adversarial training using the generated data. Through extensive validation, we show that DataFreeShield outperforms baselines, demonstrating that the proposed method sets the first entirely data-free solution for the adversarial robustness problem.

paragraphs: Improving a model's resistance to adversarial attacks commonly relies on access to substantial training data. Yet a publicly available model may include only its pretrained weights, with its original data withheld for privacy or security reasons. This paper studies how to strengthen adversarial robustness when no real data can be accessed.

A preliminary investigation shows that replacing the original dataset with data from a similar domain does not make robustness easy to obtain. DataFreeShield addresses the challenge through two connected components: generating a surrogate dataset and conducting adversarial training with that generated data. Both the data source and the robustness training procedure are therefore parts of the proposed solution.

The authors report that DataFreeShield outperforms baselines across extensive validation and describe it as the first entirely data-free solution to this robustness problem. The significance is practical for settings where pretrained weights are available but real examples are inaccessible. The reported results establish that generated training material can support improved adversarial robustness within that restricted access setting.
summary.tldr: DataFreeShield combines surrogate data generation with adversarial training to improve robustness without accessing real data.

title: DataFreeShield: Defending Adversarial Attacks without Training Data

abstract: Continual Test-Time Adaptation (CTTA) is designed to optimize the model during deployment under changing conditions. CTTA is an important problem as it enables models to remain effective and reliable in dynamic and evolving environments. However, tackling the CTTA problem is nontrivial. The model needs to be computationally and memory-efficient to rapidly update its parameters for ever-changing environments in real-time. Also, the model should generalize well to new unseen domains while maintaining its capability on previously encountered ones, as old domains can be revisited in future adaptation phases. To tackle these challenges, this paper proposes BECoTTA, a parameter/memory-efficient yet powerful framework for CTTA. We introduce Mixture-of-Domain Low-rank Experts (MoDE) that contains two core components: ?i) Domain-Adaptive Routing, which can aid in selectively capturing the domain-adaptive knowledge, and ii) Domain-Expert Synergy Loss to maximize the dependency between each domain and expert. We validate our proposed method over multiple CTTA benchmarks, getting 5.81% performance gain, while only requiring 0.001x trainable parameters. We also provide analyses of our BECoTTA, including expert assignment and target domain relation.

paragraphs: Continual test-time adaptation updates a model during deployment as its environment changes. The challenge is both computational and statistical: updates must be efficient, and learning a new domain should preserve useful capabilities for domains that may return later. BECoTTA addresses these requirements with an input-dependent collection of specialized experts.

Its central component, Mixture-of-Domain Low-rank Experts, combines domain-adaptive routing with a domain-expert synergy loss. The routing helps select knowledge suited to the current input's domain. The loss encourages stronger dependence between domains and experts, supporting specialization within the collection. Low-rank experts make this adaptation framework economical in trainable parameters and memory.

Across multiple continual adaptation benchmarks, the authors report a 5.81% performance gain while requiring 0.001 times the trainable parameters in their reported comparison. They also examine how inputs are assigned to experts and how target domains relate to one another. These findings support the approach as a way to combine selective adaptation with low parameter cost under changing deployment conditions.
summary.tldr: BECoTTA uses domain-aware routing among low-rank experts to improve continual test-time adaptation with very few trainable parameters.

title: BECoTTA: Input-dependent Online Blending of Experts for Continual Test-time Adaptation

abstract: Probabilistic Circuits (PCs) are a general framework for tractable deep generative models, which support exact and efficient probabilistic inference on their learned distributions. Recent modeling and training advancements have enabled their application to complex real-world tasks. However, the time and memory inefficiency of existing PC implementations hinders further scaling up. This paper proposes PyJuice, a general GPU implementation design for PCs that improves prior art in several regards. Specifically, PyJuice is 1-2 orders of magnitude faster than existing systems (including very recent ones) at training large-scale PCs. Moreover, PyJuice consumes 2-5x less GPU memory, which enables us to train larger models. At the core of our system is a compilation process that converts a PC into a compact representation amenable to efficient block-based parallelization, which significantly reduces IO and makes it possible to leverage Tensor Cores available in modern GPUs. Empirically, PyJuice can be used to improve state-of-the-art PCs trained on image (e.g., ImageNet32) and language (e.g., WikiText, CommonGen) datasets. We further establish a new set of baselines on natural image and language datasets by benchmarking existing PC structures but with much larger sizes and more training epochs, with the hope of incentivizing future research. Code is available at https://github.com/Tractables/pyjuice.

paragraphs: Probabilistic circuits are generative models that permit exact, efficient probabilistic inference on the distributions they learn. Their practical scale can still be limited by the time and memory costs of software implementations. PyJuice addresses this systems bottleneck with a general GPU implementation design for training larger circuits.

Its core is a compilation process that translates a circuit into a compact representation suited to block-based parallel computation. This reduces data movement and enables use of modern GPUs' Tensor Cores. The paper reports training speedups of one to two orders of magnitude over existing systems, together with two to five times lower GPU memory consumption.

Those savings allow larger models to be trained. Experiments use PyJuice to improve state-of-the-art probabilistic circuits on image and language datasets, including ImageNet32, WikiText, and CommonGen. The authors also establish baselines using existing circuit structures at larger sizes and with more training epochs. The contribution shows how implementation efficiency can expand the modeling scale available to a framework whose appeal already includes tractable inference.
summary.tldr: PyJuice compiles probabilistic circuits for efficient GPU execution, reporting major training speedups and lower memory use that enable larger models.

title: Scaling Tractable Probabilistic Circuits: A Systems Perspective

abstract: Informally, the "linear representation hypothesis" is the idea that high-level concepts are represented linearly as directions in some representation space. In this paper, we address two closely related questions: What does "linear representation" actually mean? And, how do we make sense of geometric notions (e.g., cosine similarity and projection) in the representation space? To answer these, we use the language of counterfactuals to give two formalizations of linear representation, one in the output (word) representation space, and one in the input (context) space. We then prove that these connect to linear probing and model steering, respectively. To make sense of geometric notions, we use the formalization to identify a particular (non-Euclidean) inner product that respects language structure in a sense we make precise. Using this causal inner product, we show how to unify all notions of linear representation. In particular, this allows the construction of probes and steering vectors using counterfactual pairs. Experiments with LLaMA-2 demonstrate the existence of linear representations of concepts, the connection to interpretation and control, and the fundamental role of the choice of inner product.

paragraphs: The idea that a language model represents concepts as directions sounds simple, but it leaves important questions unresolved. What precisely counts as a linear concept representation, and which geometry makes comparisons between directions meaningful? This paper addresses both questions by using counterfactuals to formalize representations in the output word space and the input context space.

The authors prove connections between these two formulations and linear probing and model steering, respectively. They then identify a non-Euclidean inner product that respects language structure in a precisely defined sense. This causal inner product supplies the geometry needed to connect the different formulations, including how projections and similarities should be interpreted.

The framework also allows probes and steering vectors to be constructed from counterfactual pairs. Experiments with LLaMA-2 demonstrate linear concept representations and their connection to interpreting and controlling the model. They also show the fundamental importance of the inner product choice. The contribution therefore clarifies both what a concept direction means and how its geometry affects practical interpretation and intervention.
summary.tldr: The paper formalizes linear concept representations and introduces a causal geometry connecting language model probing, steering, and counterfactual pairs.

title: The Linear Representation Hypothesis and the Geometry of Large Language Models

abstract: The recent embrace of machine learning (ML) in the development of autonomous weapons systems (AWS) creates serious risks to geopolitical stability and the free exchange of ideas in AI research. This topic has received comparatively little attention of late compared to risks stemming from superintelligent artificial general intelligence (AGI), but requires fewer assumptions about the course of technological development and is thus a nearer-future issue. ML is already enabling the substitution of AWS for human soldiers in many battlefield roles, reducing the upfront human cost, and thus political cost, of waging offensive war. In the case of peer adversaries, this increases the likelihood of "low intensity" conflicts which risk escalation to broader warfare. In the case of non-peer adversaries, it reduces the domestic blowback to wars of aggression. This effect can occur regardless of other ethical issues around the use of military AI such as the risk of civilian casualties, and does not require any superhuman AI capabilities. Further, the military value of AWS raises the specter of an AI-powered arms race and the misguided imposition of national security restrictions on AI research. Our goal in this paper is to raise awareness among the public and ML researchers on the near-future risks posed by full or near-full autonomy in military technology, and we provide regulatory suggestions to mitigate these risks. We call upon AI policy experts and the defense AI community in particular to embrace transparency and caution in their development and deployment of AWS to avoid the negative effects on global stability and AI research that we highlight here.

paragraphs: This position paper argues that autonomous weapons powered by machine learning pose near-future risks to geopolitical stability and open AI research. The authors focus on risks that do not require superhuman capabilities. Their concern is that replacing soldiers in battlefield roles can lower the immediate human and political costs of initiating offensive conflict.

They describe different consequences depending on the adversaries involved. Between peers, lower costs may encourage limited conflicts that risk escalating into broader war. Against weaker adversaries, they may reduce domestic opposition to aggression. The argument concerns incentives to wage war and can apply independently of other military-AI concerns, including civilian casualties.

The authors also warn that the military value of autonomous weapons could encourage an AI arms race and national-security restrictions on research. They offer regulatory suggestions and call for transparency and caution among policymakers and the defense AI community. These are policy arguments about potential consequences, intended to draw attention to risks from full or near-full military autonomy and their implications for scientific exchange.
summary.tldr: This position paper argues that autonomous weapons could lower barriers to conflict, encourage an arms race, and threaten open AI research.

title: Position: AI-Powered Autonomous Weapons Risk Geopolitical Instability and Threaten AI Research

abstract: As the use of predictive machine learning algorithms increases in high-stakes decision-making, it is imperative that these algorithms are fair across sensitive groups. However, measuring and enforcing fairness in real-world applications can be challenging due to missing or incomplete sensitive group information. Proxy-sensitive attributes have been proposed as a practical and effective solution in these settings, but only for parity-based fairness notions. Knowing how to evaluate and control for fairness with missing sensitive group data for newer, different, and more flexible frameworks, such as multiaccuracy and multicalibration, remains unexplored. In this work, we address this gap by demonstrating that in the absence of sensitive group data, proxy-sensitive attributes can provably be used to derive actionable upper bounds on the true multiaccuracy and multicalibration violations, providing insights into a predictive model’s potential worst-case fairness violations. Additionally, we show that adjusting models to satisfy multiaccuracy and multicalibration across proxy-sensitive attributes can significantly mitigate these violations for the true, but unknown, sensitive groups. Through several experiments on real-world datasets, we illustrate that approximate multiaccuracy and multicalibration can be achieved even when sensitive group data is incomplete or unavailable.

paragraphs: Evaluating predictive fairness across sensitive groups becomes difficult when group information is missing or incomplete. Proxy attributes offer an indirect way to represent those groups, but previous uses emphasized parity-based fairness. This paper investigates their use for multiaccuracy and multicalibration, which assess prediction errors and calibration across groups.

The authors prove that proxy-sensitive attributes can provide upper bounds on violations for the true sensitive groups, even when those group labels are unavailable. These bounds make the proxies useful for assessing potential worst-case fairness problems. The paper also examines model adjustment: enforcing multiaccuracy and multicalibration across proxy groups can substantially reduce violations across the true, unknown groups.

Experiments on real-world datasets illustrate that approximate multiaccuracy and multicalibration can be achieved with incomplete or unavailable sensitive-group information. The contribution therefore covers both evaluation and improvement. Proxies can help bound the fairness problem and guide corrective changes, while the stated goal remains approximate control of violations rather than treating proxy membership as identical to true group membership.
summary.tldr: Proxy-sensitive attributes can bound and help reduce multiaccuracy and multicalibration violations when true group labels are unavailable.

title: Multiaccuracy and Multicalibration via Proxy Groups

abstract: 3D vision-language grounding faces a fundamental data bottleneck: while 2D models train on billions of images, 3D models have access to only thousands of labeled scenes–a six-order-of-magnitude gap that severely limits performance. We introduce LIFT-GS, a practical distillation technique that overcomes this limitation by using differentiable rendering to bridge 3D and 2D supervision. LIFT-GS predicts 3D Gaussian representations from point clouds and uses them to render predicted language-conditioned 3D masks into 2D views, enabling supervision from 2D foundation models (SAM, CLIP, LLaMA) without requiring any 3D annotations. This render-supervised formulation enables end-to-end training of complete encoder-decoder architectures and is inherently model-agnostic. LIFT-GS achieves state-of-the-art results with 25.7% mAP on open-vocabulary instance segmentation (vs. 20.2% prior SOTA) and consistent 10-30% improvements on referential grounding tasks. Remarkably, pretraining effectively multiplies fine-tuning datasets by 2$\times$, demonstrating strong scaling properties that suggest 3D VLG currently operates in a severely data-scarce regime. Project page: https://liftgs.github.io.

paragraphs: Three-dimensional vision-language grounding has far fewer labeled scenes available than two-dimensional models have training images. LIFT-GS addresses this bottleneck by transferring supervision from established 2D foundation models into a 3D system. It uses rendered views as the connection between the two settings, without requiring 3D annotations for that supervision.

Starting from point clouds, LIFT-GS predicts 3D Gaussian representations and language-conditioned 3D masks. Differentiable rendering turns those masks into 2D views, where SAM, CLIP, and LLaMA provide supervision. Because training signals pass through the rendering process, the approach supports end-to-end learning of complete encoder-decoder architectures and is described as model-agnostic.

The authors report 25.7% mAP for open-vocabulary instance segmentation, compared with a previous best of 20.2%, alongside consistent 10–30% improvements on referential grounding tasks. They also report a pretraining benefit equivalent to doubling fine-tuning datasets. These scaling results suggest that limited data remains a major constraint on 3D grounding, and that rendered supervision can help address it.
summary.tldr: LIFT-GS transfers 2D foundation-model supervision through differentiable rendering to improve 3D language grounding without 3D annotations.

title: From Thousands to Billions: 3D Visual Language Grounding via Render-Supervised Distillation from 2D VLMs

abstract: Images are often obstructed by various obstacles due to capture limitations, hindering the observation of objects of interest. Most existing methods address occlusions from specific elements like fences or raindrops, but are constrained by the wide range of real-world obstructions, making comprehensive data collection impractical. To overcome these challenges, we propose Instruct2See, a novel zero-shot framework capable of handling both seen and unseen obstacles. The core idea of our approach is to unify obstruction removal by treating it as a soft-hard mask restoration problem, where any obstruction can be represented using multi-modal prompts, such as visual semantics and textual instructions, processed through a cross-attention unit to enhance contextual understanding and improve mode control. Additionally, a tunable mask adapter allows for dynamic soft masking, enabling real-time adjustment of inaccurate masks. Extensive experiments on both in-distribution and out-of-distribution obstacles show that Instruct2See consistently achieves strong performance and generalization in obstruction removal, regardless of whether the obstacles were present during the training phase. Code and dataset are available at https://jhscut.github.io/Instruct2See.

paragraphs: Image obstructions take many forms, and collecting training examples for every possible obstacle is impractical. Methods specialized for elements such as fences or raindrops can therefore struggle with that variety. Instruct2See proposes a unified obstruction-removal framework designed to handle both familiar obstacles and types absent from training.

The method treats removal as restoration under soft and hard masks. Visual information and textual instructions describe the obstruction, and a cross-attention unit processes those prompts to improve contextual understanding and control. A tunable mask adapter supports dynamic soft masking, allowing inaccurate masks to be adjusted in real time.

Experiments on obstacles both within and outside the training distribution show strong removal performance and generalization. The authors report that this holds in their evaluations whether or not the obstacle type appeared during training. The approach matters because it represents varied obstructions through a shared restoration task, while using prompts and adjustable masks to guide how a particular image should be repaired.
summary.tldr: Instruct2See combines multimodal prompts with adjustable masks to remove both previously seen and unseen image obstructions.

title: Instruct2See: Learning to Remove Any Obstructions Across Distributions

abstract: Social predictions do not passively describe the future; they actively shape it. They inform actions and change individual expectations in ways that influence the likelihood of the predicted outcome. Given these dynamics, to what extent can social events be predicted? This question was discussed throughout the 20th century by authors like Merton, Morgenstern, Simon, and others who considered it a central issue in social science methodology. In this work, we provide a modern answer to this old problem. Using recent ideas from performative prediction and outcome indistinguishability, we establish that one can always efficiently predict social events accurately, regardless of how predictions influence data. While achievable, we also show that these predictions are often undesirable, highlighting the limitations of previous desiderata. We end with a discussion of various avenues forward.

paragraphs: A prediction about a social event can influence the event itself. People may change their expectations and actions after hearing it, altering the likelihood of the predicted outcome. This paper revisits whether accurate prediction remains possible when forecasts participate in shaping the data they are supposed to predict.

The authors combine ideas from performative prediction and outcome indistinguishability to give a modern theoretical answer. Within their framework, they establish that accurate social predictions can always be produced efficiently, regardless of how predictions affect the data. The result addresses the feedback between forecasts and outcomes directly, showing that such influence does not by itself rule out the accuracy considered in their analysis.

The paper also shows that achievable predictions are often undesirable. This exposes a gap between satisfying previous prediction criteria and obtaining predictions one would want a social system to use. Its contribution therefore includes both an existence result and a critique of the goals used to judge success. The authors conclude by discussing possible directions for addressing that gap.
summary.tldr: Accurate, efficient prediction remains theoretically possible when forecasts shape social outcomes, but the resulting predictions can be undesirable.

title: Revisiting the Predictability of Performative, Social Events

abstract: Temporal Graph Neural Networks (TGNNs) are widely used to model dynamic systems where relationships and features evolve over time. Although TGNNs demonstrate strong predictive capabilities in these domains, their complex architectures pose significant challenges for explainability. Counterfactual explanation methods provide a promising solution by illustrating how modifications to input graphs can influence model predictions. To address this challenge, we present CoDy—Counterfactual Explainer for Dynamic Graphs—a model-agnostic, instance-level explanation approach that identifies counterfactual subgraphs to interpret TGNN predictions. CoDy employs a search algorithm that combines Monte Carlo Tree Search with heuristic selection policies, efficiently exploring a vast search space of potential explanatory subgraphs by leveraging spatial, temporal, and local event impact information. Extensive experiments against state-of-the-art factual and counterfactual baselines demonstrate CoDy’s effectiveness, with improvements of 16% in AUFSC+ over the strongest baseline. Our code is available at: https://github.com/daniel-gomm/CoDy

paragraphs: Temporal graph neural networks predict from systems whose relationships and features change over time. Explaining an individual prediction is difficult because both graph structure and event timing can matter. CoDy approaches this through counterfactual explanations: it searches for changes to the input graph that would affect a model’s prediction, making the model’s dependence on particular events easier to inspect.

The method produces explanations for individual instances and is designed to work independently of a particular temporal graph model architecture. It searches for counterfactual subgraphs using Monte Carlo Tree Search combined with heuristic selection rules. These rules use spatial relationships, temporal information, and the local impact of events to guide exploration through a large set of possible explanatory subgraphs.

Experiments compare CoDy with leading factual and counterfactual explanation methods. The authors report a 16% improvement in AUFSC+ over the strongest baseline. This provides empirical evidence that the guided search finds effective explanations in the tested settings, while retaining information about time that is central to interpreting predictions on dynamic graphs.
summary.tldr: CoDy explains temporal graph predictions by searching for counterfactual subgraphs using structural, temporal, and event-impact information.

title: CoDy: Counterfactual Explainers for Dynamic Graphs

abstract: The idea of value-aware model learning, that models should produce accurate value estimates, has gained prominence in model-based reinforcement learning. The MuZero loss, which penalizes a model’s value function prediction compared to the ground-truth value function, has been utilized in several prominent empirical works in the literature. However, theoretical investigation into its strengths and weaknesses is limited. In this paper, we analyze the family of value-aware model learning losses, which includes the popular MuZero loss. We show that these losses, as normally used, are uncalibrated surrogate losses, which means that they do not always recover the correct model and value function. Building on this insight, we propose corrections to solve this issue. Furthermore, we investigate the interplay between the loss calibration, latent model architectures, and auxiliary losses that are commonly employed when training MuZero-style agents. We show that while deterministic models can be sufficient to predict accurate values, learning calibrated stochastic models is still advantageous.

paragraphs: In model-based reinforcement learning, an environment model is useful partly because it supports accurate estimates of future value. Value-aware learning therefore trains models around the value predictions they produce. This paper investigates the theoretical behavior of these objectives, including the MuZero loss, which penalizes disagreement with the ground-truth value function.

The authors show that the usual versions of these losses are uncalibrated surrogate objectives. In this setting, optimizing the training objective does not always recover the correct environment model and value function. This identifies a mismatch between what the loss rewards and what the learning procedure is intended to recover. The paper proposes corrections to address that mismatch.

The analysis also examines how calibration interacts with latent model architectures and auxiliary training losses used in MuZero-style agents. A central distinction is that deterministic models can be sufficient for accurate value prediction, while calibrated stochastic models can still offer advantages. The result motivates choosing training objectives and model architecture together, without claiming that stochastic modeling is necessary for every accurate value estimate.
summary.tldr: The paper identifies calibration failures in value-aware model losses and proposes corrections while explaining benefits of calibrated stochastic models.

title: Calibrated Value-Aware Model Learning with Probabilistic Environment Models

abstract: Tensor regression is a powerful tool for analyzing complex multi-dimensional data in fields such as neuroimaging and spatiotemporal analysis, but its effectiveness is often hindered by insufficient sample sizes. To overcome this limitation, we adopt a transfer learning strategy that leverages knowledge from related source tasks to improve performance in data-scarce target tasks. This approach, however, introduces additional challenges including model shifts, covariate shifts, and decentralized data management. We propose the Low-Rank Tensor Transitions (LoRT) framework, which incorporates a novel fusion regularizer and a two-step refinement to enable robust adaptation while preserving low-tubal-rank structure. To support decentralized scenarios, we extend LoRT to D-LoRT, a distributed variant that maintains statistical efficiency with minimal communication overhead. Theoretical analysis and experiments on tensor regression tasks, including compressed sensing and completion, validate the robustness and versatility of the proposed methods. These findings indicate the potential of LoRT as a robust method for tensor regression in settings with limited data and complex distributional structures.

paragraphs: LoRT addresses tensor regression when the target task has too few samples to learn effectively on its own. It transfers knowledge from related source tasks while accounting for differences between tasks. These differences can involve both the regression models and the distributions of input data, making direct reuse of source information challenging.

The framework combines a fusion regularizer with a two-step refinement procedure. Its aim is to adapt transferred knowledge robustly while preserving a low-tubal-rank tensor structure, a form of compact organization in multidimensional data. This structural requirement remains part of the learning problem as information moves between source and target tasks.

For decentralized data, the authors introduce D-LoRT, a distributed version designed to retain statistical efficiency with little communication overhead. Theory and experiments on tensor regression, including compressed sensing and completion, support the methods’ robustness and versatility. The findings indicate that structured transfer can help data-scarce tensor problems even when task differences and distributed data management complicate collaboration.
summary.tldr: LoRT transfers knowledge between tensor-regression tasks while preserving low-rank structure, with a distributed variant for decentralized data.

title: Low-Rank Tensor Transitions (LoRT) for Transferable Tensor Regression

abstract: Recently, newly developed Vision-Language Models (VLMs), such as OpenAI’s o1, have emerged, seemingly demonstrating advanced reasoning capabilities across text and image modalities. However, the depth of these advances in language-guided perception and abstract reasoning remains underexplored, and it is unclear whether these models can truly live up to their ambitious promises. To assess the progress and identify shortcomings, we enter the wonderland of Bongard problems, a set of classic visual reasoning puzzles that require human-like abilities of pattern recognition and abstract reasoning. With our extensive evaluation setup, we show that while VLMs occasionally succeed in identifying discriminative concepts and solving some of the problems, they frequently falter. Surprisingly, even elementary concepts that may seem trivial to humans, such as simple spirals, pose significant challenges. Moreover, when explicitly asked to recognize ground truth concepts, they continue to falter, suggesting not only a lack of understanding of these elementary visual concepts but also an inability to generalize to unseen concepts. We compare the results of VLMs to human performance and observe that a significant gap remains between human visual reasoning capabilities and machine cognition.

paragraphs: Strong performance on some image-and-language tasks does not settle how deeply a model understands visual concepts. This paper examines that question using Bongard problems, classic visual puzzles requiring pattern recognition and abstract reasoning. The evaluation focuses on whether vision-language models can identify the concepts that distinguish the puzzle examples.

The tested models sometimes discover the relevant concepts and solve the puzzles, but they frequently fail. Even apparently elementary visual ideas, including simple spirals, cause difficulty. The authors also explicitly ask models to recognize the correct concepts. Continued failures in that setting suggest that the challenge extends beyond independently discovering which concept a puzzle is testing.

Comparisons with human performance reveal a substantial remaining gap in visual reasoning on these problems. The results suggest weaknesses in understanding elementary visual concepts and generalizing to unseen ones. Their significance is diagnostic: the evaluation separates occasional puzzle success from reliable conceptual competence and shows why broad impressions of advanced multimodal reasoning can miss persistent weaknesses on focused visual tests.
summary.tldr: Bongard puzzle evaluations reveal persistent visual concept and reasoning failures in vision-language models, with a substantial gap from humans.

title: Bongard in Wonderland: Visual Puzzles that Still Make AI Go Mad?

abstract: Vision-language instruction-tuning models have recently achieved significant performance improvements. In this work, we discover that large-scale 3D parallel training on those models leads to an imbalanced computation load across different devices. The vision and language parts are inherently heterogeneous: their data distribution and model architecture differ significantly, which affects distributed training efficiency. To address this issue, we rebalance the computational load from data, model, and memory perspectives, achieving more balanced computation across devices. Specifically, for the data, instances are grouped into new balanced mini-batches within and across devices. A search-based method is employed for the model to achieve a more balanced partitioning. For memory optimization, we adaptively adjust the re-computation strategy for each partition to utilize the available memory fully. These three perspectives are not independent but are closely connected, forming an omniverse balanced training framework. Extensive experiments are conducted to validate the effectiveness of our method. Compared with the open-source training code of InternVL-Chat, training time is reduced greatly, achieving about 1.8$\times$ speed-up. Our method’s efficacy and generalizability are further validated across various models and datasets. Codes will be released at https://github.com/ModelTC/OmniBal.

paragraphs: OmniBal addresses uneven computational work during large-scale distributed instruction tuning of vision-language models. The visual and language components differ in architecture and data distribution, so spreading training across devices can leave some with substantially more work than others. The paper identifies this imbalance in training that uses three-dimensional parallelism.

The framework coordinates changes to data, model partitioning, and memory use. It regroups examples into balanced mini-batches both within devices and across them. A search procedure finds more balanced model partitions. It also adjusts recomputation separately for each partition, using the available memory more fully. These choices are treated as connected because the work assigned to a device and its memory requirements affect one another.

Compared with the open-source InternVL-Chat training code, the authors report roughly a 1.8-fold speedup. Additional experiments across models and datasets support the method’s broader applicability. The result emphasizes coordinated workload balancing as a way to shorten training, with improvements coming from how existing computation is organized across the distributed system.
summary.tldr: OmniBal jointly balances data, model partitions, and memory use to accelerate distributed vision-language instruction tuning.

title: OmniBal: Towards Fast Instruction-Tuning for Vision-Language Models via Omniverse Computation Balance

abstract: Multi-agent frameworks can substantially boost the reasoning power of large language models (LLMs), but they typically incur heavy computational costs and lack convergence guarantees. To overcome these challenges, we recast multi-LLM coordination as an incomplete-information game and seek a Bayesian Nash equilibrium (BNE), in which each agent optimally responds to its probabilistic beliefs about the strategies of others. We introduce Efficient Coordination via Nash Equilibrium (ECON), a hierarchical reinforcement-learning paradigm that marries distributed reasoning with centralized final output. Under ECON, each LLM independently selects responses that maximize its expected reward, conditioned on its beliefs about co-agents, without requiring costly inter-agent exchanges. We mathematically prove that ECON attains a markedly tighter regret bound than non-equilibrium multi-agent schemes. Empirically, ECON outperforms existing multi-LLM approaches by 11.2% on average across six benchmarks spanning complex reasoning and planning tasks. Further experiments demonstrate ECON’s ability to flexibly incorporate additional models, confirming its scalability and paving the way toward larger, more powerful multi-LLM ensembles. The code is publicly available at: https://github.com/tmlr-group/ECON.

paragraphs: Coordinating several language models can improve reasoning, but exchanging messages between them can be computationally expensive. The paper treats coordination as a game with incomplete information. Each model holds probabilistic beliefs about the others’ strategies and selects a response accordingly, with Bayesian Nash equilibrium serving as the coordination objective.

The proposed ECON framework uses hierarchical reinforcement learning to combine independent reasoning with a centralized final output. Each model chooses responses to maximize expected reward given its beliefs about its peers. This design removes the need for costly exchanges between agents during that response-selection process, making beliefs about other models central to coordination.

The authors prove a tighter regret bound than for the non-equilibrium multi-agent schemes considered. Across six reasoning and planning benchmarks, ECON reports an average improvement of 11.2% over existing multi-LLM approaches. Further experiments incorporate additional models, supporting the framework’s scalability. The contribution joins a game-theoretic coordination objective with empirical evidence that useful collaboration can occur without extensive direct debate.
summary.tldr: ECON coordinates language models through beliefs about one another’s strategies, improving tested reasoning performance without costly inter-agent exchanges.

title: From Debate to Equilibrium: Belief-Driven Multi-Agent LLM Reasoning via Bayesian Nash Equilibrium

abstract: Decomposing hard problems into subproblems often makes them easier and more efficient to solve. With the high cost of running LLMs at scale, there is an increasing effort to decompose systems into sets of LLM-based agents, each of whom can be delegated sub-tasks. However, this decomposition (even when automated) is often intuitive, e.g., based on how a human might assign roles to members of a human team. How close are these role decompositions to optimal? This position paper argues that asymptotic analysis with LLM primitives is needed to reason about the efficiency of such problem decompositions, and that insights from such analysis will unlock opportunities for scaling such systems. By treating the LLM forward pass as the atomic unit of computational cost, one can separate out the (often opaque) inner workings of a particular LLM from the inherent efficiency of how a set of LLMs are orchestrated to solve hard problems. In other words, if we want to scale the deployment of LLMs to the limit, instead of anthropomorphizing LLMs, asymptotic analysis with LLM primitives should be used to reason about and develop more powerful decompositions of large problems into LLM agents.

paragraphs: Dividing a difficult task among language model agents may make it easier or cheaper to solve, but the division is often based on intuition about human teamwork. This position paper asks how close those designs are to efficient ones. It argues that scaling agent systems requires a more explicit analysis of how their computational costs grow.

The proposed approach treats a language model’s forward pass as the basic unit of cost. Researchers can then study the efficiency of an agent arrangement without needing to explain the model’s internal computation. This separates questions about how a particular model works from questions about how multiple calls are organized to solve a larger problem.

The authors advocate asymptotic analysis using these model-level operations to compare and develop problem decompositions. The expected benefit is insight into opportunities for scaling that human-style role assignments may obscure. This is a methodological position about designing efficient orchestration, with the claim that such analysis can reveal better ways to distribute work across agents.
summary.tldr: The paper argues for analyzing agent systems’ scaling costs using LLM forward passes as basic computational units.

title: Position: Scaling LLM Agents Requires Asymptotic Analysis with LLM Primitives

abstract: The forward pass of a Transformer can be seen as an interacting particle system on the unit sphere: time plays the role of layers, particles that of token embeddings, and the unit sphere idealizes layer normalization. In some weight settings the system can even be seen as a gradient flow for an explicit energy, and one can make sense of the infinite context length mean-field limit thanks to Wasserstein gradient flows. In this paper we study the effect of the perceptron block in this setting, and show that critical points are generically atomic and localized on subsets of the sphere.

In some weight settings the system can even be seen as a gradient flow for an explicit energy, and one can make sense of the infinite context length mean-field limit thanks to Wasserstein gradient flows. paragraphs: This paper analyzes a mathematical view of Transformer computation in which token embeddings behave like interacting particles. Layers play the role of time, and embeddings move on a unit sphere that idealizes layer normalization. This perspective turns the forward pass into a dynamical system whose collective behavior can be studied geometrically.

For some weight settings, that system follows the gradient of an explicit energy function. Wasserstein gradient flows then provide a way to describe a mean-field limit as context length becomes infinite. Within this setting, the authors focus on the effect of the perceptron block on the resulting landscape.

Their main result is that critical points are generically atomic and localized on subsets of the sphere. In this description, the limiting token distribution concentrates into point masses rather than spreading continuously across the sphere. The finding characterizes the structure of critical configurations in the studied model. It connects the perceptron block to where token mass can concentrate within this idealized account of attention dynamics.
summary.tldr: In an idealized mean-field Transformer model, the perceptron block yields critical points that are generically atomic and spatially localized.

title: Perceptrons and Localization of Attention’s Mean-Field Landscape

abstract: Vision Language Models (VLMs) are designed to extend Large Language Models (LLMs) with visual capabilities, yet in this work we observe a surprising phenomenon: VLMs can outperform their underlying LLMs on purely text-only tasks, particularly in long-context information retrieval. To investigate this effect, we build a controlled synthetic retrieval task and find that a transformer trained only on text achieves perfect in-distribution accuracy but fails to generalize out-of-distribution (OOD), while subsequent training on an image-tokenized version of the same task nearly doubles text-only OOD performance. Mechanistic interpretability reveals that visual training changes the model’s internal binding strategy: text-only training encourages positional shortcuts, whereas image-based training disrupts them through spatial translation invariance and other encoder-level inductive biases, forcing the model to adopt a more robust symbolic binding mechanism that persists even after text-only examples are reintroduced. We further characterize how binding strategies vary across training regimes and visual encoders, and show that analogous shifts occur during pre-trained LLM-to-VLM transitions. Our findings suggest that cross-modal training can enhance reasoning and generalization even for tasks grounded in a single modality.

Subsequent training on an image-tokenized version of the same task nearly doubles text-only out-of-distribution performance. The model develops a more robust symbolic binding strategy that persists when text-only examples return.

The authors compare binding behavior across training regimes and visual encoders, and identify analogous changes when pretrained language models become vision-language models. These findings suggest that cross-modal training can improve reasoning and generalization within a single modality. summary.tldr: Visual training can replace positional retrieval shortcuts with more robust symbolic binding, improving text-only generalization in controlled experiments.

title: Seeing to Generalize: How Visual Data Corrects Binding Shortcuts

abstract: Text-to-Image (T2I) models have made significant strides in visual realism and semantic consistency, yet they often perpetuate and amplify societal biases. Existing evaluation methods typically address only single-dimensional biases, lacking perspectives to uncover model biases at social-related deeper semantic levels. We introduce HoloFair, a comprehensive benchmark framework for multidimensional demographic bias analysis. Built upon our large-scale fairness-oriented dataset and the SpaFreq (Spatial-Frequency) attribute classifier, this framework proposes the Multi-attribute, Group-wise Bias Index (MGBI) metric, designed to assess both intrinsic diversity and conditional biases. Beyond evaluation, we further introduce Fair-GRPO, a reinforcement-learning-based debiasing method that alters the distribution of generative models through a designed multi-objective reward function. E.g., experiments on the SD3.5-Medium model demonstrate that Fair-GRPO significantly improves multidimensional fairness while maintaining high image quality. We also analyze potential reward hacking phenomena and provide corresponding mitigation strategies.

The paper argues that assessments focused on a single dimension can overlook deeper patterns in what a model generates.

Its Multi-attribute, Group-wise Bias Index is designed to measure both intrinsic diversity and conditional biases. summary.tldr: HoloFair evaluates multidimensional demographic bias, while Fair-GRPO improves measured fairness through reinforcement learning with a multi-objective reward.

title: HoloFair: Unified T2I Fairness Evaluation and Fair-GRPO Debiasing

abstract: Understanding what graph neural networks can learn, especially their ability to learn to execute algorithms, remains a central theoretical challenge. In this work, we prove exact learnability results for graph algorithms under bounded-degree and finite-precision constraints. Our approach follows a two-step process. First, we train an ensemble of multi-layer perceptrons (MLPs) to execute the local instructions of a single node. Second, during inference, we use the trained MLP ensemble as the update function within a graph neural network (GNN). Leveraging Neural Tangent Kernel (NTK) theory, we show that local instructions can be learned from a small training set, enabling the complete graph algorithm to be executed during inference without error and with high probability. To illustrate the learning power of our setting, we establish a rigorous learnability result for the LOCAL model of distributed computation. We further demonstrate positive learnability results for widely studied algorithms such as message flooding, breadth-first and depth-first search, and Bellman-Ford.

paragraphs: This paper studies when a graph neural network can learn to execute a graph algorithm exactly. Its guarantees apply under bounded-degree and finite-precision constraints. These conditions define the setting of the result, so the claim concerns exact learnability within that setting rather than unrestricted algorithm learning on arbitrary graphs.

The method separates learning local behavior from running the full algorithm. First, an ensemble of multilayer perceptrons learns the instructions carried out by an individual node. At inference, that trained ensemble becomes the update function of a graph neural network. The authors use Neural Tangent Kernel theory to show that the local instructions can be learned from a small training set.

The resulting graph algorithm executes without error with high probability under the stated constraints. The analysis establishes learnability for the LOCAL model of distributed computation and positive results for message flooding, breadth-first search, depth-first search, and Bellman-Ford. Its significance is a rigorous connection between learning local rules and correctly composing them into complete graph computations.
summary.tldr: Under bounded-degree and finite-precision constraints, learned local update rules enable exact graph-algorithm execution with high probability.

title: Learning to Execute Graph Algorithms Exactly with Graph Neural Networks

abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) in real-world tasks often suffers from the performance degradation due to the distribution shift between training and deployment environments. Distributionally Robust RL (DR-RL) addresses this issue by optimizing the worst-case performance over an uncertainty set of transition dynamics, providing an optimized baseline performance upon deployment. However, existing methods typically require strong data access assumptions (e.g., a generative model or comprehensive offline datasets) and mostly focus on tabular settings. In this paper, we introduce a purely online DR-RL algorithm with general function approximation that learns a robust policy directly from interaction, without any prior knowledge or pre-collected data. Our method uses a dual-based fitted robust Bellman update to jointly learn the value function and the robust backup operator. We establish the first regret guarantee for online DR-RL in terms of an intrinsic complexity measure—the robust Bellman–Eluder (BE) dimension, for general $\phi$-divergence uncertainty sets. Our regret bound is sublinear and independent of $|\mathcal{S}|$ and $|\mathcal{A}|$, and recovers sharp rates in structured regimes, providing a scalable method for practical DR-RL.

paragraphs: A reinforcement learning policy can lose performance when deployment dynamics differ from training dynamics. Distributionally robust reinforcement learning addresses this by optimizing worst-case performance within a specified uncertainty set. Existing approaches often depend on strong access to data or focus on tabular problems, limiting their scope.

The paper introduces an online algorithm that learns directly through interaction, without prior knowledge or pre-collected data. It uses a dual-based fitted robust Bellman update to learn both the value function and the robust backup operator. General function approximation allows the method to represent these quantities beyond a table of individual states and actions.

The authors establish a sublinear regret bound for general phi-divergence uncertainty sets. The bound depends on an intrinsic measure called the robust Bellman–Eluder dimension, rather than directly on the number of states or actions, and recovers sharp rates in structured settings. The guarantee ties learning difficulty to the problem's functional complexity while preserving the focus on robustness within the chosen uncertainty set.
summary.tldr: An online robust reinforcement learning algorithm learns through interaction and achieves sublinear regret governed by intrinsic functional complexity.

title: Online Robust Reinforcement Learning with General Function Approximation

abstract: Online evaluation of large language models increasingly relies on sequentially collected pairwise preferences, enabling human-aligned assessment and continuous data collection until closely performing models can be reliably distinguished. However, adaptive sampling and continuous monitoring invalidate classical fixed-sample inference, rendering existing ranking procedures largely heuristic. We propose SERPANT (Sequential E-value Ranking and Pruning via Adaptive Null Testing), a principled framework for online LLM ranking with anytime-valid guarantees. SERPANT formulates model comparison as a collection of pairwise hypothesis tests and constructs e-processes to ensure family-wise error rate control at any monitoring time. Anytime validity provides a theoretical justification for early stopping, enabling substantial cost savings from expensive human annotation. To improve efficiency, we introduce a novel tournament-based sampling strategy that adaptively selects comparisons based on past outcomes. The proposed framework is also extended to top-k model identification.

paragraphs: Online language-model evaluation often collects human preferences between pairs of responses, continuing until closely matched models can be distinguished. This creates a statistical problem: evaluators may repeatedly inspect results and choose future comparisons using previous outcomes. In that setting, ordinary methods designed for a fixed sample size no longer provide their usual guarantees.

SERPANT treats ranking as a collection of pairwise hypothesis tests. It constructs e-processes, statistical evidence processes designed for sequential monitoring, to control the family-wise error rate at any monitoring time. This means the framework accounts for the risk of erroneous conclusions across the collection of tests while allowing evaluators to keep checking the accumulating evidence.

The framework also uses a tournament-based sampling strategy that selects comparisons adaptively from past results, and extends to identifying the top-k models. Its anytime-valid guarantees provide a theoretical basis for stopping early, which can reduce expensive human annotation. The central contribution is to make adaptive comparison and flexible stopping part of a statistically justified ranking procedure.
summary.tldr: SERPANT supports adaptive online LLM ranking with statistical error control that remains valid whenever evaluation is monitored or stopped.

title: Anytime-Valid Inference for Online Ranking of Large Language Models

abstract: Meta Black-Box Optimization (MetaBBO) has emerged as a promising paradigm by employing meta learning to automatically optimize the configurations of low-level black-box optimizers. Despite its potential, the generalization of MetaBBO remains significantly constrained when facing unseen, complex objective landscapes. We identify that this bottleneck stems from a restricted performance upper bound inherent in current training mechanisms: by learning from scratch in a self-supervised or unsupervised manner, low-level learnable optimizers are never exposed to advanced, high-quality optimization behaviors, forcing them to converge on suboptimal strategies. In this paper, we propose MetaDistill, a general MetaBBO training framework designed to lift the strategy ceiling through pretraining and test-time fine-tuning. In the pretraining stage, we represent high-quality strategies from classical algorithms as expert optimization trajectories and utilize them for diversity-preserving distillation, enabling the learnable optimizer to internalize advanced optimization behaviors. In the optional fine-tuning stage, we perform self-supervised fine-tuning as a warm-start procedure to further refine the distilled knowledge on unseen tasks. We evaluate our MetaDistill framework on the BBOB test suite and three control tasks. The results demonstrate that MetaDistill significantly improves the generalization ability of various learnable optimizers compared to their original training paradigms. Our code is available at https://github.com/Roki-Xing/MetaDistill.

paragraphs: Meta black-box optimization learns how to configure an optimizer for objectives whose internal structure is not directly available. The paper identifies a training bottleneck: optimizers learning from scratch may never encounter sufficiently strong optimization behavior, limiting the strategies they acquire and their ability to handle unfamiliar, complex objective landscapes.

MetaDistill introduces a pretraining stage built from expert optimization trajectories produced by classical algorithms. The framework also offers optional self-supervised fine-tuning on unseen tasks, using the distilled optimizer as a warm start. This separates learning a stronger initial strategy repertoire from refining it for a particular new objective.

Evaluation on the BBOB test suite and three control tasks shows significantly improved generalization for several learnable optimizers relative to their original training procedures. The result supports the paper's claim that training exposure can constrain optimizer quality. Its practical contribution is a general training framework that gives learned optimizers access to advanced behavior before they must adapt to unfamiliar tasks.
summary.tldr: MetaDistill improves learned optimizers by distilling expert optimization trajectories and optionally fine-tuning on new tasks.

title: $\textttMetaDistill$: Unlocking the Performance Ceiling for Pretrained Optimizers

abstract: Although computer-use agents (CUAs) hold significant potential to automate increasingly complex OS workflows, they can demonstrate unsafe unintended behaviors that deviate from expected outcomes even under benign input contexts. However, exploration of this risk remains largely anecdotal, lacking concrete characterization and automated methods to proactively surface long-tail unintended behaviors under realistic CUA scenarios. To fill this gap, we introduce the first conceptual and methodological framework for unintended CUA behaviors, by defining their key characteristics, automatically eliciting them, and analyzing how they arise from benign inputs. We propose AutoElicit: an agentic framework that iteratively perturbs benign instructions using CUA execution feedback, and elicits severe harms while keeping perturbations realistic and benign. Using AUTOELICIT, we surface hundreds of harmful unintended behaviors from state-of-the-art CUAs such as Claude 4.5 Haiku, Claude 4.5 Opus, and Operator. We further evaluate the transferability of human-verified successful perturbations, identifying persistent susceptibility to unintended behaviors across various other frontier CUAs. This work establishes a foundation for systematically analyzing unintended behaviors in realistic computer-use settings.

paragraphs: Computer-use agents can behave unsafely even when the instructions they receive are benign. This paper studies unintended harmful outcomes in realistic operating-system workflows, moving beyond isolated anecdotes. It introduces a framework for defining these behaviors, automatically surfacing them, and analyzing how benign inputs can lead to unexpected harm.

The proposed AutoElicit system iteratively changes benign instructions using feedback from the computer-use agent’s execution. The perturbations remain realistic and benign while the search looks for harmful deviations from expected behavior. This makes the agent’s observed actions part of an automated process for uncovering difficult-to-find failures.

Using this approach, the authors surface hundreds of harmful unintended behaviors in agents including Claude 4.5 Haiku, Claude 4.5 Opus, and Operator. They also test whether human-verified successful perturbations transfer to other frontier agents and find persistent susceptibility across them. The results establish a systematic way to study this failure class and show that benign input alone does not ensure safe behavior in the evaluated computer-use scenarios.
summary.tldr: AutoElicit systematically varies benign instructions to uncover harmful unintended computer-agent behavior, finding hundreds of cases and transfer across agents.

title: When Benign Inputs Lead to Severe Harms: Eliciting Unsafe Unintended Behaviors of Computer-Use Agents

abstract: Cooperation is central to multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL), yet learned coordination can be fragile when external perturbations disrupt inter-agent interactions. Prior robust MARL methods have primarily considered value-oriented attacks, leaving a gap in robustness when interaction structures themselves are corrupted. In this paper, we propose an interaction-breaking adversarial learning (IBAL) framework that takes an information-theoretic view to construct attacks that impede coordination by perturbing agents’ observations and actions, and trains agents to perform reliably under such disruptions. Empirically, our approach improves robustness over existing robust MARL baselines across diverse attack settings and yields stronger performance even under agent-missing scenarios. Our code is available at https://sunwoolee0504.github.io/IBAL.

paragraphs: Cooperative agents depend on their interactions to coordinate, so disturbances can damage performance by breaking those relationships. The paper identifies a gap in robust multi-agent reinforcement learning: previous methods have mainly emphasized value-oriented attacks, leaving interaction structure less directly addressed. Its focus is therefore the fragility of learned cooperation when agents’ observations or actions are perturbed.

The proposed interaction-breaking adversarial learning framework, IBAL, uses an information-theoretic perspective to construct attacks that impede coordination. It also delivers stronger performance in scenarios where agents are missing. Together, these findings support treating interaction disruption as a distinct training concern. The reported benefits concern robustness in the evaluated settings, including situations where the available team itself changes.
summary.tldr: IBAL trains cooperative agents against attacks on their interactions, improving robustness across perturbations and agent-missing scenarios.

title: Interaction-Breaking Adversarial Learning Framework for Robust Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Recent advances in cross-modal few-shot adaptation treat visual-semantic alignment as a continuous feature transport problem via Flow Matching (FM). However, we argue that Euclidean-based FM overlooks fundamental limitations of flat geometry, where polynomial volume growth fails to accommodate diverse feature distributions, leading to severe path entanglement. To this end, we propose path-decoupled Hyperbolic Flow Matching (HFM), leveraging the Lorentz manifold’s exponential expansion for trajectory decoupling. HFM structures the transport via two key designs: 1) Centripetal hyperbolic alignment: It constructs a centripetal hierarchy by anchoring textual roots, which pushes visual leaves to the boundary to initialize orderly flows. 2) Path-decoupled objective: It acts as a "semantic guardrail" rigidly confining trajectories within isolated class-specific geodesic corridors via step-wise supervision. Furthermore, we devise an adaptive diameter-based stopping to prevent over-transportation into the crowded origin based on the intrinsic semantic scale. Extensive ablations on 11 benchmarks have shown that HFM establishes a new state-of-the-art, consistently outperforming its Euclidean counterparts. Our codes and models will be released.

paragraphs: Some few-shot adaptation methods align visual and textual features by transporting them continuously through feature space. This paper argues that flat Euclidean geometry can crowd these transport paths together, making diverse feature distributions difficult to accommodate. It proposes Hyperbolic Flow Matching, using the Lorentz manifold’s exponential expansion to separate trajectories.

The method first establishes a hierarchy with anchored textual roots and visual leaves pushed toward the boundary. This arrangement initializes more orderly flows. A second design supervises trajectories step by step, keeping each class within its own geodesic corridor. These constraints serve as semantic boundaries during transport, helping preserve separation between classes as features move toward alignment.

The framework also chooses when to stop transport using an adaptive diameter-based rule tied to intrinsic semantic scale. Its purpose is to avoid moving features too far into the crowded origin. Extensive ablations across 11 benchmarks report state-of-the-art performance and consistent improvements over Euclidean counterparts. The findings support combining a more expansive geometry with explicit path constraints and adaptive stopping for the evaluated few-shot adaptation problems.
summary.tldr: Hyperbolic Flow Matching separates class-specific feature trajectories and adaptively stops transport, improving reported few-shot adaptation performance.

title: Path-Decoupled Hyperbolic Flow Matching for Few-Shot Adaptation

abstract: Unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) autopilot systems typically comprise navigation and flight-control modules, and their effective scheduling is critical to achieving high flight performance. However, most existing UAV platforms adopt a split architecture in which navigation and flight control are deployed on separate hardware devices. This separation restricts system-wide observability and prevents holistic scheduling and optimization across the entire autopilot pipeline. Moreover, autonomous flight performance emerges from implicit, cross-coupled, and accumulated interactions among multiple factors, rendering traditional model-based or heuristic scheduling approaches ineffective. To address these challenges, we propose UAV$^2$, a unified and adaptive scheduling framework for UAV autopilot systems with reinforcement learning, targeting flight performance optimization. UAV$^2$ integrates navigation and flight control onto a single onboard computing platform and operating system, formulates the scheduling problem as a partially observable Markov decision process, and learns scheduling policies from runtime execution feedback. The proposed approach is trained and evaluated in a hardware-in-the-loop simulation environment. Experimental results demonstrate that the learned scheduling policy consistently outperforms fixed-rate scheduling strategies in terms of flight robustness and tracking performance.
