paragraphs: Drone autopilots depend on navigation and flight-control modules working together at appropriate times. When those modules run on separate hardware, the system has limited visibility across the full pipeline and fewer opportunities for joint scheduling. Flight performance also depends on interacting effects that accumulate over time, making scheduling difficult to capture with simple rules.

UAV² places navigation and flight control on one onboard computing platform and operating system. It models scheduling as a partially observable Markov decision process and uses reinforcement learning to choose schedules from runtime feedback. This gives the scheduler a way to learn from execution behavior while accounting for incomplete observation of the system.

Training and evaluation take place in a hardware-in-the-loop simulation environment. In those experiments, the learned policy consistently outperforms fixed-rate scheduling in flight robustness and tracking performance. The result supports coordinating computation across the integrated autopilot pipeline rather than assigning module rates independently. Its demonstrated benefit is tied to the reported simulation setup, where actual hardware participates in the evaluation.
summary.tldr: UAV² integrates autopilot modules and learns adaptive schedules that improve robustness and tracking over fixed-rate scheduling in hardware-in-the-loop simulation.

title: UAV$^2$: A Unified and Adaptive Scheduling Framework for UAV Autopilot Systems with Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Diffusion models have achieved tremendous success in image generation, but they also raise significant concerns regarding privacy and copyright issues. Membership Inference Attacks (MIAs) are designed to ascertain whether specific data was utilized during a model’s training phase. As current MIAs for diffusion models typically exploit the model’s image prediction ability, we formalize them into a unified general paradigm that computes the membership score for membership identification. Under this paradigm, we empirically find that existing attacks overlook the inherent deficiency in how diffusion models process high-frequency information. Consequently, this deficiency leads to member data with more high-frequency content being misclassified as hold-out data, and hold-out data with less high-frequency content tends to be misclassified as member data. Moreover, we theoretically demonstrate that this deficiency reduces the membership advantage of attacks, thereby interfering with the effective discrimination of member data and hold-out data. Based on this insight, we propose a plug-and-play high-frequency filter module to mitigate the adverse effects of the deficiency, which can be seamlessly integrated into any attacks within the general paradigm without additional time costs. Extensive experiments corroborate that this module significantly improves the performance of baseline attacks across different datasets and models. Code is available at https://github.com/poetic2/FreMIA.

Consequently, this deficiency leads to member data with more high-frequency content being misclassified as hold-out data, and hold-out data with less high-frequency content tends to be misclassified as member data. Moreover, we theoretically demonstrate that this deficiency reduces the membership advantage of attacks, thereby interfering with the effective discrimination of member data and hold-out data. Based on this insight, we propose a plug-and-play high-frequency filter module to mitigate the adverse effects of the deficiency, which can be seamlessly integrated into any attacks within the general paradigm without additional time costs. Extensive experiments corroborate that this module significantly improves the performance of baseline attacks across different datasets and models. Code is available at https://github.com/poetic2/FreMIA.

paragraphs: Membership inference attempts to determine whether a particular image was used to train a model. For diffusion models, many attacks use image prediction behavior to derive a membership score. This paper organizes those attacks into a common framework and identifies a frequency-related source of errors in their decisions.

The authors find that diffusion models' difficulty processing high-frequency information can distort membership scores. Training images containing more high-frequency content can be mistaken for unseen images, while unseen images with less of that content can be mistaken for training examples. Their theoretical analysis also shows that this deficiency reduces membership advantage, weakening the distinction the attacks are meant to detect.

The proposed remedy is a high-frequency filtering module that can be added to attacks within the unified framework. It aims to reduce the influence of the identified deficiency and is reported to add no time cost. Experiments across different datasets and models show substantial improvements to baseline attacks. The finding matters because image content can confound a privacy test unless the scoring process accounts for this model behavior.
summary.tldr: A high-frequency filter improves diffusion-model membership inference by reducing a content-related bias in existing attack scores.

title: Enhancing Membership Inference Attacks on Diffusion Models from a Frequency-Domain Perspective

abstract: Real-world physical sensing exhibits complex, heterogeneous noise patterns that deviate significantly from idealized simulation, posing a fundamental bottleneck for sim-to-real transfer. Existing sensor modelings typically treat depth noise as a monolithic black-box process, overlooking the distinct physical mechanisms that govern different error modalities. In this work, we introduce a physics-grounded paradigm that disentangles monolithic noise into two complementary modalities: sensing invalidation and measurement inaccuracy, enabling a tailored treatment of noise sources based on their physical origins. Building on this insight, we propose PRISM, a tripartite framework that distills 3D Visual Foundation Model features as rich spatial-semantic priors for physics-based reasoning. To address the inherent sparsity and class imbalance of invalidation regions, we develop Hierarchical Positive-Prioritized Supervision, integrating multi-scale positive-weighted objectives with a positive-preserving dynamic hard mining strategy to enforce precise artifact delineation. Extensive benchmarks demonstrate that PRISM achieves state-of-the-art fidelity in noisy depth synthesis. Furthermore, downstream robotic experiments show that PRISM facilitates a 92.1% average success rate in the real world, marking a significant improvement over monolithic baselines.

This separation enables treatment tied to their different physical origins.

The three-part framework distills features from a 3D visual foundation model to supply spatial and semantic information for physics-based reasoning. It also addresses the rarity and imbalance of invalidation regions through supervision at multiple scales. Positive-weighted objectives and dynamic hard-example mining that preserves positive examples help the model delineate these artifacts precisely.

The reported benchmarks show state-of-the-art fidelity in synthesized noisy depth. Downstream robotic experiments achieve an average real-world success rate of 92.1%, improving substantially over monolithic noise-modeling baselines. Together, these findings connect a more physically differentiated sensor model with both more realistic synthetic depth and improved performance in the evaluated robot tasks.
summary.tldr: PRISM models missing and inaccurate depth readings separately to improve sensor-noise synthesis and sim-to-real robotic performance.

title: PRISM: Learning Realistic Depth via Physics-Grounded Noise Disentanglement with Semantic-Geometric Collaboration

abstract: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) excel at tasks like zero-shot classification and cross-modal retrieval by mapping images and text to a shared space, but this requires expensive end-to-end training with massive paired datasets. Current post-hoc alignment methods reduce computational costs by connecting pretrained encoders through lightweight mappings, yet still demand substantial paired data. In this work, we investigate the potential of repurposing the classification heads of pretrained vision models as semantic prototypes. The recycling of these weights, typically discarded after pretraining, unlocks two distinct capabilities: it enables zero-shot alignment by using weights as semantic anchors, and serves as a robust data augmentation strategy by mixing these prototypes with real image-text pairs. We demonstrate that integrating our approach with several state-of-the-art post-hoc alignment techniques consistently boosts accuracy in cross-modal retrieval, zero- and few-shot classification tasks.

paragraphs: Vision-language models need image and text representations that occupy a compatible semantic space. Building that alignment can require substantial paired data, even when pretrained encoders are connected through lightweight mappings. This paper explores a source of semantic information already present in supervised vision models: the weights of their classification heads.

The authors repurpose these weights as semantic prototypes instead of discarding them after pretraining. The prototypes serve two roles. They can act as semantic anchors for zero-shot alignment, and they can augment training data by being mixed with real image-text pairs. Both uses draw additional value from the classification knowledge stored in the pretrained model.

The method integrates with several state-of-the-art post-hoc alignment techniques and consistently improves accuracy on cross-modal retrieval and zero- and few-shot classification tasks. These results show that a component commonly removed after supervised pretraining can remain useful when connecting visual and language representations. The contribution is a reusable source of semantic structure that supports alignment directly and strengthens learning from available paired examples.
summary.tldr: Recycling pretrained classification weights as semantic prototypes improves vision-language alignment through zero-shot anchoring and data augmentation.

title: Supervised Classification Heads as Semantic Prototypes: Unlocking Vision-Language Alignment via Weight Recycling

abstract: While Mamba2’s expanded state dimension enhances temporal modeling, it incurs substantial inference overhead that saturates bandwidth during autoregressive generation. Standard pruning methods fail to address this bottleneck: unstructured sparsity leaves activations dense, magnitude-based selection ignores runtime dynamics, and gradient-based methods impose prohibitive costs. We introduce GHOST (Grouped Hidden-state Output-aware Selection and Truncation), a structured pruning framework that approximates control-theoretic balanced truncation using only forward-pass statistics. By jointly measuring controllability and observability, GHOST rivals the fidelity of gradient-based methods without requiring backpropagation. As a highlight, on models ranging from 130M to 2.7B parameters, our approach achieves a 50% state-dimension reduction with approximately 1 perplexity point increase on WikiText-2. Code is available at https://github.com/Menezmic21/mamba2_ghost.

paragraphs: Mamba2 uses an expanded internal state to model temporal information, but that state creates substantial inference overhead during autoregressive generation. The paper identifies bandwidth saturation as a bottleneck. Removing scattered weights leaves activations dense, while weight magnitude alone misses runtime behavior and gradient-based selection is computationally costly.

GHOST performs structured pruning through an approximation to balanced truncation, a control-theoretic approach to reducing a system’s internal state. It jointly considers controllability and observability: how state components are affected and how they contribute to outputs. These measurements come entirely from forward-pass statistics, avoiding the need for backpropagation during selection.

The authors report fidelity comparable to gradient-based methods. Across models ranging from 130 million to 2.7 billion parameters, GHOST reduces the state dimension by 50% with an approximately one-point perplexity increase on WikiText-2. This result demonstrates a substantial state reduction with a measured language-modeling tradeoff. The approach targets the structure responsible for dense state overhead, while using runtime-sensitive information to decide what can be removed.
summary.tldr: GHOST uses forward-pass statistics to halve Mamba2 state dimensions with approximately one additional perplexity point on WikiText-2.

title: GHOST: Unmasking Phantom States in Mamba2 via Grouped Hidden-state Output-aware Selection & Truncation

abstract: Natural language to optimization (NL2Opt) requires translating unstructured text into executable mathematical models. Beyond simple syntax errors, this task suffers from silent modeling failures, where incorrect formulations execute successfully but yield invalid results. We propose Draft-and-Audit RL (DA-RL), a framework that learns optimization modeling as a two-step iterative workflow. Unlike inference-time scaffolds that rely on intermediate solver feedback to guide repairs, DA-RL optimizes a shared-parameter policy using terminal-only verification: the model is rewarded solely based on the execution of the final audited program. This constraint forces the model to internalize rubric-guided revision as a learned capability and encourages the emergence of cross-turn synergy, where the policy learns to generate drafts that are structurally amenable to self-correction.

paragraphs: Translating a written optimization problem into executable mathematics requires more than producing valid code. A program can run successfully while representing the wrong constraints or objective, yielding an invalid result without a syntax error. This paper addresses those silent formulation failures through a learned drafting and auditing workflow.

Draft-and-Audit RL uses a shared-parameter policy for two stages: constructing a draft and revising it through an audit. Training rewards depend solely on execution of the final audited program. Intermediate solver feedback does not guide the repairs, so the policy must learn to perform rubric-guided revision within the workflow itself.

This final-only reward links the quality of drafting to the success of later correction. The paper argues that the setup encourages cross-turn synergy: drafts can become structured in ways that make their errors easier for the same policy to repair. The proposed contribution is thus a training formulation for optimization modeling that treats self-revision and the preparation of revisable drafts as connected capabilities.
summary.tldr: Draft-and-Audit RL trains a shared policy to write and revise optimization programs using rewards from only the final audited execution.

title: Draft-and-Audit Reinforcement Learning for Optimization Modeling

abstract: Linear probes are a promising approach for monitoring AI systems for deceptive behaviour. Previous work has shown that a linear classifier trained on a contrastive instruction pair and a simple dataset can achieve good performance. However, these probes exhibit notable failures even in straightforward scenarios, including spurious correlations and false positives on non-deceptive responses. In this paper, we demonstrate that deception detection is inherently heterogeneous: while a single universal probe achieves modest improvements (+0.032 AUC), post-hoc oracle analysis reveals substantially higher potential (+0.108 AUC) when probes are matched to specific deception types, and synthetic validation experiments suggest this ceiling is achievable a priori when the deception type is known in advance. Our findings reveal that instruction pairs capture deceptive intent rather than content-specific patterns, explaining why prompt choice dominates probe performance (70.6% of variance). Given this heterogeneity, we conclude that organizations should define their specific threat models and deploy appropriately matched probes rather than seeking a universal deception detector.

paragraphs: Linear probes are classifiers used to monitor model representations for signs of deception. Prior approaches can work well with simple datasets and contrasting instructions, but they also produce false positives and rely on spurious correlations. This paper studies why a detector that works for one kind of deceptive behavior may struggle with another.

A single universal probe gives a modest AUC improvement of 0.032. An oracle analysis performed after evaluation finds greater potential, an improvement of 0.108, when probes are matched to particular deception types. Synthetic validation experiments suggest that this higher level can be approached when the deception type is known beforehand. The distinction between retrospective matching and advance knowledge is central to interpreting the result.

The authors find that contrasting instruction pairs capture deceptive intent rather than content-specific patterns, with prompt choice explaining 70.6% of performance variance. Their practical recommendation is to define the deceptive behaviors an organization needs to detect and choose probes accordingly. The findings support targeted monitoring, with performance depending strongly on how the detector's training setup matches the threat.
summary.tldr: Deception probes perform differently across deception types, and matching probes to known threats shows greater potential than a universal detector.

title: One Probe Won’t Catch Them All: Towards Targeted Deception Detection

abstract: Federated bilevel optimization is widely used for nested learning problems across distributed clients, such as federated hyperparameter tuning and meta-learning under privacy and communication constraints. Most existing formulations assume fixed client data distributions, which can be violated by performativity, where deployed decisions reshape client behavior and data collection, inducing client-specific, decision-dependent distribution shift. We study federated bilevel performative prediction, where both upper-level (UL) and lower-level (LL) objectives are evaluated under client-dependent, decision-dependent distributions. We formalize the federated bilevel performatively stable (FBPS) point under a decoupled-risk perspective and provide sufficient conditions for its existence and uniqueness. We then develop two federated methods to compute the FBPS solution: FBi-RRM, which converges linearly under a contraction condition, and FBi-SGD, a communication-efficient stochastic method based on federated hypergradient estimation with convergence guarantees under diminishing step sizes when sensitivities are sufficiently small. Experiments on strategic regression and meta strategic classification validate the predicted stability thresholds and demonstrate improved meta-generalization over non-performative baselines, and CNN-based classification further demonstrates the practical effectiveness of the proposed methods in nonconvex neural network settings.

paragraphs: Distributed learning can involve nested optimization, as in hyperparameter tuning or meta-learning across clients. Standard formulations often assume each client’s data distribution stays fixed. This paper studies what happens when deployed decisions change client behavior and data collection, so both levels of the optimization operate on distributions that depend on the decisions themselves.

The authors define a federated bilevel performatively stable point using a decoupled-risk perspective and establish sufficient conditions for its existence and uniqueness. They propose two methods for computing it. FBi-RRM converges linearly when a contraction condition holds. Classification with convolutional networks also demonstrates practical effectiveness in nonconvex settings. The contribution links decision-induced distribution changes to both algorithm design and stability conditions, while keeping the formal guarantees tied to the assumptions under which they were established.
summary.tldr: The paper develops federated bilevel learning methods for decision-dependent data distributions, with conditional stability guarantees and supporting experiments.

title: Federated Bilevel Performative Prediction

abstract: Graph Contrastive Learning (GCL), which trains graph encoders by maximizing similarity between positive samples and minimizing it between negative ones, has emerged as a mainstream graph pre-training paradigm. It is widely recognized that positive samples are essential in GCLs. Ideally, maximizing the similarity of positive samples enables graph encoders to capture intrinsic semantic and patterns of graph data. However, we discover an interesting phenomenon: GCLs can achieve competitive performance even without positive samples. This motivates us to revisit the fundamental mechanism of positive samples in GCLs. From the perspective of Dirichlet energy, we theoretically finds that message passing, a key mechanism in graph encoders, trivializes the maximization of positive samples, preventing GCLs from effectively learning from positive samples. To address this, we propose SPGCL to mitigate the trivialization caused by message passing and restore the learning efficacy of positive samples. Specifically, we find that high Dirichlet energy features help positive samples provide effective learning signals while low Dirichlet energy features contribute little to positive learning signal but is useful for positive sampling. Based on this, SPGCL propagates only high Dirichlet energy features and uses low energy features to construct a probability matrix for reliable positive sampling. Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of SPGCL.

paragraphs: Graph contrastive learning typically brings positive examples closer together in representation space while separating negatives. This paper starts from a surprising observation: competitive performance can persist even without positive samples. That raises the question of whether the positive-pair objective is supplying the useful learning signal normally attributed to it.

The authors analyze the issue through Dirichlet energy and identify message passing as a source of trivialization. Their account is that message passing makes positive similarity too easy to maximize, weakening what the encoder learns from that objective. They distinguish high-energy features, which support effective positive learning signals, from low-energy features, which contribute little to that signal but remain useful for selecting positive pairs.

SPGCL assigns these features different jobs. It propagates only high-Dirichlet-energy features and uses low-energy features to build a probability matrix for reliable positive sampling. Experiments demonstrate the approach's effectiveness. The contribution is a mechanism-based explanation for weak positive learning and a corresponding redesign that separates learning from positive examples from choosing them.
summary.tldr: SPGCL separates graph features used for positive-pair learning from those used for sampling, addressing trivialization caused by message passing.

title: Revisiting Positive Samples in Graph Contrastive Learning: From the Perspective of Message Passing

abstract: Discrete diffusion language models (dLLMs) provide a fast and flexible alternative to autoregressive models (ARMs) via iterative denoising with parallel updates. However, their evaluation is challenging: existing metrics conflate denoiser approximation error with sampler-induced error from the sampling dynamics, a problem that does not arise for ARMs whose autoregressive sampling exactly reflects the learned probability model. We introduce a sampler-centric oracle framework that replaces learned denoisers with an exact Hidden Markov Model posterior derived from a ground-truth Markov chain, isolating sampler-induced error in a controlled setting. We show that few-step discrete diffusion samplers are not distributionally correct even under an oracle denoiser, with transition-level mismatch that vanishes only as the number of steps approaches the sequence length. Moreover, improvements in negative log-likelihood (NLL), generative perplexity (GenPPL), or MAUVE do not imply correct sampling. Code is available at https://luhantang.github.io/dllm_sampler/.

However, their evaluation is challenging: existing metrics conflate denoiser approximation error with sampler-induced error from the sampling dynamics, a problem that does not arise for ARMs whose autoregressive sampling exactly reflects the learned probability model. We introduce a sampler-centric oracle framework that replaces learned denoisers with an exact Hidden Markov Model posterior derived from a ground-truth Markov chain, isolating sampler-induced error in a controlled setting. paragraphs: Discrete diffusion language models generate text through repeated denoising steps that can update positions in parallel. Evaluating them is difficult because errors can come from either the learned denoiser or the sampling procedure. Ordinary evaluation combines these sources, making it hard to tell whether better denoising would fix an observed sampling problem.

The paper builds a controlled framework that replaces the learned denoiser with an exact posterior from a Hidden Markov Model based on a known Markov chain. Removing denoiser approximation error exposes errors introduced by the sampling dynamics themselves. This lets the authors assess whether the sampler reproduces the intended distribution even with perfect denoising information.

In this setting, few-step samplers remain distributionally incorrect. Transition-level discrepancies disappear only as the number of sampling steps approaches the sequence length. Improvements in negative log-likelihood, generative perplexity, or MAUVE also do not imply correct sampling. The findings distinguish better evaluation scores from faithful reproduction of a model’s intended probability distribution.
summary.tldr: An exact-denoiser evaluation shows that few-step discrete diffusion sampling can distort the intended distribution despite improved standard metrics.

title: Is Your Diffusion Sampler Actually Correct? A Sampler-Centric Evaluation of Discrete Diffusion Language Models

abstract: Process Reward Models (PRMs) are rapidly becoming the backbone of LLM reasoning pipelines, yet we demonstrate that state-of-the-art PRMs are systematically exploitable under optimization pressure. We introduce a three-tiered diagnostic framework that applies increasing adversarial pressure to quantify these vulnerabilities. Static perturbation analysis uncovers a fluency-logic dissociation: high invariance to surface-level style changes (reward changes $<$0.1) yet inconsistent detection of logically corrupted reasoning, with different models failing on different attack types. Adversarial optimization demonstrates that gradient-based attacks inflate rewards on invalid trajectories, with reward landscapes exhibiting wide, exploitable peaks. RL-induced reward hacking exposes the critical failure mode: policies trained on AIME problems achieve near-perfect PRM rewards ($>$0.9) while ground-truth accuracy remains below 4%, with 43% of reward gains attributable to stylistic shortcuts. These findings reveal that current PRMs function as fluency detectors rather than reasoning verifiers, creating systematic blind spots that undermine their use as training signals. We release PRM-BiasBench and a diagnostic toolkit to enable robustness evaluation before deployment.

paragraphs: Process reward models score intermediate reasoning and can guide language-model training. This paper tests whether those scores remain trustworthy when systems actively optimize them. Its diagnostic framework applies three increasing levels of pressure: fixed perturbations, gradient-based adversarial optimization, and reinforcement learning against the reward model.

Static tests find little sensitivity to surface style changes but inconsistent detection of logical corruption, with different models vulnerable to different attacks. Gradient-based attacks then raise rewards for invalid reasoning trajectories, exposing broad regions of exploitable high scores. Under reinforcement learning on AIME problems, policies obtain rewards above 0.9 while actual answer accuracy remains below 4%; stylistic shortcuts account for 43% of the reward gains.

These findings demonstrate a substantial gap between earning a high reasoning reward and producing correct reasoning in the evaluated systems. The authors characterize current reward models as responding to fluency more reliably than verifying logic. They release PRM-BiasBench and a diagnostic toolkit to support robustness evaluation before these models are used as training signals.
summary.tldr: Adversarial tests show that process reward models can assign very high rewards to incorrect reasoning, making them exploitable training signals.

title: Reward Under Attack: Analyzing the Robustness and Hackability of Process Reward Models

abstract: Steering diffusion models toward conditions unseen during training typically requires either retraining with conditional inputs or per-step gradient computations, both of which incur substantial computational overhead. We present NA-RFM, a general recipe for efficiently steering unconditional diffusion models without gradient guidance during inference, enabling fast controllable generation. The method combines two offline-computed signals: noise alignment, a high-noise correction from PCA statistics of the target examples and the full data, and Recursive Feature Machine (RFM) activation steering, which learns a target-discriminative direction from labeled forward-process activations. During sampling, noise alignment provides coarse control at high noise, while the RFM direction is reused over intermediate/late timesteps through lightweight activation edits. Experiments on CIFAR-10, ImageNet, CelebA, and fine-grained bird species show improved target accuracy over gradient-based post-hoc guidance baselines, improved FID on the class-guidance benchmarks, and substantial inference speedups. Code: https://github.com/isotrivial/na-rfm.

During sampling, noise alignment provides coarse control at high noise, while the RFM direction is reused over intermediate/late timesteps through lightweight activation edits. paragraphs: Steering an unconditional diffusion model toward a desired category often requires conditional retraining or repeated gradient calculations during generation. NA-RFM develops control signals offline and reuses them while sampling. Its aim is to direct an existing model toward conditions it was not trained to receive as inputs, with less inference overhead.

The method combines two signals that act at different noise levels. Noise alignment uses principal-component statistics from target examples and the full dataset to make a broad correction early in sampling. A Recursive Feature Machine learns a direction that distinguishes the target from labeled forward-process activations. Lightweight edits along that direction provide control during intermediate and later sampling steps.

Experiments cover CIFAR-10, ImageNet, CelebA, and fine-grained bird species. NA-RFM improves target accuracy over the gradient-based post-hoc guidance baselines evaluated, improves FID on class-guidance benchmarks, and provides substantial inference speedups. These findings support dividing control into an early statistical correction and reusable internal activation edits, avoiding gradient guidance during inference.
summary.tldr: NA-RFM steers unconditional diffusion models using offline noise corrections and reusable activation edits, improving control and inference speed in reported experiments.

title: General and Efficient Steering of Unconditional Diffusion Models

abstract: The core challenge of Test-Time Reinforcement Learning (TTRL) lies in estimating rewards without access to ground-truth supervision. Existing TTRL methods predominantly rely on majority voting to generate pseudo-labels, under the assumption that the most frequent answer among sampled trajectories is correct. However, we observe that this assumption frequently breaks down in complex reasoning tasks, where correct solutions often constitute a logical minority. As a result, rare yet correct trajectories are systematically undervalued by majority-voting-based approaches. To address this limitation, we propose Self-Reflective Test-Time Reinforcement Learning (SR-TTRL), a novel framework that leverages self-reflective verification to produce high-fidelity pseudo-labels. Specifically, given multiple sampled trajectories for a problem, SR-TTRL first groups trajectories according to their final answers and selects one representative from each group to form a candidate pool. Each candidate trajectory is then summarized to preserve its core reasoning steps while reducing verbosity. Finally, the model performs self-reflection over the candidate pool, critically evaluating and selecting the most plausible trajectory as the pseudo-label. Empirically, SR-TTRL achieves substantially higher pseudo-label fidelity and sample efficiency than prior majority-voting-based TTRL methods. Extensive experiments across diverse benchmarks and model families demonstrate that SR-TTRL consistently outperforms majority-voting baselines and significantly improves generalization to novel problems. For example, SR-TTRL improves the Pass@1 accuracy of Qwen3-8B on AIME24 from 29.1 to 55.8 (a gain of +26.7), exceeding standard TTRL by an additional +9.1. The code will be released at: https://github.com/JIA-Lab-research/SR-TTRL.
originalAbstract: The core challenge of Test-Time Reinforcement Learning (TTRL) lies in estimating rewards without access to ground-truth supervision. Existing TTRL methods predominantly rely on majority voting to generate pseudo-labels, under the assumption that the most frequent answer among sampled trajectories is correct. However, we observe that this assumption frequently breaks down in complex reasoning tasks, where correct solutions often constitute a logical minority. As a result, rare yet correct trajectories are systematically undervalued by majority-voting-based approaches. To address this limitation, we propose Self-Reflective Test-Time Reinforcement Learning (SR-TTRL), a novel framework that leverages self-reflective verification to produce high-fidelity pseudo-labels. Specifically, given multiple sampled trajectories for a problem, SR-TTRL first groups trajectories according to their final answers and selects one representative from each group to form a candidate pool. Each candidate trajectory is then summarized to preserve its core reasoning steps while reducing verbosity. Finally, the model performs self-reflection over the candidate pool, critically evaluating and selecting the most plausible trajectory as the pseudo-label. Empirically, SR-TTRL achieves substantially higher pseudo-label fidelity and sample efficiency than prior majority-voting-based TTRL methods. Extensive experiments across diverse benchmarks and model families demonstrate that SR-TTRL consistently outperforms majority-voting baselines and significantly improves generalization to novel problems. For example, SR-TTRL improves the Pass@1 accuracy of Qwen3-8B on AIME24 from 29.1 to 55.8 (a gain of +26.7), exceeding standard TTRL by an additional +9.1. The code will be released at: https://github.com/JIA-Lab-research/SR-TTRL.

paragraphs: Test-time reinforcement learning needs a way to judge answers without access to ground truth. A common approach treats the most frequent sampled answer as correct. This paper identifies a weakness in that strategy: on difficult reasoning problems, correct solutions can be a minority, so voting can reward repeated mistakes and undervalue successful reasoning.

SR-TTRL replaces frequency-based selection with a self-reflective comparison. It groups sampled reasoning trajectories by final answer and chooses one representative from each group. Each representative is summarized to retain its central reasoning while reducing verbosity. The model then compares these candidates and selects the most plausible trajectory to supply a pseudo-label for learning.

Across the reported benchmarks and model families, the approach improves pseudo-label fidelity, sample efficiency, and generalization to new problems relative to majority-voting methods. For Qwen3-8B on AIME24, Pass@1 rises from 29.1 to 55.8, exceeding standard TTRL by another 9.1 points. The findings support examining competing reasoning paths rather than treating answer popularity as the primary evidence of correctness.
summary.tldr: SR-TTRL improves test-time learning by comparing representative reasoning paths instead of assuming the most common answer is correct.

title: Beyond Majority Voting: Self-Reflective Test-Time Reinforcement Learning for LLM Reasoning

abstract: Audio provides critical situational cues, yet current Audio Language Models (ALMs) face an attention bottleneck in long-form recordings where dominant background patterns can dilute rare, salient events. We introduce NAACA, a training-free NeuroAuditory Attentive Cognitive Architecture that reframes attention allocation as an auditory salience filtering problem. At its core is OWM, a neuro-inspired Oscillatory Working Memory that maintains stable attractor-like states and triggers higher-cognition ALM processing only when adaptive energy fluctuations signal perceptual salience, triggering higher-level reasoning. On XD-Violence, NAACA improves AudioQwen’s average precision (AP) from 53.50% to 70.60% while reducing unnecessary ALM invocations. Furthermore, qualitative case studies on the Urban Soundscapes of the World (USoW) dataset show that OWM captures novel events and subcategory shifts while remaining robust to transient pauses and ambient urban noise.

paragraphs: Long recordings can contain rare, meaningful sounds surrounded by dominant background patterns. Audio language models may struggle to allocate attention to those events. NAACA addresses this as a filtering problem: determine when the audio becomes perceptually salient, then invoke the language model for higher-level processing. The architecture operates without additional training.

Its central component is Oscillatory Working Memory, a neuro-inspired mechanism that maintains stable, attractor-like states. Adaptive changes in its energy signal when incoming audio warrants further attention. This gives the system a persistent state for monitoring sound and a trigger for escalating selected moments to the audio language model, linking event sensitivity with selective computation.

On XD-Violence, NAACA increases AudioQwen’s average precision from 53.50% to 70.60% while reducing unnecessary model invocations. Qualitative studies on Urban Soundscapes of the World show detection of novel events and shifts between subcategories, alongside robustness to short pauses and ambient noise. The quantitative result supports the evaluated detection improvement, while the urban examples illustrate how the memory mechanism responds to changing soundscapes.
summary.tldr: NAACA uses oscillatory working memory to trigger audio-model reasoning at salient moments, improving detection while reducing unnecessary invocations.

title: NAACA: Training-Free NeuroAuditory Attentive Cognitive Architecture with Oscillatory Working Memory for Salience-Driven Attention Gating

abstract: We propose Re-FORC, an adaptive reward prediction method that, given a query, enables prediction of the expected future rewards as a function of the number of future thinking tokens. Re-FORC trains a lightweight adapter on reasoning models, demonstrating improved prediction with longer reasoning and larger models. Re-FORC enables: 1) early stopping of unpromising reasoning chains, reducing compute by up to 26% compared to fixed-budget cutoffs, while maintaining accuracy, 2) optimized model and thinking length selection that outperforms the largest model alone— reaching 1.7 percentage points higher peak accuracy while needing up to 12% less compute to match the largest model’s accuracy, 3) adaptive test-time scaling, which increases accuracy by 9.9 percentage points (on average at maximum compute) over confidence-based baselines. Re-FORC allows dynamic reasoning with length control via cost-per-token thresholds while estimating computation time upfront.

Re-FORC allows dynamic reasoning with length control via cost-per-token thresholds while estimating computation time upfront.

paragraphs: Reasoning models face a resource-allocation problem: additional thinking can help, but its value varies across queries and reasoning paths. Re-FORC predicts expected future reward as a function of how many additional thinking tokens a model uses. This provides a forecast of the benefit of continuing, rather than relying only on a fixed token allowance.

The method trains a lightweight adapter on reasoning models. Prediction improves with longer reasoning and larger models in the reported experiments. Its forecasts support stopping unpromising chains, selecting a model and thinking length together, and allocating extra computation adaptively. Cost-per-token thresholds provide length control, while the method also estimates computation time upfront.

Early stopping reduces compute by up to 26% versus fixed-budget cutoffs while maintaining accuracy. Joint selection reaches peak accuracy 1.7 percentage points above the largest model alone and matches its accuracy with up to 12% less compute. Adaptive scaling improves accuracy by 9.9 percentage points on average at maximum compute over confidence-based baselines, supporting reward forecasts as a useful allocation signal.
summary.tldr: Re-FORC predicts the value of additional thinking tokens to adapt reasoning length, model choice, and computation allocation.

title: Re-FORC: Adaptive Reward Prediction for Efficient Chain-of-Thought Reasoning

abstract: Adapting Detection Transformers to Incremental Object Detection (IOD) poses a systemic challenge, as set-based optimization is inherently destabilized by sequential learning. In this work, we identify Gradient Dilution as the root cause of performance degradation, wherein optimization signals required to preserve old knowledge are progressively weakened. This phenomenon manifests as a cascading erosion of preservation gradients in magnitude, direction, and support coverage, driven by three tightly coupled factors: Signal Dispersion, where foreground gradients are overwhelmed by background noise; Assignment Drift, where stochastic query–target matching induces inconsistent gradient trajectories; and Support Attrition, where gradients from retained samples insufficiently cover the old-class feature space, weakening decision boundaries under interference from new classes. To counteract this, we propose FAS, a unified framework that Focuses, Aligns, and Sustains gradient flow throughout incremental learning. Specifically, we introduce prior-injected queries to focus discriminative signals by filtering background interference at the source. We further propose deterministic anchor distillation to align query–target assignments and enforce semantic consistency across stages under unstable matching. Finally, we devise manifold-support replay to sustain distributional support of old classes, counteracting representational erosion induced by continual updates. Extensive experiments show that FAS restores robust optimization dynamics and outperforms state-of-the-art methods, achieving over 5.0 AP improvement in the challenging 40+10$\times$4 incremental setting.

paragraphs: Detection Transformers must learn new object classes while maintaining earlier detection abilities in incremental learning. This paper attributes degradation to gradient dilution: the training signals that preserve old knowledge weaken in strength, consistency, and coverage. It identifies three connected mechanisms that progressively undermine those preservation signals.

Background interference overwhelms foreground signals, changing query–target assignments produces inconsistent update directions, and retained samples provide insufficient coverage of earlier classes. The proposed FAS framework addresses each mechanism. Prior-injected queries focus useful signals, deterministic anchor distillation stabilizes assignments and semantic consistency, and manifold-support replay maintains broader support for old-class representations.

This coordinated design treats preservation as a property of the full optimization process, spanning which signals dominate, where they point, and which portions of old knowledge they cover. Experiments report more robust optimization and performance beyond leading methods, including an improvement of over 5.0 AP in the 40+10×4 incremental setting. The findings support the paper’s account that several coupled disruptions must be addressed to sustain old detection capabilities.
summary.tldr: FAS preserves earlier object-detection knowledge by strengthening, aligning, and sustaining the training signals that sequential learning otherwise erodes.

title: Focus, Align, and Sustain: Counteracting Gradient Dilution in Incremental Object Detection

abstract: The periodicity misalignment remains a challenge problem in generating time-series data across multiple domains. The fundamental processing unit of attention in time-series modeling has long been restricted to either individual points or fragmented segments, limiting their ability to capture and adapt to complex periodic patterns inherent in diverse domains. To address this, we introduce Winformer, first to extend this processing unit from individual points to sliding windows, establishing a unified window-wise attention paradigm. Leveraging the adaptive window-alignment kernels derived from the frequency decomposition, Winformer brings semantically richer window representations, and effectively captures and transfers complex periodic patterns across domains. Extensive experiments on 12 real-world datasets demonstrate Winformer’s effectiveness, achieving an average performance gain of 10.67% over SOTA baselines.
originalAbstract: The periodicity misalignment remains a challenge problem in generating time-series data across multiple domains. The fundamental processing unit of attention in time-series modeling has long been restricted to either individual points or fragmented segments, limiting their ability to capture and adapt to complex periodic patterns inherent in diverse domains. To address this, we introduce Winformer, first to extend this processing unit from individual points to sliding windows, establishing a unified window-wise attention paradigm. Leveraging the adaptive window-alignment kernels derived from the frequency decomposition, Winformer brings semantically richer window representations, and effectively captures and transfers complex periodic patterns across domains. Extensive experiments on 12 real-world datasets demonstrate Winformer’s effectiveness, achieving an average performance gain of 10.67% over SOTA baselines.

paragraphs: Generating realistic time series requires capturing recurring patterns whose alignment can vary across domains. The paper argues that attention built around individual points or fragmented segments has difficulty representing and adapting to these periodic relationships. Winformer changes the unit that attention processes, making sliding windows central to the model.

Its window-wise attention uses adaptive alignment kernels derived from frequency decomposition. These kernels help align windows according to periodic structure, producing representations that carry richer meaning than isolated point comparisons. The design is intended to capture complex recurring patterns and transfer them across domains, directly addressing periodicity misalignment in time-series generation.

Experiments on 12 real-world datasets show an average performance improvement of 10.67% over state-of-the-art baselines. The reported finding supports the value of combining window-level processing with frequency-derived alignment. The contribution is specifically about how attention represents and matches temporal structure: choosing a richer processing unit gives the model a way to account for patterns that extend across multiple observations.
summary.tldr: Winformer uses frequency-aligned window-wise attention to improve the generation of time series with complex periodic patterns.

abstract: We present a novel algorithm for computing a training set consistent subset for the nearest neighbor decision rule. The algorithm, called FCNN rule, has some desirable properties. Indeed, it is order independent and has subquadratic worst case time complexity, while it requires few iterations to converge, and it is likely to select points very close to the decision boundary. We compare the FCNN rule with state of the art competence preservation algorithms on large multidimensional training sets, showing that it outperforms existing methods in terms of learning speed and learning scaling behavior, and in terms of size of the model, while it guarantees a comparable prediction accuracy.
originalAbstract: We present a novel algorithm for computing a training set consistent subset for the nearest neighbor decision rule. The algorithm, called FCNN rule, has some desirable properties. Indeed, it is order independent and has subquadratic worst case time complexity, while it requires few iterations to converge, and it is likely to select points very close to the decision boundary. We compare the FCNN rule with state of the art competence preservation algorithms on large multidimensional training sets, showing that it outperforms existing methods in terms of learning speed and learning scaling behavior, and in terms of size of the model, while it guarantees a comparable prediction accuracy.

paragraphs: The paper introduces FCNN, an algorithm that selects a smaller subset of training examples for nearest-neighbor classification. The selected subset is consistent with the training set, preserving the required training classifications under the nearest-neighbor decision rule. This addresses the practical question of how much training data a nearest-neighbor model needs to retain.

FCNN has several stated computational properties. Its result does not depend on the order of the training examples, and its worst-case running time grows subquadratically with training-set size. It also converges in few iterations. The algorithm is likely to select points near the decision boundary, concentrating the retained examples around locations where classification decisions change.

Experiments compare FCNN with leading competence-preservation methods on large, multidimensional training sets. FCNN performs better in learning speed, scaling behavior, and model size, while maintaining comparable prediction accuracy. These results support the method as a way to reduce the stored model and accelerate its construction without sacrificing comparable predictive performance in the reported comparisons.
summary.tldr: FCNN efficiently selects a compact, training-consistent nearest-neighbor subset and achieves comparable prediction accuracy in the reported comparisons.

title: Fast condensed nearest neighbor rule

abstract: This paper introduces a new approach to actionvalue function approximation by learning basis functions from a spectral decomposition of the state-action manifold. This paper extends previous work on using Laplacian bases for value function approximation by using the actions of the agent as part of the representation when creating basis functions. The approach results in a nonlinear learned representation particularly suited to approximating action-value functions, without incurring the wasteful duplication of state bases in previous work. We discuss two techniques to create state-action graphs: offpolicy and on-policy. We show that these graphs have a greater expressive power and have better performance over state-based Laplacian basis functions in domains modeled as Semi-Markov Decision Processes (SMDPs). We present a simple graph partitioning method to scale the approach to large discrete MDPs.
originalAbstract: This paper introduces a new approach to actionvalue function approximation by learning basis functions from a spectral decomposition of the state-action manifold. This paper extends previous work on using Laplacian bases for value function approximation by using the actions of the agent as part of the representation when creating basis functions. The approach results in a nonlinear learned representation particularly suited to approximating action-value functions, without incurring the wasteful duplication of state bases in previous work. We discuss two techniques to create state-action graphs: offpolicy and on-policy. We show that these graphs have a greater expressive power and have better performance over state-based Laplacian basis functions in domains modeled as Semi-Markov Decision Processes (SMDPs). We present a simple graph partitioning method to scale the approach to large discrete MDPs.

paragraphs: This paper learns representations for action-value functions, which assign values to choices made in particular states. Earlier work used Laplacian basis functions constructed from states. The proposed approach includes the agent's actions when constructing the representation, making the basis functions directly reflect the state-action setting of the approximation problem.

The authors obtain the basis functions through a spectral decomposition of a state-action manifold. This yields a learned nonlinear representation and avoids duplicating state bases across actions as in previous work. They discuss both off-policy and on-policy methods for building the state-action graphs on which the representation depends.

The paper reports greater expressive power and better performance than state-based Laplacian basis functions in domains modeled as semi-Markov decision processes. It also presents a simple graph partitioning method for scaling to large discrete Markov decision processes. Together, these contributions address what information the representation contains and how the graph-based construction can be made workable for larger problems.
summary.tldr: Spectral bases learned from state-action graphs improve action-value representations and outperform state-only Laplacian bases in the studied semi-Markov domains.

title: Learning state-action basis functions for hierarchical MDPs

abstract: We present a family of incremental Perceptron-like algorithms (PLAs) with margin in which both the “effective” learning rate, defined as the ratio of the learning rate to the length of the weight vector, and the misclassification condition are entirely controlled by rules involving (powers of) the number of mistakes. We examine the convergence of such algorithms in a finite number of steps and show that under some rather mild conditions there exists a limit of the parameters involved in which convergence leads to classification with maximum margin. An experimental comparison of algorithms belonging to this family with other large margin PLAs and decomposition SVMs is also presented.
originalAbstract: We present a family of incremental Perceptron-like algorithms (PLAs) with margin in which both the “effective” learning rate, defined as the ratio of the learning rate to the length of the weight vector, and the misclassification condition are entirely controlled by rules involving (powers of) the number of mistakes. We examine the convergence of such algorithms in a finite number of steps and show that under some rather mild conditions there exists a limit of the parameters involved in which convergence leads to classification with maximum margin. An experimental comparison of algorithms belonging to this family with other large margin PLAs and decomposition SVMs is also presented.

paragraphs: This paper studies incremental classification algorithms that resemble the Perceptron but explicitly pursue a large margin. A margin describes how confidently a separating boundary places examples on their assigned sides. The authors introduce a family of algorithms whose behavior is governed by the number of mistakes made during learning, using rules that involve powers of that count.

Two parts of learning follow these rules: the effective learning rate and the condition that determines misclassification. The effective learning rate is the ordinary learning rate divided by the length of the weight vector. Controlling this ratio connects the size of an update to the current scale of the classifier, while controlling the misclassification condition shapes when an update is triggered.

The authors examine when these algorithms converge after finitely many steps. Under conditions described as relatively mild, they identify a parameter limit in which convergence yields a maximum-margin classifier. This is a conditional limiting result, not a claim that every parameter choice reaches the maximum margin. The paper also presents experimental comparisons with other large-margin Perceptron-like algorithms and decomposition SVM solvers.
summary.tldr: Mistake-count rules control incremental classifiers that approach maximum-margin classification in a parameter limit under stated conditions.

title: Approximate maximum margin algorithms with rules controlled by the number of mistakes

abstract: This paper extends many of the recent popular reinforcement learning (RL) algorithms to a generalized framework that includes least-squares temporal difference (LSTD) learning, least-squares policy evaluation (LSPE) and a variant of incremental LSTD (iLSTD). The basis of this extension is a preconditioning technique that tries to solve a stochastic model equation. This paper also studies three signicant issues of the new framework: it presents a new rule of step-size that can be computed online, provides an iterative way to apply preconditioning, and reduces the complexity of related algorithms to near that of temporal difference (TD) learning.
originalAbstract: This paper extends many of the recent popular reinforcement learning (RL) algorithms to a generalized framework that includes least-squares temporal difference (LSTD) learning, least-squares policy evaluation (LSPE) and a variant of incremental LSTD (iLSTD). The basis of this extension is a preconditioning technique that tries to solve a stochastic model equation. This paper also studies three signicant issues of the new framework: it presents a new rule of step-size that can be computed online, provides an iterative way to apply preconditioning, and reduces the complexity of related algorithms to near that of temporal difference (TD) learning.

paragraphs: This paper organizes several reinforcement learning algorithms into a generalized framework. It includes least-squares temporal difference learning, least-squares policy evaluation, and a variant of incremental least-squares temporal difference learning. Bringing these methods together provides a common way to describe algorithms that otherwise appear as separate procedures.

The framework is based on preconditioning while attempting to solve a stochastic model equation. Preconditioning changes how the equation is handled during computation, making it the central mechanism through which the paper relates and extends the included algorithms. The work also develops an iterative way to apply this mechanism, so the framework includes a concrete computational procedure.

Two further contributions address practical use. The authors introduce a step-size rule that can be computed online, allowing it to be determined during learning. They also reduce the complexity of related algorithms to near that of temporal difference learning. These results matter together: the framework connects existing methods while addressing the cost of applying preconditioning and selecting update sizes.
summary.tldr: A preconditioning framework unifies several temporal-difference methods and reduces related computational costs toward those of TD learning.

title: Preconditioned temporal difference learning

abstract: Given multiple possible models for a protein structure, a common sub-task in in-silico Protein Structure Prediction is ranking these models according to their quality. Extant approaches use MLE estimates of parameters to obtain point estimates of the Model Quality. We describe a Bayesian alternative to assessing the quality of these models that builds an MRF over the parameters of each model and performs approximate inference to integrate over them. Hyper-parameters are learnt by optimizing a list-wise loss function over training data. Our results indicate that our Bayesian approach can significantly outperform MLE estimates and that optimizing the hyper-parameters can further improve results.
originalAbstract: Given multiple possible models for a protein structure, a common sub-task in in-silico Protein Structure Prediction is ranking these models according to their quality. Extant approaches use MLE estimates of parameters to obtain point estimates of the Model Quality. We describe a Bayesian alternative to assessing the quality of these models that builds an MRF over the parameters of each model and performs approximate inference to integrate over them. Hyper-parameters are learnt by optimizing a list-wise loss function over training data. Our results indicate that our Bayesian approach can significantly outperform MLE estimates and that optimizing the hyper-parameters can further improve results.

paragraphs: Protein structure prediction can produce several candidate structures, leaving a separate question: which candidates are most trustworthy? This paper addresses that ranking problem. Existing approaches described in the abstract estimate model parameters by maximum likelihood and then use those fitted values to produce a single assessment of quality.

The proposed alternative represents the parameters of each candidate with a Markov random field, a probabilistic model of their relationships. It then uses approximate Bayesian inference to integrate over those parameters. This makes the quality assessment depend on a range of parameter possibilities rather than only one fitted setting. The method also learns hyperparameters from training data by optimizing a loss that evaluates rankings as whole lists.

The reported results indicate that this Bayesian treatment can substantially outperform maximum-likelihood estimates, with further improvement from hyperparameter optimization. The contribution therefore combines uncertainty-aware quality assessment with training directed at the actual task of ordering candidate protein structures.
summary.tldr: A Bayesian method ranks candidate protein structures by integrating over model parameters and learning hyperparameters with a ranking-focused loss.

title: A Bayesian approach to protein model quality assessment

abstract: A popular approach to collaborative filtering is matrix factorization. In this paper we consider the "probabilistic matrix factorization" and by taking a latent variable model perspective we show its equivalence to Bayesian PCA. This inspires us to consider probabilistic PCA and its non-linear extension, the Gaussian process latent variable model (GP-LVM) as an approach for probabilistic non-linear matrix factorization. We apply approach to benchmark movie recommender data sets. The results show better than previous state-of-the-art performance.
originalAbstract: A popular approach to collaborative filtering is matrix factorization. In this paper we consider the "probabilistic matrix factorization" and by taking a latent variable model perspective we show its equivalence to Bayesian PCA. This inspires us to consider probabilistic PCA and its non-linear extension, the Gaussian process latent variable model (GP-LVM) as an approach for probabilistic non-linear matrix factorization. We apply approach to benchmark movie recommender data sets. The results show better than previous state-of-the-art performance.

paragraphs: Matrix factorization is a common approach to collaborative filtering, including predicting movie preferences from rating data. This paper examines probabilistic matrix factorization through a latent-variable perspective. The authors show that it is equivalent to Bayesian principal component analysis, connecting a recommendation method to a broader probabilistic approach for representing data through hidden variables.

That equivalence motivates the next step. The authors consider probabilistic principal component analysis and its nonlinear extension, the Gaussian process latent variable model, as tools for probabilistic matrix factorization. The nonlinear model extends the kind of relationship that the latent representation can express. The paper thus builds its proposed recommendation approach from a conceptual connection between existing model families.

The approach is evaluated on benchmark movie-recommendation datasets, where the authors report performance better than the previous state of the art. This is an empirical result for those benchmarks. Its significance is that the latent-variable reinterpretation leads to a useful nonlinear alternative, linking a theoretical modeling relationship to improved recommendation results in the reported evaluations.
summary.tldr: A connection between probabilistic matrix factorization and Bayesian PCA motivates a Gaussian-process nonlinear model with improved movie-recommendation benchmark results.

title: Non-linear matrix factorization with Gaussian processes

abstract: One of the most successful semi-supervised learning approaches is co-training for multi-view data. In co-training, one trains two classifiers, one for each view, and uses the most confident predictions of the unlabeled data for the two classifiers to ``teach each other''. In this paper, we extend co-training to learning scenarios without an explicit multi-view representation. Inspired by a theoretical analysis of Balcan et. al (2004), we introduce a novel algorithm that splits the feature space during learning, explicitly to encourage co-training to be successful. We demonstrate the efficacy of our proposed method in a weakly-supervised setting on the challenging Caltech-256 object recognition task, where we improve significantly over previous results by (Bergamo & Torresani, 2010) in almost all training-set size settings.
originalAbstract: One of the most successful semi-supervised learning approaches is co-training for multi-view data. In co-training, one trains two classifiers, one for each view, and uses the most confident predictions of the unlabeled data for the two classifiers to ``teach each other''. In this paper, we extend co-training to learning scenarios without an explicit multi-view representation. Inspired by a theoretical analysis of Balcan et. al (2004), we introduce a novel algorithm that splits the feature space during learning, explicitly to encourage co-training to be successful. We demonstrate the efficacy of our proposed method in a weakly-supervised setting on the challenging Caltech-256 object recognition task, where we improve significantly over previous results by (Bergamo & Torresani, 2010) in almost all training-set size settings.

paragraphs: Co-training uses two classifiers trained on different views of the same data. Each classifier supplies confident predictions on unlabeled examples to help teach the other. This paper addresses a practical obstacle to that arrangement: many learning problems provide a single feature representation without an explicit division into two useful views.

The authors introduce an algorithm that splits the feature space during learning. The split is chosen specifically to encourage successful co-training, drawing inspiration from an existing theoretical analysis. Constructing the views becomes part of the learning procedure, allowing the two-classifier teaching process to be applied when a suitable multi-view representation is not already supplied.

The method is evaluated in a weakly supervised object-recognition setting on Caltech-256. The abstract reports significant improvements over the cited previous results in almost all training-set size settings. These findings support the effectiveness of the learned feature decomposition for that task and show how co-training can be extended beyond problems with an explicit multi-view input representation.
summary.tldr: The method learns a feature split that enables co-training from a single view and improves weakly supervised object recognition in the reported evaluation.

title: Automatic Feature Decomposition for Single View Co-training

abstract: The exponential increase in the availability of online reviews and recommendations makes sentiment classification an interesting topic in academic and industrial research. Reviews can span so many different domains that it is difficult to gather annotated training data for all of them. Hence, this paper studies the problem of domain adaptation for sentiment classifiers, hereby a system is trained on labeled reviews from one source domain but is meant to be deployed on another. We propose a deep learning approach which learns to extract a meaningful representation for each review in an unsupervised fashion. Sentiment classifiers trained with this high-level feature representation clearly outperform state-of-the-art methods on a benchmark composed of reviews of 4 types of Amazon products. Furthermore, this method scales well and allowed us to successfully perform domain adaptation on a larger industrial-strength dataset of 22 domains.

Hence, this paper studies the problem of domain adaptation for sentiment classifiers, hereby a system is trained on labeled reviews from one source domain but is meant to be deployed on another. We propose a deep learning approach which learns to extract a meaningful representation for each review in an unsupervised fashion. Sentiment classifiers trained with this high-level feature representation clearly outperform state-of-the-art methods on a benchmark composed of reviews of 4 types of Amazon products. Furthermore, this method scales well and allowed us to successfully perform domain adaptation on a larger industrial-strength dataset of 22 domains.

paragraphs: A sentiment classifier trained on reviews from one domain may need to operate in another domain where labeled reviews are difficult to obtain. This paper addresses that transfer problem. Its motivation is the breadth of review domains: gathering separate annotated training collections for all of them is difficult.

The proposed approach uses deep learning to extract a meaningful representation of each review without supervision. Sentiment classifiers then use those higher-level features. This separates learning a representation of review text from learning the sentiment prediction itself, with the aim of making training on a labeled source domain useful when the classifier is deployed elsewhere.

On a benchmark covering four Amazon product types, classifiers using the learned representation clearly outperform the state-of-the-art methods considered. The authors also report successful adaptation on a larger dataset spanning 22 domains. Together, these findings provide evidence for both classification effectiveness in the benchmark and scalability across a broader collection of domains. They support representation learning as a practical component of sentiment-domain adaptation.
summary.tldr: Unsupervised deep representations improve sentiment-domain adaptation on a four-domain benchmark and scale to a 22-domain dataset.

title: Domain Adaptation for Large-Scale Sentiment Classification: A Deep Learning Approach

abstract: Ensembles of classification and regression trees remain popular machine learning methods because they define flexible non-parametric models that predict well and are computationally efficient both during training and testing. During induction of decision trees one aims to find predicates that are maximally informative about the prediction target. To select good predicates most approaches estimate an information-theoretic scoring function, the information gain, both for classification and regression problems. We point out that the common estimation procedures are biased and show that by replacing them with improved estimators of the discrete and the differential entropy we can obtain better decision trees. In effect our modifications yield improved predictive performance and are simple to implement in any decision tree code.

During induction of decision trees one aims to find predicates that are maximally informative about the prediction target. To select good predicates most approaches estimate an information-theoretic scoring function, the information gain, both for classification and regression problems. paragraphs: A decision tree is built by choosing questions that divide the data into informative groups. Many tree-learning methods score candidate questions using information gain, which estimates how much a split reveals about the prediction target. The quality of that estimate therefore affects which branches the learning procedure creates.

The paper identifies bias in commonly used information-gain estimation procedures. It replaces their underlying entropy estimates with improved estimators, addressing discrete entropy for classification and differential entropy for regression. The intervention changes how candidate splits are evaluated while retaining the familiar idea of selecting informative questions.

The authors report that these modifications produce better trees and improve predictive performance. They also describe the changes as straightforward to implement in decision-tree code. This matters because a widely used component of tree training can influence the final model even when the surrounding learning procedure is unchanged. The contribution focuses on improving that statistical estimate rather than introducing an entirely new family of predictive models.
summary.tldr: Improved entropy estimators reduce bias in split scoring and yield decision trees with better predictive performance.

title: Improved Information Gain Estimates for Decision Tree Induction
